items.title: Bolsonaro's party accepts Brazil election defeat, but he refuses to concede
paragraphs: Opposition presidential candidate Sen. Flavio Bolsonaro speaks after the presidential election runoff in Brasilia, Brazil, Oct. 25. Eraldo Peres/AP hide caption

BRASILIA, Brazil — Brazil's Liberal Party, the party of defeated presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro, has acknowledged the results of Sunday's presidential election, recognizing incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva's victory. But Bolsonaro himself has yet to formally concede defeat.
The party's president, Valdemar Costa Neto, said in a statement Monday that the party recognizes the election results but believes "questions raised about the vote" still need to be clarified.

The concession came as President Trump questioned the election's legitimacy, telling reporters Monday, "I didn't take sides, but it looked like another rigged election." Trump offered no evidence of fraud.
Bolsonaro initially said he would seek to annul the election results, citing alleged irregularities, including a last-minute extension of voting hours.

On Sunday, the Supreme Court ordered polling stations to remain open for two additional hours, until 7 p.m., following an appeal by Lula's campaign, which cited public transportation disruptions. Bolsonaro's campaign also requested an extension, citing heavy rain in southern Brazil.

In a video posted Monday, Bolsonaro shifted his approach, saying he would seek to have Lula's election victory disqualified over alleged abuses of political and economic power. "The law must apply to everyone," he said. "The competition must be fair and equal, which did not happen." Bolsonaro did not provide any evidence for this claim.
Bolsonaro also said Brazil's Federal Police had ordered him to surrender his passports after he visited his father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, in Brasília.
The former far-right president is under house arrest after being sentenced to 27 years in prison for his role in the 2022 coup attempt against Lula.

"I was ordered right on the street to hand over my passports, and I'm also prohibited from leaving the country," he said in the video. Bolsonaro said the order was based on remarks by his brother Eduardo, who lives in the U.S., suggesting he should leave Brazil if he lost the election. The passport order was issued by Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes in connection with a separate investigation.
Lula won just over 51% of the valid votes, or approximately 64.2 million, compared with more than 48%, or nearly 59.8 million, for Bolsonaro.
The result marked a major comeback for Lula, who trailed his challenger in the first round, and put the breaks on a run of right-wing electoral victories in Latin America.

Supporters of Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva celebrate in São Paulo on Oct. 25, after Lula won reelection with over 51% of the vote, defeating Flávio Bolsonaro. Alexandre Schneider/Getty Images hide caption

Lula's victory celebrations rang out across Brazil on Sunday night. Near downtown Rio de Janeiro, supporters hugged, shouted and sang the national anthem. Gains in major cities, including Rio de Janeiro and São Paulo, helped Lula overcome his first-round defeat, along with support from younger, older and working-class voters.
In his victory speech in São Paulo, Lula singled out young people who had helped mobilize support for his campaign.

"I wanted to thank the Brazilian people for the generosity they have shown me for a long time," he said. "And in this second round, I want to thank the Brazilian youth for their generosity in taking to the streets. They took to the streets to defend democracy in the country."

17-year-old Brisa Pereira cast her first vote at a busy polling place in one of Brasília's sprawling suburbs. She said Lula's journey from poor factory worker to president had inspired her. She also wanted to send a message to Trump and what she described as his push to dominate Latin America.
"It's not the '90s anymore. We have rights, and Donald Trump can't speak for all of America," Pereira said.

Lula had to win over voters across different demographic and geographic groups to defeat Bolsonaro. He gained more than 10 million additional votes compared with the first round, helped by increased turnout and support from voters who had backed other candidates or had previously stayed away from the polls.
"No wonder pollsters said a Lula victory was almost impossible," said Thiago Vidal, a political analyst with Prospectiva consultants.
"This was a nationwide victory, a systemic victory — from top to bottom, and from left to right," Vidal said.

The decisive margin gives Lula a mandate to govern, Vidal said, but the next four years will be challenging. Bolsonaro's Liberal Party made significant gains in Congress, leaving Lula facing a conservative opposition and a deeply divided electorate.

Vidal said Lula also learned important lessons about communicating with voters, particularly through social media. The president, who had relied more heavily on traditional media, embraced a more digital campaign in the final weeks.

Brazilian lawmaker André Janones embraces President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva as he delivers a victory speech after winning a fourth term in the presidential runoff on Oct. 25. Andre Penner/AP hide caption
"Part of that has to do with communication, and part of that therefore has to do with Lula, setting aside the traditional media and becoming more digital," Vidal said.

Much of that shift was credited to André Janones, a congressman from the bellwether state of Minas Gerais who helped direct Lula's online campaign. Janones used Instagram and WhatsApp to reach younger voters and mobilize supporters. His WhatsApp channel, dubbed "Lula's Army," attracted over 10 million followers.
In an election-night Instagram post, Janones captured the spirit of the celebrations with a message summing up the campaign: "Nothing is more powerful than when the people unite."

items.title: Discursive Verses: Jay-Z, the Super Bowl and playing with house money
paragraphs: SANTA CLARA, CALIFORNIA - FEBRUARY 08: Jay-Z looks on prior to the start of Super Bowl LX between the Seattle Seahawks and the New England Patriots at Levi's Stadium on February 08, 2026 in Santa Clara, California. Kevin C. Cox/Getty Images hide caption

It's no small irony that Jay-Z, the best personification of hip-hop's hopes and dreams, built his success by emulating America's worst excesses. Avarice. Greed. Domination. In turn, we idolized him for showing us "how to move in a room full of vultures." The streets he hustled in were made savage by design. The industry he conquered was out to vanquish him first. Indoctrinated by the same vampiric systems, we learned to praise those willing to sacrifice humanity — whether theirs or others' — in order to scale from the bottom up. The oppressor-oppressed dialectic can be funny that way. If you're not careful, you start to become the monster you're running from.

According to an announcement from the NFL, Jay-Z will headline the 2027 Super Bowl halftime show in February. He's reached a new pinnacle. Not the first rapper to play the halftime show, but the first act with the power to plug himself into that highly coveted slot. The gig even came with a $25 million paycheck, if you count the 2019 deal his entertainment agency Roc Nation scored to book the NFL's annual Super Bowl lineup. The game is to be sold, as the saying goes. And this time, a true player got to set the rules of engagement. After seven years of curating the talent — and pushing rap to the forefront in unprecedented fashion — he's poised to stick the proverbial feather in his Yankees fitted. Yet, hip-hop's response has been ambivalent. Some of us don't know whether we want to slow clap or slapbox with the god.

Whether it's viewed as a crowning achievement or the culmination of a deal that made Jigga the perfect "Black face" to whitewash the NFL's sullied image — per Colin Kaepernick's recent recounting (comments Jay-Z has not responded to) — ultimately depends on which version of the story hip-hop's most valuable hustler can convincingly sell. Like water to a whale.

Fresh off a PR crisis himself, Jay-Z's been engaged in his own rebranding campaign this year. It follows the recently recanted rape allegations made in a civil lawsuit that named Jay-Z and Sean "Diddy" Combs as co-defendants. (Jay-Z vehemently denied the allegations from the start and pursued a defamation and extortion lawsuit against the filing attorney, Tony Buzbee, which was also recently dismissed by an appellate court. Combs also denied the allegations against him and was sentenced to more than four years in prison on prostitution-related charges.) Surviving such a public smear campaign lent new meaning to the 30th anniversary of Reasonable Doubt. "We played enough defense, 2026 is all offense," as he told GQ's senior associate editor Frazier Tharpe in March. So he brought back the umlauts over his chosen name. He sheared off the Basquiat locs grown for both his daughter, Blue Ivy, and his deceased uncle. And he sold out Yankee Stadium three nights in a row.

That was the underlying message of his anti-protest freestyle on night one. With smug confidence, he responded to the backlash for making his vinyl reissue available exclusively at Target in the middle of a grassroots Black boycott to combat the retailer's DEI policy reversal.
"They say I sold out. Yeah, I did sell out. Three nights. I sold Yankee Stadium the hell out," he rapped a capella as a prelude to "Politics As Usual."

There's this erroneous idea that Jay-Z's image rehab is oddly out of character. It's bolstered by the belief that he's always been oblivious to what the general public thinks. He can afford to be. But the truth is he's always been keenly aware and blatantly responsive to critique — whether cultural or personal in nature. When he likened himself to "Che Guevara with bling on / I'm complex" on "Public Service Announcement (Interlude)," it was in direct response to former Village Voice and Vibe journalist Elizabeth Méndez Berry, who provoked him to consider the contradictions he laid bare by donning a diamond-encrusted Jesus piece atop a t-shirt featuring the Cuban revolutionary's face. "The piece was smacking Che Guevara upside the head," Méndez Berry recently told The Ringer's Joel Anderson. "Communism and capitalism colliding with every step."

When Harry Belafonte called out Jay and Beyoncé by name in 2012 and 2013 to criticize Black celebrities for "turn[ing] their back on social responsibility," Jay clapped back. "My presence is charity," he said in an interview with hip-hop journalist Elliott Wilson. His response also showed up in criminal justice reforms he pushed to address disproportionate rates of incarceration in the Black community. Even Decoded, his 2010 book written with dream hampton, was a first-person explainer meant to contextualize his lyrics with the liner notes of his lived experience.

His latest explanatory foray, the eight-episode HBO documentary Jay-Z in 8, pairs him with former Def Jam founder and producer/guru Rick Rubin. Appropriately set in the austere environs of France's former stock exchange, they sit across from one another for deep listening sessions of Jay's discography meant to trigger revelations. He covers the Che Guevara moment again. He talks about what it meant to confront his dad — who abandoned the family when Jay was 11 — just one month before his death. They talk generational trauma and family secrets. He even fills in some unredacted details from his hustling era. Mostly, he tics and bobs his head to the beat like rap's Rainman, shuffling through stored volumes of lyrics famously composed and committed to memory without ever having touched a pen.

No one does this dance between dualities better. Encoding performances for those who lived it. Translating rhymes for those consuming from a privileged distance. This Duboisian double consciousness is what makes him such an articulate marketer of the American Dream, a propaganda artist for Black excellence and capitalist exploits.

For Jay, crossing over didn't come through rapping. It came through his extracurricular moves. The brand sponsorships. The lucrative partnerships. Essentially, he became a cultural broker. The gatekeeper handing the key for entry over to the highest bidder. He played a key role in unlocking the Nets-NBA deal for developer Bruce Ratner that made Barclays Center the catalyst for gentrifying Brooklyn. Jay gained a minority ownership stake (.067 percent); longtime Brooklynites got displaced. He gave cover for Roger Goodell and the NFL to sidestep Colin Kaepernick's protests on behalf of Black America. The league's billionaire owners got a pass; racial injustice got performative slogans and empty charitable initiatives.

"Over and over, Jay is the one that powerful whites use to quiet Negro protests so they can make more money together," former hip-hop journalist Touré recently said, likening Jay-Z to a house Negro who repeatedly aligns himself with the white power structure while claiming to represent Black folks' come-up. The same conclusion is drawn by prominent video essayist F.D Signifier, who categorizes Jay-Z as part of the "Black misleadership class."

But the biggest condemnation actually comes from Jigga himself. In the final episode of Jay-Z in 8 — the documentary he co-executive produced — Jay also calls out so-called race hustlers and house Negroes who act as "extortionists" that "go to one place and say: You want our support? Give us the money." It's as if he doesn't realize how much his own actions resemble the behavior he's side-eyeing. "We['re] not getting it as a race together," he says. "We're slowly getting there separately, but it's not a concerted effort of us to align our powers and our finances to benefit our community."

We could blame Jay, but as he once rapped on "P.S.A.," he didn't invent the game. He "just rolled the dice, trying to get some change." When he hits that Super Bowl halftime stage at SoFi Stadium next year, he'll be playing with a pocketful of house money.

items.title: A 'Green Army' is out to thwart El Niño flooding
paragraphs: Even without the interference of El Niño, Nairobi, Kenya is prone to flooding. Above: Motorists drive through heavy rains in the Kibera community on March 14. Flooding that month took over 100 lives in the capital city. Donwilson Odhiambo/Getty Images hide caption
Nairobi is a city of rivers, streams and almost six million people.

For weeks, Kenya's bustling capital has braced for potentially catastrophic floods, as forecasters predict the strongest El Niño event on record this winter. Globally, this year's Super El Niño will likely peak in November or December and continue into early 2027. But Nairobi isn't just watching and waiting.

On a sunny October day near the city center, a team of workers in reflective vests shovels dirt and clears debris from the bank of a river. It's unseasonably hot — and hot days usually suggest there's an unusually strong rainy season ahead.

"The best thing to do is to be prepared," says Alex Oyando, a 30-year-old worker. "These drainage troughs are full of different things. When we remove the dirt, the water can flow — and it prevents flooding."

Nairobi frequently experiences catastrophic flash floods. More than 100 people died during rain-induced flash floods last March, and residents have pressured Kenya's government to do more to prevent these disasters in the future.

As part of the preparations, Nairobi's county government has mobilized the "Green Army," a youth-employment program of more than 4,000 people. While generally assigned to trash pickups and city greening projects, the workers have been out in full force to prepare for El Niño, clearing drainages and dismantling illegal structures like food stalls. These buildings are generally constructed by the community without government permits and are at an increased risk of collapsing during natural disasters.

Earlier this month, Oyando and his colleagues widened a drainage ditch that runs along a busy road lined with stalls selling clothing. Piles of fabric, plastic bottles and other litter often build up in the stream, triggering flash floods.
While the pay isn't as much as he could make elsewhere, Oyando admits, the shifts are manageable and not too grueling.
"It's something that gives me an opportunity to make a living," he says.

Many of Oyando's colleagues live or grew up in Nairobi's low-income neighborhoods, which are the hardest hit by flash floods. Aging drainage infrastructure and clogged waterways can cause stormwater to build up. When it rains, he says, it's not unusual for his street to fill with water and flood his home.

"The infrastructure we've had in place for decades was tailored for a population of not more than 2 million people," says Bramwell Simiyu, the chief officer of disaster management for Nairobi's county government. "We're now talking about a daytime population of close to 7 million."

Kenya's federal government has put in place a $385 million plan to widen Nairobi's waterways, build affordable housing and improve the city's trash pickup and sewer system by the end of 2027. In addition, the program supports a national youth employment program called Climate WorX, which is working with the Green Army on El Niño preparations.
Now, Simiyu says, the county is preparing supplies and evacuation centers for the rainy season.
"We're also preparing for a worst-case scenario, where up to about 20,000 households may be affected — mostly in the low -income settlements," Simiyu said.

In these settlements, the demolition of illegally built structures, such as food hawker stalls, has caused an outcry. Tobias Sifuna, a supervisor for Green Army teams in the Kamukunji area of Nairobi, says it's a necessary step.
"These are small kiosks that are built illegally, by the community — without the authorization from the county government," Sifuna said.
But nearby communities rely on them, for income and for daily shopping.
Wycliffe Ochieng, a 32-year-old fruit vendor, says many workers in central Nairobi now have nowhere to buy an affordable hot lunch during the day.
"Now, we have to sleep without food because we can't afford it," Ochieng says.

When the county government destroys the shops, it's the community that feels the loss — whether or not the floods eventually come. But it's these neighborhoods that were hit the hardest by the floods during the last rainy season. Ochieng himself had to sleep outdoors, because he could not reach his home in the floodwaters.
"This place, it's like an ocean when it's raining," Ochieng says. "When the flood came, all the food stalls were swept away."

His friend, a woman who owned a food stall, died as she tried to escape. He lost his own stand, a small grocery, as well. He struggled to rebuild his business in a new neighborhood, where customers no longer knew him by reputation.
"After the flood I really suffered. It was hard to put food on the table," Ochieng says.
He says he hopes the county can do more to prevent flooding and safeguard livelihoods. There are only so many times he can rebuild his life from scratch.
"We are all scared. I fear if El Niño comes, I won't come back again."
For stories about life in our changing world, subscribe to NPR's Global Health newsletter.

items.title: ‘Meaningless as a laptop screensaver’: reviewers slate Musk’s AI-made Odyssey film
paragraphs: Elon Musk has released an AI-generated rival to Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey after pledging to make a version “true to the art of Homer”.
Having criticised the hit movie in the summer, the tycoon said he would use Grok Imagine to make a “historically accurate” adaptation.
The initial results have been released on X in the form of a seven-minute episode made in conjunction with Wonder Studios, a London-based startup.
Musk had objected to Nolan’s casting choices – such as black actor Lupita Nyong’o as Helen of Troy – and used the blockbuster as a vehicle for reciting his views on diversity, equity and inclusion.
The Tesla tycoon had promised to make a “full-length movie” version of Homer’s poem before the year ends but is sticking to a film released in episodes.

The first episode starts with Odysseus agonising over whether to join the Greek forces in their attempt to sack Troy. He then sails from Ithaca, his home island, with his men crying out for “vengeance” before they make land and start fighting.
The episode ends after 10 years of conflict, with Odysseus holding, ominously, a wooden figurine of a horse.

Xavier Collins, the co-founder of Wonder Studios, said the first episode was made in less than two weeks with a creative team of three, including the US-based director Dev Walker. It is understood to have cost tens of thousands of dollars. Nolan’s version cost $250m (£188m) and was shot in multiple locations over 91 days with a vast crew. It has made $1.8bn at the box office.
Despite Musk’s criticisms of Nolan’s film, the creative team behind the latest take on Homer are supporters of the summer blockbuster.

Collins said he was a “huge fan” and told the Guardian: “We were not given any direction to make it [Musk’s version] anti-woke or anything like that. We were given the opportunity by one of the world’s best frontier labs to work on one of the best stories ever told.
“The brief was ‘help us understand the technology, where it’s strong, where it could use improvement’.”

Peter Bradshaw’s review in the Guardian gave it one star, saying: “Every single dramatic moment – Odysseus’s cod-insanity and his agreeing to fight, taking leave of his family, the hardship and adventure of the sea journey and the climactic decision – is all as motiveless and meaningless as the movement of shapes on a laptop screensaver.”

The episode on the Grok Imagine X account has received 7.3m views and some harsh feedback, with a reviewer in the Telegraph saying: “You can feel your eyeballs twitch as it unfolds in all its sloppy gruesomeness.”
Collins said Wonder aimed to make the next episode an improvement on the first and would address criticism, including the historical accuracy of its boats and rapid pacing.

“We are going to take a look at all of the comments and all of the things we could have done better and see if we can improve it. The goal is that the next episode we make is radically better than the last,” he said.
Wonder has also worked with Google DeepMind to produce an AI-generated video for the Lewis Capaldi track Something in the Heavens.

items.title: Will a new strategy help protect Northern Ireland's nature?
paragraphs: Agriculture and environment correspondent, BBC News NI
A new strategy to restore and enhance protection for nature in Northern Ireland has been launched by the agriculture and environment minister.
About 40% of the plants and animals in protected sites across Northern Ireland fall short of meeting the standard for "favourable condition".
And just one of 49 priority habitat types - like ancient and native woodlands, blanket bogs and species-rich grasslands - have favourable status.
The Nature Recovery Strategy sets out a long-term framework based on science for tackling biodiversity loss and restoring habitats.
The Nature Recovery Strategy sets out a long-term framework based on science for tackling biodiversity loss and restoring habitats
Minister Andrew Muir said supporting nature was "not just a nice thing to do", but "a moral obligation to future generations".
But the minister acknowledged that money would be needed to address the challenges.
And just one of 49 priority habitat types - like ancient and native woodlands, blanket bogs and species-rich grasslands - have favourable status
The strategy highlights the importance of nature as providing the food we eat, the water we drink and the air we breathe.
Muir said nature must be put "back at the heart of everything we do, because when nature thrives, people flourish.
"It is essential to a strong economy, healthier communities and a more resilient Northern Ireland.
"With so much of our natural world lost, we must protect what remains, restore what has been damaged and create new habitats at scale."
Many places in Northern Ireland support rare or threatened plants, animals and habitats.
They can be legally designated to help ensure better management and protection of those species.

There are hundreds of such designated sites across Northern Ireland, covering around 10% of the land and 38% of coastal waters - classed as Areas of Special Scientific Interest; Special Areas of Conservation (SACs) which have international biodiversity importance; Ramsar Sites which cover wetlands of international importance; Special Protection Areas (SPAs); and Marine Conservation Zones (MCZs).
That should lead to work to protect the species and habitats they have been designated for.
But the Office for Environmental Protection found not enough sites are being designated and the condition of those that have been is worsening.
The number of sites that were in favourable condition dropped from 61.7% in 2008, to 51.5% in 2024.
It is now investigating how those sites are being managed, external by the Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs, after it found implementation of the designation fell short.
Northern Ireland is one of the most nature-depleted areas in the world, according to the 2023 State of Nature Report.
It found 12% of species here are under threat of extinction, and the number of flowering plants had declined by 14% since 1970.

The Nature Recovery Strategy identifies six external pressures affecting nature and biodiversity - invasive species; climate change; human impact through inappropriate development; land and sea-use change; increased intensive farming; pollution.
It says these must all be addressed effectively to allow nature to thrive.

items.title: Rare call with Putin on Ukraine was ‘substantive’ but ‘significant differences’ remain, say Finnish and Norwegian leaders – Europe live
paragraphs: Norway’s Jonas Gahr Støre has offered a bit more colour on his and Stubb’s call with Russia’s Putin in a huddle with journalists in Helsinki just now.

He and Stubb had been initially given only 20 minutes to talk to Putin, but ended up speaking for 90 minutes, in a conversation he described as “substantive, focused on the issues at hand, and professional.”

“Much of what he said was already known – he [Putin] recalled his views on how the conflict evolved since 2014 – and we stated our positions. These are well-known views, which we were able to acknowledge and respond to,” he said.
The talks touched on what can be done to tackle most pressing issues, including attacks on energy infrastructure and in the Black Sea.
But Støre conceded “there remain significant differences in our respective positions,” reiterating Norway’s continued support for Ukraine.
“We stand with Ukraine, defend its right to self-defence, and emphasise the need for a diplomatic path to end this war in a lasting and just manner,” he said.
Støre also stressed that he and Finland’s Stubb spoke on behalf of their two countries only, “and no one else.”
Responding to criticism of their call from Denmark’s Frederiksen (11:26), he said that “all our partners and allies were informed in advance and received a detailed account afterwards.”

“If one assumes that the current situation – where communication from the American administration to Moscow serves as the sole channel for discussing Ukraine outside of Ukraine – is the only way, then one is entitled to that view. I believe it is important that other voices are heard as well.”
Støre also stressed that the importance of the meeting in Abu Dhabi, first agreed as a result of the Oslo consultations that he and Stubb hosted.
In a brief section of the briefing in English, Støre again focused on pushing back against Frederiksen’s criticism:

“I believe that talking, having the right messages, is not wrong. Today these messages [are] coming out of the American administration; that is the only thing reaching Moscow. So [now] there are [also] voices from two neighbouring states, speaking on behalf of Finland and Norway, not speaking on behalf of others, but … in full compliance with the coalition of the willing who share view on the nature of this war and how with has to end.”

Sweden’s prime minister, Ulf Kristersson, has insisted that any peace “must be achieved on Ukraine’s terms,” joining a growing chorus of sceptical voices after an earlier call between Finland and Norway’s leaders and Russia’s Vladimir Putin.
Talking to reporters, Kristersson said that any peace settlement “must be brought about through strength, and not through appeasement towards Russia.”

“If talks lead to that, then talks are good. But my experience so far – based on the reports we received from German and French attempts at dialogue [with Moscow] – is that the results have been very, very modest.”
Kristersson added that given Russia’s continued aggression against Ukraine, “I see nothing to suggest that they are seeking peace.”
“But we will surely receive an update on those discussions later today, and I am interested in that,” he said.

German chancellor Friedrich Merz said on Tuesday that attempts by ⁠the US and Russia to end the war in Ukraine “can never find solutions without Ukraine” ⁠and said any ⁠talks ​must also include European countries.
Merz was speaking at the Yusof Ishak Institute in Singapore as ⁠he described diplomatic efforts to build a negotiating format with Moscow.
He said the end of ⁠the war depended “only on one person” and framed continued backing ​for Kyiv as a ‌defence of Europe’s political ‌order.

He said “as long as he [Putin] does not want ‌to end the war, we will support Ukraine” and that Europe was not just defending Ukraine’s territorial integrity but also “the entire political order of the European continent”.

Merz added that Russia, Ukraine, the United States and European countries ‌should be at the negotiating table and warned against a scenario where “Russia, perhaps China and the ​United States of America” end the war without Ukraine.
Poland’s prime minister Donald Tusk has also responded to Stubb and Støre’s engagement with Putin, giving a detailed account on the European consultations ahead of and after the call.

Speaking before the cabinet meeting in Warsaw, Tusk said the call followed “consultations with me, among others, but primarily with president Zelenskyy and the US side … that it would be good for European politicians to have a working contact given the planned ceasefire talks that may take place in Abu Dhabi.”
He said the UAE talks between Russia, Ukraine, and the US are provisionally planned for 4 November.

Tusk confirmed he had been briefed on plans for the call beforehand, with Norway’s Støre assuring him that he and Stubb were ready to take political responsibility for this rare engagement with Putin, and would stick to the agreed position of the coalition of the willing.

He said Finland’s Stubb then briefed him after the call, saying “both sides maintained their positions,” and that “the European side’s impression during the call was one of very restrained optimism” about the chances of making progress in Abu Dhabi.

Tusk said he was “very cautions” about engaging with Russia and urged Stubb and Store to be “vigilant” in their talks with Putin, as “Russia’s agenda and interests are quite precisely defined, and that one should harbour any illusions about getting an agreement.”
He said Stubb and Støre also told Putin that the security of Nato’s northern and eastern flanks were “non-negotiable”.

Poland’s PM also stressed that despite the resumed dialogue, “nothing changes” in Europe’s “full support for Ukraine,” or collective views on “the [broader] security architecture and security guarantees for Ukraine.”

“We should not have any illussions; it is clear what the Russian side is playing at, but I will remain in constant contact with all those who possess the good will and the belief that an agreement is possible – or at the very least, a ceasefire before winter.”

Without specifying the source of his claim, Tusk said that “three, four nights ago,” “Russia lost 2,500 men” during one night. “This gives us an idea of ​​just how dire the further consequences of this war could be.”

So [now] there are [also] voices from two neighbouring states, speaking on behalf of Finland and Norway, not speaking on behalf of others, but … in full compliance with the coalition of the willing who share view on the nature of this war and how with has to end.”

Russia is exploring the possibility ⁠of ⁠cooperation with ​partners from the ⁠United States in the resource-rich ⁠Arctic, president ​Vladimir ‌Putin ‌told a conference ‌of gas-exporting countries in Moscow.
Putin did not specify ‌whether the joint projects under consideration ​would involve extracting natural gas ⁠or other resources.

Three tankers carrying Russian diesel are en route to the United States, with a fourth expected to depart Wednesday, Moscow said, part of a deal that triggered a fierce Ukrainian and European backlash.
US president Donald Trump this month struck an agreement with Russia’s president Vladimir Putin to ease sanctions in exchange for Moscow releasing diesel onto global markets.
The measure was seen as an attempt to lower fuel prices for American consumers ahead of the US midterm legislative elections on 3 November and drew sharp criticism from Ukraine and its allies.

“At present, three tankers” with Russian fuel are on their way to the United States, Russian deputy prime minister Alexander Novak told reporters on Tuesday. A fourth was expected to set off on Wednesday, he added.

The first US-bound tanker with Russian diesel departed last week. According to data from the maritime tracking firm Kpler, it loaded nearly 300,000 barrels of diesel at the Primorsk terminal and was headed to New York.

In other news, the Netherlands has dropped (again) from the 2027 Eurovision song contest as public broadcaster NPO reversed its plans to pick up the baton after another broadcaster pulled out in August.

The withdrawal is linked with “sensitivities” over Israel’s participation in the competition, NPO’s media director Jurre Bosman said, acknowledging the issue continues to “elicit various reactions in society and causes discussion and division.”
“Therefore, after consultation with the Board of Broadcasters, the NPO has decided to forgo participation in 2027,” he added.

This is the second time a Dutch broadcaster has dropped out of the competition: in August, the Avrotros, which usually selects the Dutch entry and broadcasts the show, had pulled out, paving the way for NPO to step in.

Ireland and Spain have also declared they will not take part in the 2027 competiton because of Israel’s involvement, and the Czech Republic pulled out over financial constraints. Iceland and Slovenia also didn’t take part.
The 2027 Eurovision song contest will take place in Bulgaria’s Black Sea city of Burgas, after singer Darina Yotova, performing as Dara, won this year’s contest in Austria with “Bangaranga”.

Meanwhile, Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, has warned that Russia’s Vladimir Putin is “testing us and testing Nato’s resolve” as he condemned hybrid threats and “state-sponsored terrorism” from Russia.
Streeting repeated his recent warnings that “we have to be ready for a scenario in which the United Kingdom and the Nato alliance finds itself at war with Russia”. He went on:

Not because we want war – we have no quarrel with the Russian people, and we have no desire for war with Russia; Nato is a defensive alliance – but when Putin gives assurances that he has no intentions to provoke a war with Nato, we are reminded of what he said about Ukraine only days before the invasion.
Speaking in Warsaw alongside Poland’s defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, Streeting stressed Nato is ready “to defend every inch of Nato territory” and will continue its support for Ukraine.
The more ready we are to face against Russia, to defend every inch of Nato territory, the less likely we are to find ourselves in that scenario.
Poland is one of our greatest and certainly our most reliable friend in Europe, and we value and treasure this friendship very much.
The partnership is “not simply about our shared history,” but also “our shared determination that in that contest between freedom and tyranny, the United Kingdom and Poland will not be bystanders.”
He said that UK forces will next month take part in major exercises as part of the multinational force for Ukraine.

Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskyy stressed that “real de-escalatory steps are needed regarding our energy and infrastructure” ahead of critical winter months, as he responded to the reported call with Putin.
In his debrief with Finland’s Stubb and Norway’s Støre, the leaders also discussed preparations for the Abu Dhabi talks next month.
“Finland and Norway, as countries that border Russia, have a particular interest in sound and reliable security arrangements.
We also discussed various formats for our engagement with partners in Europe that could be useful in further supporting diplomacy, our defence, and our shared security.
There must be peace, de-escalation is needed, and Russia must stop dragging out the war.”

The Kremlin’s readout from Putin’s call with Stubb and Støre offers some more revealing lines from the Russian side, which perhaps show why Frederiksen (and no doubt other leaders) remain deeply sceptical of the idea that these discussions can change anything.

Putin “recalled the root causes” of the Russian invasion of Ukraine, the Kremlin said, and stressed that any peace settlement could only be reached with “full and unconditional considerations of the legitimate interests of the Russian Federation,” and as we know these tend to be phrased in a very expansive way.
He also blamed the EU and Nato for “confrontational policies,” which in his view “are leading to a prolongation of hostilities.”
The three leaders agreed to keep talking, so expect these issues to come up again.
But not everyone seems to be particularly convinced by the joint Finnish-Norwegian initiative.

Denmark’s Mette Frederiksen told the country’s broadcaster DR that she was “very sceptical” about this “independent initiative by Norway and Finland,” stressing “it has not been coordinated with the rest of us.”

“I see no signs that Russia desires peace with Europe – neither in the hybrid warfare taking place every single day, nor in Ukraine, where they are launching fierce and aggressive attacks on a daily basis.
I believe we should keep Europe united, rather than going it alone.”
She told DR that she didn’t know “what they think can be achieved by this.”

“We have previously emphasised – in very clear terms, on behalf of the rest of Europe – whenever others have gone it alone and traveled to Moscow, that it is crucial for us Europeans to stand together. That is something many of us have fought for all these years,” she said.
Russian news agency Tass has a bit more on the Stubb/Store/Putin call from the Russian side.
The agency it’s the first time the leaders spoke by phone since the full-scale invasion in March 2022.
The leaders agreed to continue contacts and discussed the upcoming meetings in Abu Dhabi.
Finland’s Stubb has just confirmed his call with Zelenskyy.
“Norwegian PM @jonasgahrstore and I had a good phone call with @ZelenskyyUa.
We discussed our prior call with President Putin. Finland and Norway will continue to support Ukraine, and the efforts to find a just and lasting peace.”
Stubb and Støre are now reportedly briefing Ukraine’s Zelenskyy on their talks, according to AFP.

There were some rumours making rounds this morning that the Finnish president Alexander Stubb and Norway’s Jonas Gahr Støre, who hosted the US-Ukrainian talks in Oslo last week, may have been active again.
And we now have a formal confirmation: the pair spoke on the phone with Russia’s Vladimir Putin to discuss the latest on Ukraine.
Their call was “a follow-up” to the Oslo meeting, Stubb’s office said in a statement, as the Nordic pair wants to advance their diplomatic efforts to end the Russian war of aggression in Ukraine.

“Finland and Norway border Russia. They are firm supporters of Ukraine. The aim of the call was to convey messages directly regarding future negotiations to help to end the war to President Putin. The call was related to the upcoming meetings to be held in Abu Dhabi,” the statement read.
The trilateral talks between Russia, Ukraine, and the US in Abu Dhabi are expected in early November.

“Norway and Finland have always promoted peace and security in our region. The two countries have a shared interest in stability and predictability in the Baltic Sea region and the High North. This was highlighted in the call.”
Curiously, the statement noted that “Stubb and Støre took the call as leaders of their respective countries and did not speak on the behalf of Europe as a whole.”
Reacting after the call, Stubb called the discussions “frank and substantive,” saying that “ending the war requires direct discussions” with Russia.
“The war comes with enormous human and material costs. The suffering and destruction will impact generations. In the call we stressed the importance of de-escalation”, Norway’s Støre added.
The head of Ukraine’s president Zelenskyy’s office, Kyrylo Budanov, has confirmed that the ceasefire in Oleshky is in operation.
“Ukrainian Parliament Commissioner for Human Rights Dmytro Lubinets has headed to the site and will be responsible for coordinating the process. We are in constant contact with him.

It is critically important that this mission to rescue our people be carried out successfully and safely. I am sincerely grateful to everyone involved in carrying out and supporting this operation. Every Ukrainian life is priceless.”

Russia and Ukraine have started a localised ceasefire to allow for ⁠a humanitarian operation to begin in the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky, but Russian strikes continued in other parts of the country, including Kyiv.

Overnight, Russia launched 16 ballistic missiles and more than 280 drones, with at least 15 people injured in Kyiv, with further attacks in the Chernihiv, Chernivtsi, Dnipro, Donetsk, Kharkiv, Kherson, Odesa, Sumy, Vinnytsia, Zaporizhzhia regions.

“A serious escalation in Russia’s operation against our logistics. Almost everywhere, Russia’s targets were the energy sector, logistics, and ordinary urban infrastructure,” Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said.

He added that “the artificial and prolonged delays in the delivery of interceptor packages for Patriot and Nasams systems … are directly helping Russia achieve the objectives of its terrorist campaign.”
“Every such delay means another Russian strike on one facility or another. Unfortunately, strikes are taking place every day. Russia is constantly taking new steps toward escalation.”
I will also be looking at the latest updates from Serbia after Sunday’s parliamentary elections, France after last night’s proposals seeking to end student protests, and elsewhere.
It’s Tuesday, 27 October 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.

items.title: No more horses in the streets of New York – level 1
paragraphs: New York City wants to stop horse carriages in Central Park by 2028. Many people say that working in the city is bad and dangerous for horses.

A bad accident with a horse happens some time ago. A tourist dies. Now, city leaders want to ban the rides. Drivers and workers are sad and angry. They will lose their jobs. They say that carriages are an old tradition. It belongs to New York since the 1800s. City leaders want to help the workers and keep the horses safe.
Many visitors say that it is time to keep the animals safe. There are other ways to see the park than using horses.
Difficult words: horse carriage (a vehicle with wheels which a horse or more horses pull), ban (an official stop), tradition (something what people do for a long time).

items.title: No more horses in the streets of New York – level 2
paragraphs: New York City is planning to ban horse-drawn carriages in Central Park by June 2028. Animal rights groups criticized the carriages for years and said the horses work in unsafe conditions alongside cars.

Support for the ban grew stronger after a tourist died in an accident involving a carriage. While the city mayor supports the new law, drivers and union workers are fighting against it. They say the carriages are a famous tradition from the 1800s and that the ban will destroy many jobs. The city plans to help workers transition and promises that the horses will not be killed.
While some tourists will miss the classic rides, many people believe it is time to stop using horses for entertainment.

Difficult words: union (an official organization of workers formed to protect their rights and interests), transition (the process or period of changing from one state or job to another), entertainment (activities provided for people to enjoy).
You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

items.title: No more horses in the streets of New York – level 3
paragraphs: New York City lawmakers will vote on a bill to ban Central Park’s historic horse-drawn carriages by June 2028.

Activists have long argued that operating horses on busy city streets is inhumane and unsafe. Support for the ban surged following a fatal accident in which a young tourist died when a horse bolted. City officials, including the mayor, support the phase-out and propose transition plans to compensate owners and protect horses from being slaughtered. However, the proposal faces strong opposition from drivers and the Transport Workers Union, who argue that the tradition has existed since the 1800s and provides a livelihood for hundreds of workers.
While some visitors regret losing an iconic city tradition, others welcome the change and point to modern alternatives that don’t involve animal labor.

Difficult words: inhumane (causing unnecessary suffering to people or animals; without kindness), bolt (to suddenly run away out of control, usually because of fear or shock), phase-out (ending or stopping something gradually over a period of time).

items.title: MP calls for rethink of pre-poll voting amid heightened security concerns in wake of Haines incident
paragraphs: A Liberal-National MP has called for a rethink of pre-poll voting at federal elections, including potentially shortening the amount of time booths are open, amid concerns of threats to voters and volunteers.

Security risks to politicians and their staff have been front and centre this week, as parliament returned after the alleged attack on Helen Haines, which left the independent MP in a serious but stable condition after both her legs were amputated.
The member for the Queensland electorate of Groom, Garth Hamilton, said the risk of having members of the public and volunteers lined up at booths near car parks or roads needed to be assessed.
“I’ve had three elections and I’ve witnessed three interactions between cars and people at pre-poll, two accidental, one wasn’t,” Hamilton said on Tuesday.
“The threat is already there, the potential is already there in a heightened environment.”

Pre-polling booths usually open one to two weeks before an election. The Toowoomba-based politician said the length of the pre-polling period, the allocation of resources at centres and the role of postal voting were all measures that could be considered to lower the risk to voters and staff.

“What we obviously want is not in any way to restrict anybody’s access to democracy, but we also want to make sure that it’s done in a safe way,” Hamilton said. “There’s a reasonable conversation to be had on the shape of pre-poll in Australia, if these threats are increasing, and that’s what we’re hearing from the AFP.”

Australians are increasingly choosing to vote early ahead of polling day. More than 9m votes, or 56%, were cast at early voting centres, according to the Australian Electoral Commission’s 2025 election report.
It is understood Jerome Laxale, a Labor MP who chairs the parliamentary inquiry into the 2025 election, raised safety and his committee’s interim report on the issue at a caucus meeting on Tuesday.

The report recommends the electoral commission reviews the resourcing requirements and duration of pre-poll voting to ensure adequate arrangements are in place, noting the rising number of people opting to cast their ballot early.

The AEC advised the committee that shortening the pre-poll period would not decrease early voting, but would instead “compress the growing demand into a shorter period and increase operational risks, such as queues and shortages of appropriate venues”.
Laxale, who has represented the NSW seat of Bennelong since 2022, said it was incumbent on the parliament to provide a safe and welcoming atmosphere at a polling booth.
“Democracy doesn’t collapse, it just crumbles,” he said.

“If people go, ‘you know what? I don’t want to deal with that. I’m not going to vote,’ then that has a snowball effect, which will undermine and erode our democratic process. Voting has to be safe and secure.”
Submissions to the inquiry detailed neo-Nazis turning up to booths with speakers, volunteers being bullied and harassed and voters leaving polling centres in tears.
The independent MP Monique Ryan said candidates, volunteers, and campaign workers facing threats of violence should be given clear guidance for how they might engage with federal and state police.
“We need to go back to democracy sausages and bake sales, not voters feeling intimidated and harassed as they approach polling booths,” she said.

items.title: Greens push for human override in aged care assessment after ombudsman’s scathing report into algorithm tool
paragraphs: The Greens leader, David Shoebridge, has used a scathing report from the commonwealth ombudsman to press the government to use the last two sitting weeks of parliament to restore human override to its “unfair” aged care assessment tool.

The 104-page ombudsman report, published on Monday, recommends the government change legislation so that aged care workers assessing older Australians for home support packages can amend the outcome when the algorithm-driven assessment tool makes an incorrect decision on funding.

Known as the Integrated Assessment Tool (IAT), the ombudsman found it is leading to unfair outcomes, and has undermined the public’s confidence in aged care. Assessors meet older people, complete a questionnaire about their needs, and an algorithm then decides whether funding should be allocated, and at what level.
“People are tearing their hair out at what’s happening,” Shoebridge said.

“We’ve got aged care workers who are trying to help their clients … and the computer just says no. The ombudsman has told us now that this has been unfair from the moment it was conceived of. That it’s producing arbitrary and unfair outcomes for people who are at a stage of life where they desperately need help and support.”

State health officials were so alarmed by algorithmic changes to the IAT, introduced in November, that they kept a log of hundreds of cases where vulnerable older Australians were severely under-assessed, Guardian Australia previously revealed.

In a joint statement, the aged care minister, Sam Rae, and the health minister, Mark Butler, said the government will “consider the Ombudsman’s report carefully” and are acting on some of its recommendations. The government has commissioned an independent review of how the IAT assesses and prioritises people.
Of the 10 recommendations made, six were accepted and two, including instating human override for assessors and amending the aged care legislation, were noted.
“We have two more sitting weeks of parliament, where the Senate and the House of Reps can come to some arrangement and put in place a human override for aged care,” Shoebridge said.

Rae said that a new escalation pathway had already been introduced, allowing a wrong outcome to be escalated for review by a delegate, “adding a further layer of human oversight and nuance to the assessment system”.

“Our response aligns with the principles of the ombudsman’s report, allowing for human discretion to overturn assessment decisions that are not fit for purpose in a way that is fair and responsible for all older people.”

The commonwealth ombudsman, Iain Anderson, said: “I think that assessors being able to change decisions because they appear to be clinically inappropriate is really important, and so I am concerned that the escalation pathway will not necessarily do that”.
An aged care assessor with more than four decades of nursing experience, who spoke to Guardian Australia on condition of anonymity, said escalation pathways are not good enough.

“The delegate has not sat in front of that older person,” she said. “The delegate has not laid eyes on that person. I have.” She said while she escalates cases to a delegate in her workplace, who received special training to review cases, this adds time and administrative work.
She said she and her colleagues are experiencing severe anxiety and distress due to their work.

“I’m too scared to ‘accept’ on the algorithm’s decision, but I have no choice,” she said. “It feels like I’m telling the algorithm and the government, ‘great choice’ and sometimes I need to walk away from the computer because I can’t hit the button.

“It’s not Sam Rae or Mark Butler that then has to face the client. They’re not standing there after spending hours with clients, some of them in tears, and then telling them what the outcome is. I want the ministers to come to work with me and see what is happening.”

She said she has become “so anxious, and I get so agonised over every question that I ask my clients, that it puts me into a situation where I’m not finishing my work on time, I’m not reaching my KPIs, I’m working weeknights and weekends, and I am considering leaving this job.”

The shadow aged care minister, Anne Ruston, told the ABC’s Radio National on Tuesday that “the government needs to actually put proper human override back in,” describing the escalation pathway as “only a Band-Aid on a symptom”.
Independent senator David Pocock accused the government of “resisting attempts to fix a problem it created”.
“The Senate has offered a solution, the Ombudsman has now backed it, and the government needs to explain why it’s still standing in the way,” he said.
“The Ombudsman’s findings are extraordinary, including a finding that the department responsible for designing this system didn’t even understand the legal framework it had created.”

items.title: Guardian Essential poll: One Nation and Labor’s primary vote on par as discontent with Albanese rises
paragraphs: One Nation’s primary vote is back on par with Labor in the latest Guardian Essential poll, with Anthony Albanese’s public disapproval rising to its equal highest on record and more Australians than ever before believing the country is on the wrong track.
But Australians are still not convinced One Nation or the Coalition would do a better job than the current government, with Labor still the most trusted party on the economy and managing the country.
“This is a sobering poll for Labor, but not a ringing endorsement of One Nation either,” Peter Lewis, the executive director of Essential Media, said.

The Guardian Essential poll of 1,087 Australians, conducted last week, found Labor and One Nation neck and neck on 28% of the primary vote each. The Coalition is further back on 23%. Both conservative parties have improved their votes since last month, when One Nation was on 25% and the Coalition on 22%.
The poll took place early last week, after the alleged attack on the respected independent MP Helen Haines.

Labor lost a point from September’s 29%, coinciding with a further deterioration of Albanese’s personal approval ratings, and amid increasing scrutiny of the government’s handling of the economy, inflation and cost-of-living issues.

Disapproval of Albanese rose two points to 56%, the equal highest in Essential’s polling since he became prime minister in 2022. Albanese’s approval rating was 38%, also up one point, for a net approval of -18.
Albanese’s disapproval has been this high only once before, in August, when his approval was even lower at 35%, for a net approval of -21 that month.

The opposition leader, Angus Taylor, scored a 35% approval and 40% disapproval, for a net approval of -5 – a marked improvement since September, when his approval rating was just 31% and his disapproval 43%.

The poll also showed a new high number of Australians saying they felt the nation was going in the wrong direction, adding to the midterm malaise for Labor. In October, 61% of respondents said they thought the country was on the wrong track, with just 25% believing it was on the right track.

Essential’s “wrong track” number has been steadily increasing over Labor’s time in office, up from just 38% in May 2023. But it increased markedly between late last year, when it was 46% in October 2025, and early this year when it rose to 54% in January and has not dipped below 50% since.

Voters are also quick to blame the government for economic and cost-of-living issues. Asked what was most responsible for the rising cost of living from a list of factors, 32% of voters nominated government spending as the top cause. That was far above global events such as the war in the Middle East (which 24% nominated as the top cause) and supermarket price gouging (19%).
“The key markers are historic low levels for Labor midway through the term, but the electorate is clearly not settled on any viable alternative,” Lewis said.
“A key challenge is the perception that it’s local factors, rather than the global chaos emanating from the White House, which is to blame for cost-of-living pressure.”

The poll asked Australians which party they trusted on key issues, and what voters thought One Nation could do if it won government. When voters were asked which party was trusted to “ensure the economy works in the interests of everyday Australians”, Labor led on 32%, followed by One Nation on 29% and the Coalition far back on 18%.
Some 21% of voters said they didn’t see any difference.
On which party was trusted to “manage the country generally”, Labor again led on 31%, with One Nation (25%) and the Coalition (23%) further back.

Voters also gave their verdict on how One Nation would govern. While 43% of voters said they thought Pauline Hanson’s party would manage immigration better than current settings, 33% said they thought it would be worse. Only 20% of voters thought One Nation would handle relationships with trading partners such as the US and China better, with 39% believing it would do a worse job.

One Nation also received mixed verdicts on how it would manage energy policy (29% of voters said better, 36% said worse), cost of groceries (27% better, 37% worse), managing a crisis like a pandemic (23% better, 41% worse) and management of the economy (29% better, 39% worse).

items.title: This AI billboard might be too ballsy for its own good
paragraphs: Recently, billboard ads have been getting daring. From brands ditching their logos to wild guerrilla marketing, we've seen some real out-of-the-box thinking, but this latest ad from AI company Notion might be the most gutsy yet.

Placing itself shoulder to shoulder with the competition, Notion's confident ad proves that it stands out against its rivals. Dividing critics with its bold and minimalist billboard design, the ad proves that creative bravery is a priceless tool for standing out in a crowded market.
i can’t even tell who the billboard is for 😭 https://t.co/jclLv2cdtBOctober 26, 2026

The billboard in question features a lineup of AI logos including Claude, Perplexity, Grok Bot, ChatGPT and, of course, Notion front and centre. It might seem a little barmy to place yourself among the competition in your own ad, but it's this very confidence that makes Notion's ad shine.

"As much as I hate to admit it, this is a really great ad," a user on X wrote. "No words, just app icons. There’s mystery over who paid for it. There's controversy over why certain apps should be there. It's bold and makes a statement," they added. "Super cool and smart, or super dumb?" another added.

I, for one, am in the "super cool" camp. Given that most AI logos look the same, Notion's simple letterblock logo instantly stands out against the competition. The neutral ground of the logo lineup only helps Notion to emerge among its competitors, suggesting a certain edge against the competition.

While some have criticised the billboard for being too vague, I think that's where its strength emerges. The best adverts often spark conversation, and Notion's bold billboard is not only a symbol of confidence, but a conversation prompt about where the brand belongs in the AI sphere.

paragraphs: It could also see a reduction in the number of sheep from 1,500 to 500 with the number of cattle quadrupled to 200.
The government grant was announced on Monday at the UN Global Biodiversity Conference, COP17, taking place in Armenia.

Craig Bennett OBE, chief executive of the Wildlife Trusts, said the funding would "take us another step closer to realising our vision for one of the largest nature recovery projects England has ever seen".
He added it was a "stamp of approval" for the project on the back of "millions generously donated by philanthropists, charitable funds and thousands of members of the public".

items.title: Parents who killed their baby have sentences increased
paragraphs: A couple who "fatally battered" their three-month-old son have had their "unduly lenient" sentences for murder increased.
Klevi Pirjani, 38, and 35-year-old Nivalda Pirjani, from Wirral, Merseyside, were sentenced in April to a minimum of 19 years and 15 years in April over the death of their son, 13-week-old Miguel.
The Court of Appeal has now increased Klevi Pirjani's sentence to 21 years and six months, while Nivalda Pirjani will have to serve 17 years and nine months.
Miguel was taken to Alder Hey children's hospital in November 2024. He had severe head injuries and died five days after being admitted.
Miguel was found to have suffered 41 separate bone fractures in at least four separate incidents.

The Attorney General, Ellie Reeves, referred their sentences to the Court of Appeal, with barristers for the government arguing that the original sentences did not "meet the justice of this terrible case".

Lord Justice Jeremy Baker, sitting with Mr Justice Goose and Mr Justice Hilliard, said the pair subjected their son to "routine" assaults which increased in severity, and culminated in his "particularly callous" murder.

He said: "We take the view that the resulting sentences significantly underestimated the aggravating factors, to the extent that not only do we consider that the minimum terms were unduly lenient, but that we should set them aside."

Bill Emlyn Jones KC, for the Attorney General, said in written submissions that Miguel's death was caused by an assault by his parents on 24 November 2024, which involved "a heavy blow, or series of blows, to the right side of his head".

Paramedics arrived two minutes after his parents called 999 following Miguel suffering a cardiac arrest at their home in Percy Road, Seacombe, Merseyside, but he never regained consciousness and was pronounced dead five days later.

Emlyn Jones said that while the boy was in hospital, a "wider picture of long-standing physical abuse emerged", including the discovery of multiple fractured ribs, fractured legs and a fractured sternum suffered across several incidents before the fatal attack.
He also said that while it could not be ascertained whether Klevi Pirjani or Nivalda Pirjani inflicted the fatal violence, "whichever it was, they did so with the encouragement of their partner".
Sentencing them in March, Mr Justice Andrew Baker said the pair were "in this together, encouraging each other" to attack their "defenceless" son.
He said that who "fatally battered" the infant "remains the guilty secret of a warped relationship, in which you came first for each other to an unnatural degree".
Rupert Bowers KC, for Nivalda Pirjani, acknowledged in court that "of course" her sentence was lenient, but that the sentencing judge "considered all of the factors".

He said: "There is nothing that would indicate that the sentences he passed are beyond the ambit of reasonableness, or an error of principle, so that this court should interfere with his exercise of discretion, having heard all the evidence."
Sarah Vine KC, for Klevi Pirjani, also said her client's sentence was "undoubtedly lenient, but not unduly, and leniency in itself is not a vice".
Klevi and Nivalda Pirjani, watching proceedings from HMP Wakefield in Yorkshire and HMP Styal in Cheshire respectively, showed no reaction as their sentences were increased.

items.title: Rare dinosaur skeleton goes to auction in New York with £4.5m price tag
paragraphs: The mounted skeleton of a newly-identified dinosaur once mistaken for a young Tyrannosaurus rex is up for auction - with a price-tag of at least $6m (£4.5m).
Nicknamed "Jodi", the roughly 10-foot-tall (3m) skeleton will be auctioned by Sotheby's in New York. The sale comes a year after researchers confirmed that the skeleton belongs to a distinct genus.

The Late Cretaceous carnivore is expected to fetch up to $9m when it goes under the hammer on Tuesday. The auction comes after Sotheby's sold a Tyrannosaurus rex, dubbed "Gus", for a record $50.1m (£37.4m) in July.
The sales comes as some in the scientific community debate whether dinosaur remains should be sold privately.
Sotheby's described "Jodi" as an "excellent exhibition-ready" skeleton with about 191 fossil-bone elements and a "beautifully preserved, virtually complete skull".

The auction house added that the Nanotyrannus is "one of only three such skeletons known to science." The specimen is the first to come to market since the existence of the genus was confirmed by US researchers last October, Sotheby's said.

Megan Jenkins, a palaeontologist at the University of Portsmouth, told BBC Radio 4's Today programme on Tuesday that Nanotyrannus "was for a very long time believed to be sort of a teenager of T. rex".
"But it's a lot smaller and its a lot more gracile. So it's very sort-of sleek, slender, [with] blade-like teeth for slicing through meat," Jenkins said.
Tyrannosaurus rex and Nanotyrannus lived alongside one another during the same geological period approximately 67 million years ago.
"Jodi" was initially exhibited as a juvenile T. rex at London's Frieze Masters international art fair in October 2023, before the Nanotyrannus genus was classified.

The skeleton was discovered in the US state of Montana by rancher Jodi Pierson on her land in the Hall Creek Formation, a heavily studied geological site. It was later excavated by commercial palaeontologist Clayton Phipps.

Phipps also discovered the famous "Dueling Dinosaurs" fossil. That specimen, which shows the remains of a Nanotyrannus and Triceratops apparently in combat, was found eight miles (13km) away from "Jodi" in 2006.

The "Dueling Dinosaurs" discovery became crucial to the research published by Lindsay Zanno and James Napoli that classified Nanotyrannus as separate from T. rex. Their paper ended decades of debate over whether the dinosaurs were distinct from one another.
The auction of "Jodi" comes as some scientists warn that auctions could herald a new era in fossil collecting by the ultra-rich.
Researchers told the BBC after the sale of "Gus" that such remains should be exhibited in public spaces where they can be more freely studied.

Prof Steve Brusatte, a palaeontologist at the University of Edinburgh and consultant on the Jurassic Park films, told BBC World Service's What in the World programme in July that the T. rex's auction was "concerning".

"I don't know of any museum or university that can afford a price tag like that," he said. "Imagine if the Mona Lisa was just owned by a super-wealthy person and it wasn't on display and people couldn't see it, couldn't enjoy it."
He said that the time that he hoped such a sale didn't become a trend, adding it could adversely affect scientific research and public education.
Responding to today's auction, Brusatte called it "harrowing" that "Jodi" could disappear from public view.

"We've really just found out that Nanotyrannus is real, and now one of the best skeletons is about to be sold to the highest bidder, and it's harrowing to think it could disappear into the vaults of a collector rather than displayed on a museum where it can wow and inspire kids and families and the public at large," he told the BBC.
But Jenkins told the Today programme on Tuesday there were two sides to the debate, and that a lot of time, effort and money went into excavating the specimens.

"I don't begrudge the people involved for wanting to sell it for such a large amount of money," she said. "Although its a scary prospect, actually a lot of them have ended up in the public eye... these things without a doubt will end end up in a museum at some point."

items.title: Norway and Finland leaders hold rare call with Putin
paragraphs: Finland's President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre have held a joint call with Vladimir Putin - a rare contact between the Russian president and European leaders.
The aim was looking at "future negotiations to help to end the war" in Ukraine, their offices said. They said their initiative was not on behalf of "Europe as a whole".
After the call, Putin said "confrontational" EU and Nato policies were prolonging the war which began when Russia launched a full-scale invasion in 2022.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has spoken to the two Nordic leaders after their conversation with Putin. Last week, Zelensky met them as well as US special envoy Steve Witkoff in Oslo.
The Ukrainian leader said he was grateful for the "active support" of his Finnish and Norwegian counterparts.
Tuesday's phone call was held from the Finnish capital Helsinki.

"Finland and Norway border Russia," Stubb and Støre said. They said they had initiated the call to "discuss Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine and the diplomatic efforts to end the war and promote peace and stability in Europe".
"The war comes with enormous human and material costs," the Norwegian prime minister said. "The suffering and destruction will impact generations."
Tuesday's phone call was "frank and substantive", Stubb said, explaining that the war's outcome will "have a direct impact on our and the broader European security".
Relations between the US, Ukraine and its European allies have been souring since US President Donald Trump agreed to lift some sanctions from Russia - allowing it to export oil to the US.
Stubb and Støre said they had taken the initiative to continue discussions held in the Norwegian capital on 20 October, after which Witkoff travelled on to St Petersburg to meet Putin.
After the talks, Ukraine, Russia and the US agreed to resume three-way negotiations that Russia had stopped for months.
After speaking to the two Nordic leaders, Zelensky said part of their discussions with Putin had centred on the upcoming trilateral talks to be held in Abu Dhabi in November.
Zelensky said he had discussed with them "various formats for our engagement with partners in Europe that could be useful in further supporting diplomacy, our defense, and our shared security".
Stubb and Støre are the first European leaders to contact Vladimir Putin since French President Emmanuel Macron's conversation with him in July 2025.
Denmark's Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said she was "very sceptical" of Tuesday's dialogue between her Nordic neighbours and Moscow.
"It hasn't been co-ordinated with any of the rest of us," she told Danish broadcaster DR.
Moscow regularly accuses European leaders of prolonging the war by supplying Ukraine with weapons.
But last weekend, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said having a European negotiator at the peace talks table would be "good".
