items.title: Etsy's crackdown on AI slop is welcome, but it shows how far things have slipped
paragraphs: It's good to have rules. But there's only so far you can go without needlessly stating the obvious. You wouldn't, for example, expect to see signs in restaurant kitchens saying "Don't serve raw chicken". Store managers don't email their cashiers telling them to "Give customers the correct change". These things are common sense, and don't generally need to be said out loud.
So why is Etsy suddenly telling its sellers: "The photo of the product you're selling should actually be the photo of the product you're selling"?

Last week the marketplace for handmade goods made an important-sounding announcement: that every listing must now include at least one unedited photo of the actual item, shot against a real background.

It also specifically banned the use of AI image generators for patterns, recipes and instructions for customers. It's outlawed listings created by bots. And while it's still okay to see AI-generated art on Etsy, you need to be clear about that fact, so buyers know exactly what it is they're buying.
AI on Etsy: What's Allowed and What's Changing - YouTube
All of which sounds great. But I can't help feeling we never should have got to the place where any of this was necessary.

Admittedly, Etsy had to do something, because the complaints are mounting fast. Full-time creator Kara Lynne summed it up on X, writing: "I can't explain how infuriating it has been to purchase a crochet pattern, only to open the PDF and realise it's fully AI-generated, doesn't make sense, and definitely doesn't match what the finished product should be." Quite.

That's the world that AI is delivering to us. Someone spending their hard-earned money and an evening of their life on instructions that were never going to work. Multiply that by thousands of buyers and you can see how big the problem has become, both for shoppers and the majority of Etsy sellers, who are trying to do everything properly yet end up being tarred with the same brush.

So what Etsy has said does make sense, although it does make you wonder why they haven't acted sooner. Despite its folksy image, this is a company with a market cap of $7.81 billion, after all. You'd think they'd have enough cash to hire a few people to keep an eye on this stuff.

Still, at least Etsy now seems to be pulling in the same direction as much of the creative world. The company now follows Spotify pulling 50 million AI tracks, Snap keeping gen-AI content out of its recommendations and LinkedIn, well, at least adding a button to report it.

Etsy's new rules won't fix everything. But they do acknowledge what should have been obvious: that when people buy something "handmade", they want to know whether a human actually made it. Baby steps, of course, but at least they're steps in the right direction.

Tom May is an award-winning journalist specialising in art, design, photography and technology. He is the author of the books The 50 Greatest Designers (Arcturus) and Great TED Talks: Creativity (Pavilion). Tom was previously editor of Professional Photography magazine, associate editor at Creative Bloq, and deputy editor at net magazine.

items.title: UK and EU officials to discuss freedom of movement
paragraphs: British and European officials will discuss the future options for the UK's relationship with the EU, Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds has told the BBC.
Officials on both sides are expected to begin discussions about a range of options, including free movement, before the EU summit on 20 November.
However, Downing Street has insisted the government's current focus is on achieving new deals in areas such as food and youth mobility at the summit.
Reynolds said no "assumptions" had been made about what the UK's future relationship with Brussels could look like.
Andy Burnham has said he wants an "honest discussion" about the prospect of returning to free movement between the UK and EU.
But the prime minister has been clear any major changes to the UK-EU relationship would require a mandate at a general election, which is due by 2029.

He has vowed to stick by the red lines in Labour's 2024 manifesto, with no return to freedom of movement, the EU single market or customs union, for the duration of this parliamentary session, which will end by 2029.
Freedom of movement, which allows EU citizens to travel, live, study and work in any member country, is a precondition of membership of the EU's single market.
The single market enables goods, services and people to move freely between member states, with countries also applying many common rules and standards.
Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today programme, Reynolds said current discussions ahead of the summit are around food and drink, electricity and emissions trading.
He said: "What the prime minister has also said, quite rightly, is we face a series of policy changes on the European side that will affect us.
"We need to get as little uncertainty as possible, we need to have a way to resolve what our long-term relationship will be and he is going to set that out after the summit.
"He is going to be frank with the British people about what the trade-offs are but no assumptions have been made on that."
Pressed on whether UK officials are talking to the EU about freedom of movement Reynolds said: "They will be talking to them about what the future options for our relationship might be.
"But here and now, the focus should be on the summit and the tangible difference improvements we're going to make."
A government spokesperson stressed there were no current discussions on freedom of movement.
"We are working with the EU on the areas set out and agreed ahead of the UK-EU Summit and within the manifesto red lines," the spokesperson added.

Burnham is far more willing to have a public conversation around Brexit than his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer, whose government was nervous about reopening a debate that proved so contentious in the past.

Some people within the Labour Party had been urging Sir Keir to go further and there is a widely held view that Burnham's comments are likely to go down well with voters tempted by the Liberal Democrats and Greens.
But there is nervousness among Labour MPs with small majorities in Brexit-supporting, Reform-facing constituencies.

Labour MP Melanie Onn, whose constituency Great Grimsby and Cleethorpes backed leaving the EU, told the Today programme Burnham risked losing trust by talking about going beyond the 2024 manifesto at a future election.
"I don't think that the scars have healed for many people around the country so I do think this is an unnecessary conversation to be having at this time," she said.

Onn, who lost her seat in 2019 to the Conservatives but won it back in 2024, warned against re-opening the conversation, saying: "Trust is incredibly important, it's hard-earned and easily lost, and on this matter I think that we should tread incredibly carefully."

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage told BBC Breakfast that "Andy Burnham has no mandate to be in Brussels, to be negotiating any of this" and called for the prime minister to put his ideas to the public in a general election.
On Monday, Burnham left the door open to a potential referendum on freedom of movement with the EU.

The prime minister caused some confusion when he told broadcasters that he would not reintroduce free movement without a referendum, but Downing Street later said no decisions had been made on whether a public vote would be needed.
Housing Secretary Angela Rayner told the BBC on Sunday that no options for the UK's future relationship could be taken off the table.
But Burnham did appear to draw some red lines of his own when he told the Sunday Times, external that he would not be in favour of the UK joining the euro or the border-free Schengen zone.
The fact the prime minister has not been willing to say the same thing about free movement is being seen in Westminster as evidence that he believes it is a genuine option.

items.title: Two charged over alleged plot to assist Iran in RAF Fairford incident
paragraphs: Two British nationals have been charged over an alleged plot to assist Iran's intelligence service as part of the investigation into the incident at RAF Fairford in September.
Mohmed Ahmad Abdulkarim, 24, from Westminster, has been charged with assisting a foreign intelligence service under Section 3 of the National Security Act.

Nouman Essghir, also 24 and from Westminster, has been charged under Section 4 of the same act with entering a prohibited place for a purpose prejudicial to the UK on 22 August - weeks before he was arrested near the airbase in Gloucestershire alongside four other men.
The pair will appear at Westminster Magistrates' Court on Tuesday.
A major incident was declared after three suspicious vans were seen near the US-operated airbase on 27 September.
Dozens of residents were evacuated and a large cordon was put up in the area around the base. No explosive materials were found in the vans by police but a quantity of petrol was seized.

Essghir, from Westminster, was one of five men arrested near the scene in Gloucestershire on suspicion of committing offences under the Explosives Act and later on suspicion of preparation of a terrorist act. All five were released on police bail the following day, but Essghir was re-arrested on 20 October.

A 25-year-old UK-Iranian national who was also re-arrested on that date on suspicion of assisting a foreign intelligence service has now been released without charge. He remains on police bail after his initial arrest on 1 October on suspicion of preparation of terrorist acts.
The re-arrests in October led to detectives interviewing Abdulkarim.
Eight men have been arrested as part of the counter-terror police investigation.
Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor said the release of the five men on police bail in September had raised significant questions and speculation about the investigation for members of the public.
He stressed that tactics used by counter-terror police can appear "illogical" at times but said that "there will always be a good reason or rationale behind them".
"In this case, this decision-making has led to swifter progress, better evidence, and ultimately us securing the charges that I've announced today," he added.
US President Donald Trump at the time said he was "surprised" the men had been released, saying: "We would not have released them."
Taylor said counter-terror police had seen "a range of incidents in recent months that we believe have been directed by the Iranian state".
Iran has previously denied any involvement in the incident at RAF Fairford.
The base has been used as a forward operating location by the US Air Force (USAF) for decades.
In recent months, the US has flown B-1 and B-52 bombers from the base to the Middle East, after the UK approved a request for it to be used for defensive strikes against Iran.
After the incident in September the US pulled its bombers out of the base and returned them to America.
Trump said the aircraft were removed due to "some threats" to the base, without giving specific details.

items.title: Scotland's recycling rates fall to lowest level in five years
paragraphs: Waste experts have warned that landfill space in Scotland is rapidly running out
Scotland environment, energy and rural affairs correspondent
Scotland's recycling rate has fallen to its lowest level in five years, according to figures from the Scottish Environment Protection Agency (Sepa).
The Scottish government's environmental regulator says households recycled 42.8% of waste in 2025 - down from 44.3% the previous year.
According to a roadmap set by the Scottish government in 2010, recycling rates should have hit 70% last year but are falling well short.
The share of waste processed at an incinerator remained broadly the same at 82% but the amount being diverted to landfill fell by 10%.
Recycling rates vary massively by local authority. South Ayrshire's residents recycled 55% of their waste, compared to 26% in Glasgow.
The islands have the lowest rates, with Orkney recording a figure of just 18.2%.
A total of 2.31 million tonnes of waste was created by households in 2025, which represents a fall of just 1,500 tonnes.
Recycling rates have remained similar - at about 45% - for more than a decade.
The biggest change has been seen in the way black bag waste is treated.
A rapid growth in the construction of energy-from-waste plants, which generate electricity by burning rubbish, has seen a shift away from landfill.
But this has not happened quickly enough to meet a landfill ban which was due to come in at the start of the year. It has now been effectively delayed to 2028.
The figures do not reflect a disruption to Scotland's waste management by the long-term repairs being carried out to the incinerator at Polmadie in Glasgow.
The Glasgow Recycling and Renewable Energy Centre in Glasgow was shut down in April this year, with much of the waste being diverted to other incinerators or landfill.
The centre is operated, along with a facility at Dunbar, by Viridor.
Karen MacCormick from the company says waste incineration is a greener option than landfill because it can also generate electricity.
She added: "When it's in landfill you've got the landfill gasses, you've got methane, etc.

"This is a more sustainable way of dealing with the waste, coming through an energy recovery facility, and obviously we can create something at the end of it which is low carbon energy going straight to the grid."
A deposit return scheme for bottles and cans, which has seen recycling rates increase significantly in other countries, has been repeatedly delayed.
Experts have also suggested that the lack of consistency in what is collected by local authorities across the country makes it confusing for households.
While some councils take glass at the kerbside, for example, others are forced to drop them off at bottle banks.
Research from Zero Waste Scotland also suggests that more than half of the waste placed in black bins could be recycled.
Sepa's chief scientific officer, Dr Richard Allan, says the figures highlight an "ongoing challenge" with how waste is managed.
He added: "It's clear that where waste ends up is important, but we need to focus on preventing waste in the first place and recycling more of that material when it is produced."
Kim Pratt, senior circular economy campaigner at Friends of the Earth Scotland, said there had been a "shocking decline" in recycling rates.
She said this showed that Scotland had "lost its way", with households missing the 2025 target of 70% recycling "by a mile".

"Recycling levels have stalled in Scotland since the Scottish government encouraged a new generation of waste incinerators to be built, meaning that household waste which could have been recycled is being burned instead," she said.
"The Scottish government is expected to consult on new circular economy targets this year.
"If these are to be meaningful, it must learn the lessons from the past – setting targets is the easy part, meeting them requires real commitment and planning that puts people and nature first."
The Scottish government has been approached for comment.

Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.

A new NPR/PBS News/Marist poll reveals that Democrats hold significant advantages in the midterm elections and are favored to gain control of the U.S. House. But there are also signs suggesting that a potential wave may be limited. The poll highlights key issues influencing voters; one in three Americans face financial hardships, and four in 10 say their personal finances are worsening. Preserving democracy resonates with Democrats and independents, while immigration ranks as the top issue for MAGA supporters.

A member of the League of Women Voters of Greater Cleveland helps hold the flag during the national anthem before a basketball game on Oct. 26, 2026 in Cleveland, Ohio. Jason Miller/Getty Images hide caption

A federal judge today hears arguments in the Trump administration's bid to compel California to set aside ballots from voters it alleges may not be citizens. This comes after an appeals court last night declined the administration's request to get involved.

Israelis are voting today in an election that will shape their country's future. This marks the first time since the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas attacks that Israelis can choose their leaders. Voters will decide whether to keep Israel's far-right, longest-serving prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, or replace him with Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief promising more diplomacy and less extremism. Here's what you need to know about the leading candidates, the issues shaping the vote and what could happen next.
Woman stretching back during remote work break at home office Olga Pankova/Getty Images/Moment RF hide caption

Hours of screen time at your desk can turn you into a stiff, bleary-eyed version of yourself. Prolonged sitting can take a real toll, but a few smart habits can help reset your body and mind. Here are Life Kit's best strategies to help with the discomfort and health risks that can come from sitting at a desk all day.

Lubelo Mthenjana performs a magic trick involving fire during the annual junior magic contest at the College of Magic in Cape Town, South Africa. Tommy Trenchard for NPR hide caption

Forget flying brooms. Cape Town is home to South Africa's real-world Hogwarts: the College of Magic. Every Saturday, almost 200 students ages 10 to 18 attend classes in a variety of things, including puppetry, mime and clowning, juggling, card tricks, illusions, mentalism, stage magic, theater production and escapology. In 1980, David Gore and a friend came up with the idea of starting a magic school. At the time, South Africa was grappling with apartheid, a brutal system of racial segregation. But from day one, the establishment was multiracial, even though state schools were still strictly segregated. Almost 50 years later, the College of Magic continues to stand out in a city that remains deeply divided along racial and economic lines. These photos capture how the school has turned young dreamers into magicians.

items.title: Büro Ziyu Zhuang designs Chinese museum cluster to "blend seamlessly" into meadow
paragraphs: Chinese architecture studio Büro Ziyu Zhuang embedded four cultural buildings, including a viewing tower and a rammed-earth workshop, into parkland in Xianning, China, to create the Zi Museum.
Located along Zishan Lake in Xianning, Hubei Province, the project comprises four public buildings designed to complement the guest houses of the Ziyouji resort on the other side of the lake.
The centrepiece of the project is the 3,000-square-metre Zi Museum, which features a multi-faceted, layered structure made from pale concrete and was organised around a central courtyard.
Büro Ziyu Zhuang (BUZZ) created three separate access points into the museum at various levels, to follow the natural elevation of the landscape.

On the ground floor, the museum has flexible gallery spaces and a garden restaurant, with a lower-level entranced located near the main traffic route to make installation setup and collection storage easier.
At the front of the museum, a path from the main building leads to a viewpoint closer to the lake.
Visitors can also go from the viewpoint into the museum’s central courtyard and straight to the viewing ramp onto the museum’s rooftop.

“Visitors who are here for nature viewing are able to bypass the interior gallery space, accessing the rooftop viewing platform directly from the outdoor park, while a different circulation was created for those who are here for the gallery exhibitions,” explained BUZZ.
“This allows serious academic exhibition and relaxed social gathering to co-exist in the same building,” it continued.
BUZZ organised the interiors of the museum as an “open labyrinth”, the studio said.
Galleries, public passages, rest and hospitality areas are intertwined to create a free-flowing viewing experience that was designed to evoke the sense of wandering in a Chinese garden.
Next to the museum sits another viewpoint, described by the studio as a “meditation tower”, which features stairs that circulate around a hollow core at its centre.
These continue underground, where they lead to a sunken courtyard wrapped in metal mesh.
The tower can be used as a viewpoint, as well as for small outdoor gatherings and exhibitions.
The third building, a rammed-earth workshop, was designed to seamlessly embed into the landscape.
Like the museum building, this also has a walking ramp, which leads up to a grass-covered rooftop while slightly revealing the entrance below.
Nearby sits the final building, a bookshop with an overhanging roof design that creates a sheltered entrance facing the main street.
It gently steps down towards the lake, where its glass facade opens up to create views over the parkland and lake.

BUZZ aimed to encourage visitors to explore freely between the four buildings. Rather than designing a set route, the studio wanted to create access to the public art space from every direction of the park.
“The overall project manifests as a continuous, open expansion of green space, which provides the flexibility needed for diverse future operations,” BUZZ said.

“There are no forced axes or rigid zoning between individual buildings; instead, they are connected organically through gentle slopes, undulating lawns, and landscaped pathways, blending seamlessly into the existing meadow,” it continued.
Büro Ziyu Zhuang was founded by architect Ziyu Zhuang in 2016. It now has offices in Beijing, Shanghai and Berlin.
The studio also recently unveiled an UFO-shaped gallery that sinks into grassland in Inner Mongolia, as well as an observatory in China that resembles a “spaceship or alien form”.

items.title: This creative agency’s website is giving me Tumblr 2000s vibes, and I’m here for it
paragraphs: I've been writing about websites since the late 2000s, when I got a job on one of Creative Bloq's forerunners, a web design title called net magazine. And believe me, in the two decades that have passed by since, I've visited a lot of creative agency websites.

If you look at a lot of anything, you tend to get snow blindness after a while. And so it's been with me. Through my tired and cynical eyes, most agency sites look like they've been built by the same person.

Looping showreel? Check? Big, bold type? Check. Meaningless waffle about how the studio is “building brands that matter” (barf). Check. An imposing contact form you sense no one human will ever be bothered to fill out? Check. I could go on, but you get the point.

That's why an email from Denver’s Bound Agency made me smile this morning. Its subject line described their new website, built by Denver studio Wunder Werkz, as "Messy, meaningful and made by humans". And it did not disappoint.

The logo is a handwritten scrawl. The navigation icons are wobbly doodles: a slice of cake, an arrow, a signpost, a camera. There are acres of white space (well, soft lilac space to be precise). And scrolling down the tiles feels like I'm flicking through a fanzine.

A collage of Dolly Parton and Tim Curry pictures, all big blonde hair and glam-rock make-up, overlaid with the words: “Pack your wigs, divas. We’re being called home.” A Juno Calypso photo of a woman in a pink heart-shaped bath, pinned with a paperclip. A Spotify playlist titled The Dregs of Summer. A Victorian paper-doll bust. If you spent any time on Tumblr in the late 2000s, it all feels very familiar.

While it's not a carbon copy of the era, many of the hallmarks are there. Found imagery, ironic captions, mixtapes, and a sense that someone’s personal taste is the whole point. Personally, I’m here for it.

So why take this approach? Bound's founder Lauren “Lolo” Butts notes that in 13 years, their website has never won them a single client. “New business almost always comes from word of mouth,” she explains. “So this revamp wasn’t about lead-gen. It was about building a beautiful, fun place that feels like the person you were already told to talk to.”

I find this super-refreshing. It frees the site from having to do lots of boring jobs. There’s no “About us” page and no list of the services the agency offers. Instead, it’s a playground. You can pull a tarot card. You can rearrange a grid that keeps changing. You can build and share a cake. You can browse an estate sale guide called Let’s Go Hunting!

Almost a year ago I wrote about a tactile rebellion against slick, synthetic design, and turns out my article headline, "Messy, meaningful and made by humans", were the very words Bound used in their email to me. Flattery will get you everywhere, as they say; but I do genuinely feel this site lives up to that promise.
Every logo, doodle and arrow on the site is in Lauren's own handwriting. And even the eyeballs subtly signal an agency willing to look clients in the eye.

You can’t prompt your way to this kind of personality in Claude; it can only come from somewhere real. And for potential clients, this site is a handy vibe check. If it holds your attention, you’re probably the kind of client they want. If it doesn’t, you’ve both saved yourselves a meeting.
In short, it's a great example of a classic design maxim: why describe your message, your point of view, when you can just show it?

Tom May is an award-winning journalist specialising in art, design, photography and technology. He is the author of the books The 50 Greatest Designers (Arcturus) and Great TED Talks: Creativity (Pavilion). Tom was previously editor of Professional Photography magazine, associate editor at Creative Bloq, and deputy editor at net magazine.

items.title: Netherlands pulls out of Eurovision over Israel participation
paragraphs: NPO chair Jet de Ranitz said the organisation had held discussions with broadcasters about participating next year.
"In those discussions, we initially felt there was sufficient support to return. Unfortunately, we were unable to find a suitable format for this.
"As a result, we must conclude that it is currently too early to participate in the Eurovision Song Contest in 2027.
"Due to the sensitivities surrounding the themes currently at play, we have decided to take a step back for the time being."
NPO acknowledged that some Dutch fans may be disappointed, but that the contest would still be aired in the Netherlands.

Eurovision Song Contest director Martin Green said he was "deeply sorry" that the Netherlands would not take part, but added that "we understand their decision, and we respect the strength of feeling behind it".
Green added that organisers recognise that opinions about the contest "differ widely, both within countries and between them", adding: "We do not dismiss any of those views.

"At the same time, we believe the Eurovision Song Contest matters in a divided world. It is one of the few moments each year when people from across Europe and beyond come together around music, creativity and shared experience.
"That spirit of unity is what the contest has always stood for, and we are committed to protecting it."
Green said they looked forward to welcoming a Dutch entry again when they "feel the time is right".

items.title: See all 14 winning interiors selected in the Dezeen Awards public vote
paragraphs: The results of the interiors public vote for Dezeen Awards 2026 have been announced, with 14 projects selected as winners by Dezeen’s readers.

Projects voted as readers’ favourite include a co-working space in Berlin that offers “more than a boring desk”, as well as a “quietly magical” Toronto cafe that provides a family-friendly third place.
Also winning this year’s public vote is an office in Kyiv featuring vintage furnishings, artworks, and quirky touches such as leftover paint swatches.
Dezeen Awards 2026 public vote winners revealed this week
Dezeen Awards 2026, in partnership with Trimble, will reveal all public vote winners this week. The architecture winners were announced yesterday and the design winners will be revealed tomorrow.

items.title: Abu Dhabi reveals design for youth concert hall by the late Frank Gehry
paragraphs: Abu Dhabi‘s Department of Culture and Tourism has unveiled plans for a concert hall dedicated to young musicians, designed by Canadian-American architect Frank Gehry before his death.
Expected to open in January 2027 in the Mina Zayed port district, the Youth Orchestra Abu Dhabi will contain a 600-seat concert hall and 18 rehearsal rooms.
The orchestra building, designed by Gehry before he died in December last year, will have a more pared-back appearance compared to the fluid, organic forms for which the architect is famed.
Renders show a two-tiered building with long, straight rooflines and tall glass facades broken up by white panels.
Inside, wood will line the staircases and balcony walkways, and the top floor will open onto rooftop terraces.
Youth Orchestra Abu Dhabi will provide free access to musical education programmes for children aged six to nine, with the first cohort enrolling 100 students.

“The Youth Orchestra Abu Dhabi is an important investment in our future and in our commitment to making culture and creativity accessible to all,” said Department of Culture and Tourism Abu Dhabi chairman Mohamed Khalifa Al Mubarak.

“Through its free access to world-class music education programmes, we are creating opportunities for young people to discover their talent, develop their potential and experience the lifelong benefits that music can bring,” he continued.

“As Abu Dhabi continues to strengthen its position as a global centre for culture and creativity, and as a UNESCO Creative City of Music, institutions such as this ensure the next generation has every opportunity to participate in, contribute to and shape our cultural future, while preserving the rich musical traditions that form an important part of our heritage.”
Elsewhere in Abu Dhabi, construction is underway on Gehry’s Dar al Funoon Abu Dhabi, a performing arts venue cloaked in a rippling, fabric-like exterior.
The architect’s long-awaited Guggenheim Abu Dhabi is expected to open to the public on Saadiyat Island on 11 December.
The images are courtesy of the Department of Culture and Tourism Abu Dhabi.

items.title: What is Nasa's Artemis III mission? And what comes next?
paragraphs: Artemis III has been described by Nasa as the most complicated mission it's ever attempted.
It involves four astronauts, three rocket launches, three different spacecraft and two dockings. It will last for 14 days, although it could be extended to 17 days if needed.

The first rocket to launch will be Blue Origin's New Glenn rocket, blasting off from Florida. It will be carrying its prototype lander called Blue Moon. No astronauts will be on board and the lander will be placed into low Earth orbit.

Then Nasa's Space Launch System rocket will launch from the Kennedy Space Center in Florida, carrying four Artemis III astronauts in the Orion capsule. This is the same type of rocket and spacecraft used for the Artemis II mission, which saw astronauts fly around the Moon and back to Earth.
Orion will also be placed into orbit around the Earth, and the crew will spend two days checking out their spacecraft.
Then on day three of its flight, Orion will dock with the Blue Origin's Blue Moon. The crew will open the hatch and enter the lander, where they will spend two days checking out its systems.

On flight day six, SpaceX's huge Starship rocket will blast off, also from Florida. The upper stage of its rocket, called "the Ship" is the prototype lander (although it has not yet been fitted out as a lander and lacks life support systems) and this will be placed in low Earth orbit.

Nasa's Orion spacecraft and its crew will undock from the Blue Moon lander and then dock with the SpaceX Ship. This will be a shorter demonstration lasting for two hours, and the Artemis III crew will not enter the SpaceX lander.
Once undocked, the Orion crew will spend the rest of their mission carrying out additional tests of their capsule and carrying out science experiments, before returning home.

The overarching ambition behind Artemis is to establish a long-term human presence on the Moon. Nasa's Moon Base programme — unveiled in May 2026 by the agency's administrator, Jared Isaacman — sets out three phases:
Before 2029: robotic landers and hopping drones will survey the south polar region and deliver scientific instruments
From 2029 onwards: repeated crewed missions will expand the site
By the mid-2030s: Nasa envisages "semi-permanent" habitats with astronauts living on the Moon for extended stays

A working base would allow sustained scientific research, the testing of technology bound for future Mars missions, and the eventual extraction of lunar resources. It would also keep the United States ahead of China in a renewed space race.
Many in the field doubt that Nasa's timetable can be met.
Experts are concerned about the slow pace of the development of SpaceX;s Starship lunar lander and the absence of any in-orbit refuelling tests.
But the biggest set back was on 28 May 2026, when Blue Origin's only launch pad at Cape Canaveral was seriously damaged after a rocket exploded during an engine test.
Rebuilding the New Glenn launch pad is expected to take many months. When SpaceX lost a pad in 2016 it took 15 months to rebuild it — and SpaceX had other pads to fall back on.
Blue Origin does not, which calls into question the company's ability to provide the Blue Moon Mk2 needed for one of the lunar landings.

"It would not surprise me at all if China gets [to the moon] first," the Open University's Dr Simeon Barber told the BBC. The limiting step, he said, was the lander — the most challenging piece of the mission's technical architecture, and the one least under Nasa's direct control.

items.title: How Aldi is pushing down grocery prices
paragraphs: WASHINGTON, DC - MAY 02: An Aldi grocery store is pictures on May 02, 2025 in Washington, DC. The discount grocery chain more plans to add over 225 new stores in the U.S. in 2025 as part of a five-year growth plan to add 800 stores by the end of 2028. (Photo by Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images) Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images/Getty Images North America hide caption
Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images/Getty Images North America

In the summer of 2020, I lived briefly in Ithaca, New York. It's the only time I've lived near Aldi, the grocery store known for low prices. I went twice, and I thought it was fine, but underwhelming. I appreciated the low prices, but it didn't have everything I needed. The store was small and a bit shabby.

I didn't know it yet, but those are the exact ingredients that have made Aldi the fastest-growing grocery chain in America. Per Bloomberg, Aldi plans to have more than 3,000 American locations by the end of 2028, which would be more than any other chain but Walmart. In 2024, Aldi generated some $29 billion in U.S. sales, which is more than Trader Joe's.

Aldi is a German company known for having low, low prices, and it deserves that reputation. Food reporter Deena Shanker told me that her experience comparison shopping over many months was that Aldi either matched Walmart on price or was a bit cheaper. Grocers like Wegmans and Kroger have announced defensive price reductions, and an analysis published in late 2023 of Lidl, another German grocer with a very similar model to Aldi's but fewer U.S. stores, found that grocery chains reduced their markups ~7 percent in areas where Lidl stores opened.
All to say: Aldi is disrupting the grocery business and actually lowering prices even as the cost of food—at restaurants and other grocery stores—goes up and up.
Maybe this sounds a bit humdrum. But I found it totally intriguing and perplexing, because…

One necessary but not sufficient explanation for Aldi's low prices is that management is obsessed with efficiency and cutting unnecessary costs. There's no music in stores, because speakers (and licensing fees for muzak) cost money. The staff places products on shelves still in the cardboard boxes they were trucked in on, because artfully unpacking fruits, bread, and jerky sticks would mean higher labor costs. The shabbiness is intentional — it's the cost of cheaper groceries.

But other grocery chains are similarly obsessed with efficiency. Here's one of my favorite examples about Costco, courtesy of Zachary Crockett and The Hustle: "In another instance, reengineering a container of cashews from a circle to a square shape allowed Costco to stack more items in a single truck, reducing the number of shipments by 24,000 pallets per year. For shoppers, this meant cheaper nuts."
Instead, Aldi's disruptively low prices rely on two primary tactics:

Aldi's low prices made their stores very attractive during periods like the Great Recession and today's inflationary era. The Great Recession, especially, enabled their current growth. But if all Aldi offered was bargain prices in shabby stores, customers might flee to Costco, Kroger, or Whole Foods when the economy recovered.

So another key to Aldi's success is that it's fun. Aldi has a famously chaotic-good middle aisle with rotating buys like fun toys, German spätzle, and advent calendars that contain 24 festive cheeses. And its U.S. stores have expanded their offerings (a bit) to attract higher-income customers: Aldi doesn't just have the cheapest apples, but the cheapest honey crisp apples. Not just super-duper cheap wine but well-priced "premium" wine.

Instead of being a sad place to shop when you're low on cash, Aldi has more flea-market energy: a place anyone might go to hunt for good deals and fun finds. Aldi is beloved; many customers arecult-like in their devotion. In some cases, customers line up for new store openings like early iPhone releases.

My main takeaway from researching and analyzing Aldi for several weeks (foran episode of Gastronomics!) is that there's always something new under the sun. American grocery stores are a mature market. They seem pretty stable equilibrium-y. But they are dynamic and always changing. Aldi didn't need futuristic tech to disrupt the industry; just a strategy developed 80 years ago, then tweaked for the American market. In healthy markets, there's always a way in for new competitors.
My other takeaway is greater appreciation for the famous business idiom: "There are only two ways to make money in business: One is to bundle; the other is to unbundle."

The clearest example of bundling and unbundling is probably television. Cable companies bundled hundreds of TV channels together and charged one high fee for all of them. Then streaming services like Netflix made money by unbundling television — by allowing people to pay for just Netflix. Which felt liberating! For a few years. But now customers are annoyed about subscribing to so many streaming services. So streamers are teaming up to form bundles, like getting Disney, Hulu, and HBO Max all for one reduced price. Now, to make money, you gotta bundle.

Even the person who coined the phrase about bundling and unbundling didn't think it's literally the only way to make money. Still, I often failed to see (un)bundling as a powerful framework outside of the media industry. Until I realized that Aldi is unbundling the grocery store.

For a long time, grocery stores got more bundled. People once went to the baker, the butcher, and the greengrocer. Then the super market put all those things under one roof. And then Walmart, Target, and Costco created superstores where you could buy groceries and clothes and big-screen TVs.

Now Aldi is reversing this process by unbundling the grocery store. Not only does Aldi not have the big-screen TVs and dupes of Lululemon hoodies and pants, it doesn't even have everything on your grocery list. Aldi unbundled the part of the grocery business it can do super cheaply, and it intentionally locates Aldi stores near competitor grocery stores so shoppers can easily go grab the last few things on their list (the rest of the bundle).
With this in mind, I've started seeing bundling and unbundling at work in more and more industries. If you look closely at your own, I suspect you will, too.

My third takeaway is that I just didn't live in Ithaca long enough to grok Aldi. If I'd been there longer, I bet I would have made Aldi part of a multi-store strategy. I get it now! Aldi, please come to Colorado (where I live)!
At the start of this post, I asked three questions inspired by Aldi's expansion. The first two, which are about how Aldi achieved a comparative advantage, I feel like I've answered.

The third was whether the American economy can still deliver a bounty of affordable food. I think the way Aldi's growth pressured competitors to keep prices low shows that grocers are not the right target of our ire over food prices. But grocery stores are just one slice of the food world.

items.title: Photos reveal walkable Oxford Street as first phase of pedestrianisation begins
paragraphs: Almost a kilometre of Oxford Street in central London has been permanently closed off to vehicle traffic as pedestrianisation of the major shopping street and thoroughfare began yesterday.
Nearly a kilometre of the two-kilometre-long street – the stretch between Orchard Street and Great Portland Street – is now fully pedestrianised.
Traffic, including cars, buses, taxis and private hire vehicles, cycles, scooters and pedicabs, will not be allowed on this part of Oxford Street and will instead be routed via side streets.
Photographs from the unveiling yesterday show the road decorated with a large sign reading “Oxford St” and green bollards keeping out traffic.

The design for the pedestrianisation was made by local architecture studio East, which is working with landscape architecture studio JL Gibbons and urban design studios Gehl and Publica on the project.
Meanwhile, architecture studio Hawkins\Brown has been developing a long-term vision for the entirety of the street, which stretches from Tottenham Court Road to Marble Arch.

This first pedestrianised section is now undergoing a transition period, during which the East team will add new signage, seating and planters to make the area more visitor-friendly. The full transformation is expected to begin in 2027 and be completed by 2028.

“As we have seen from Borough High Street to Eltham, from Croydon to Green Lanes, London’s high streets are the public face of the city in all its diversity, its greenery and its energy,” East director Julian Lewis said.
“We design to preserve and support this energy, maintaining the ebbs and flows of these places which make our neighbourhoods unique.”

The transformed section of Oxford Street will feature two new squares, one close to Holles Street and the other close to Duke Street. These will be marked with a new surface dressing that will make the ground level across the carriageway.
Trees will also be added in “sculptural pots”, East said, before being planted into the ground for the permanent scheme.
London mayor Sadiq Khan had originally announced plans to make Oxford Street traffic-free almost a decade ago, in 2017, but they were blocked by Westminster Council.
East revealed updated renders of its vision for the final scheme earlier this month.
