items.title: AI-driven disinformation running rampant on social media before US midterms, experts warn
paragraphs: Social media feeds are awash with an unprecedented flood of AI-driven disinformation ahead of November’s US midterm elections, according to experts, who warn many posts are probably “slipping through the cracks”.
As tens of millions of Americans prepare to cast their vote, social media companies have scaled back their efforts to protect voters from lies meant to manipulate elections.

While the backlash against Facebook after the Cambridge Analytica scandal prompted social media giants to bolster their trust and safety operations, a counter-backlash from the right over fears of speech restrictions – which intensified after Elon Musk’s takeover of X, formerly Twitter, and the election of Donald Trump in 2024 – has led to significant layoffs from relevant teams.
Artificial intelligence has made it easier than ever to launch a disinformation campaign. And platforms are increasingly relying on AI, rather than human intervention, to respond.

“You can run an information operation now with quality that was impossible in 2016 for super, super cheap,” said Frances Haugen, a former Facebook data engineer turned whistleblower and advocate for transparency and accountability in big tech. Operatives playing dirty tricks can get around content moderation rules “because you can just keep tweaking the post a little bit each time you create them, and some of them are going to get through”, she said.

Campaigns from Pennsylvania to Texas have been scrambling to respond to lies that have surfaced, and spread rapidly, online. Unlike previous elections, they find themselves in a quandary: who, exactly, do they turn to when fabrications and falsehoods propagate?
Meta Platforms, the Facebook and Instagram owner, and X did not respond to requests for comment. YouTube, owned by Google, said all its users are subject to the same guidelines.

James Talarico, the high-flying Democrat running for US Senate in Texas, took time off from campaigning earlier this month to recover from the flu. But many social media feeds hosted another – false – reason for his absence: that he was supposedly being treated at a mental health facility in Ohio.

The claim was a complete fabrication, pushed by a rightwing “provocateur” who published a deceptively edited phone call with a hospital staffer. Talarico’s campaign released security-camera video showing him at home in Texasand the candidate publicly clarified he had never even been to Ohio.
But the lie circulated – and was stoked – for several days.

The Digital Democracy Institute of the Americas (DDIA) tracked its propagation, and how the misinformation mutated as it was picked up by conservative Spanish-language media. What began as a viral lie about Talarico being hospitalized in Ohio became a false claim in Spanish that he had attempted suicide.

The case “illustrates a recurring challenge in countering election disinformation”, DDIA’s researchers wrote. Lies evolve and shift as they spread, “making the original correction insufficient to address every version of the story”.
Social media platforms enforce their terms of service “more congruently” in English than other languages including Spanish, according to Roberta Braga, the founder and executive director of DDIA.

“There’s a lot less guardrails in place from the companies to deal with Spanish language, especially now that they’ve walked back a lot of their own investments in content moderation, and they’ve moved toward doing community-centered content moderation, like Community Notes-style things,” said Braga. “Now that they’re using AI to do a lot of the content moderation, even more is likely slipping through the cracks.”

Ken Paxton, Talarico’s Republican opponent in Texas, also launched a campaign advert earlier this year using AI-generated footage of Talarico – a Presbyterian seminarian – supposedly rewriting the Bible.

“I think Texans are fed up with these kind of lies in our politics,” Talarico told NBC News in September. “These AI deepfake ads don’t add anything to our civic discourse. They don’t do anything to elucidate the choice that’s in front of voters.”
Online hit squads behind election disinformation once operated on the fringes. Today, their work may be amplified by official government sources.

When viral posts on X and rightwing blogs claimed that an undocumented immigrant arrested in central Pennsylvania was an active field worker and canvasser for Democrat Janelle Stelson’s congressional campaign, staffers set the truth sprinting, trying to to catch up with a lie.

As they did, however, an official statement from the Department of Homeland Security amplified the claim. “It’s unbelievable that Janelle Stelson would employ an illegal alien to work on a congressional campaign, let alone a pervert who exposed himself in public,” declared Charles Wall, the deputy director of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

But the campaign released records showing that the immigrant, Chimaobim Adedayo Igbojekwe, had no paid position on the campaign, despite an initial police incident report stating that Igbojekwe claimed to be a campaign worker. They hold the claim provably false.
The campaign of Stelson’s opponent, Republican congressman Scott Perry, continues to run ads with the claim.

The Stelson campaign sent cease-and-desist letters to the media. A Fox News reporter took down a post on X about the indecent exposure arrest. Activists at Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington launched a complaint accusing the DHS of violating the Hatch Act, which limits the political activities of government employees.

“Trump has made clear that he intends to interfere in the elections,” said Nora Benavidez, a civil rights and free speech attorney with Free Press, a non-profit advocating for media independence. Trump “has leveraged agencies across the federal government, whether it’s the US Postal Service or DHS – you name it”, she added.

Stelson’s campaign has yet to complain directly to the social media platforms: Meta’s Facebook, Elon Musk’s X, Google’s YouTube or others. But a spokesperson said the campaign “continues to consider every legal avenue to fight the false claims in Perry’s ads”.
The dominant social media platforms do have clear rules – based on specific, limited definitions – on how to handle misinformation driven by AI during election campaigns.

Meta requires advertisers to disclose the use of synthetic images and AI-generated content with election ads, and enforces automated labeling on AI-generated images identified through Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity (C2PA) metadata. It also bans posts and ads that misrepresent voting dates, locations or legal requirements, as well as threats of violence.

But the company does little active moderation of political commentary, beyond the exclusion of unsolicited political content from its recommended posts. An analysis by Free Press noted that Meta had narrowed its historical restrictions in 2023 to allow debate around the legitimacy of past election cycles.

In 2023, YouTube also stopped removing content that falsely claimed the 2020 election or other past US presidential elections were marred by “widespread fraud, errors or glitches”, stating that the removals had curbed misinformation, but also had a chilling effect on political speech.
“All users” of YouTube, including political candidates and campaigns, “are subject to the same community guidelines … and have access to the same public reporting tools,” according to the platform.

It defines election misinformation narrowly, however: content that misleads voters about the time, place, means or eligibility requirements for voting or false claims that could materially discourage voting are banned. Claims that a candidate on the ballot is somehow ineligible, or calls to hack a polling site’s computers or incite violence at election locations, are also forbidden. “We also review government requests closely to determine if content should be removed because it violates a law or our policies,” YouTube’s spokesperson wrote in response to inquiries.

Google has a likeness detection system and allows civic leaders to request removal of a video when an AI-generated image falsely depicts their words or deeds. But a direct lie that falls outside these lines could propagate without intervention.

Instead of relying on takedowns, Google prefers to amplify authoritative news outlets and election boards in search queries and underneath high-stakes civic videos via contextual “information panels”.

X, formerly known as Twitter, abandoned internal safety reviews after its acquisition by Musk, replacing it with the crowdsourced “Community Notes” program. Its civic integrity policy bars false information about how to vote and suppression schemes. The platform also supposedly restricts synthetic media designed to mislead, though experts argue that the policy amounts to little without enforcement.

“When you stop being able to focus on content because the AI will just slightly tweak it until it gets through, you have to focus on what are the systems of distribution,” Haugen said. “What are the biases? What are the ways we have feedback systems, cycles, that allow the community to provide feedback, that allows it to be damped down?”

items.title: ‘My social life completely plummeted’: gen Z is fighting back against big tech
paragraphs: Nelissa Moukoudi, 19, a university student in Canada, noticed a shift once she joined Instagram and TikTok.
“My social life completely plummeted and it felt like my life was only [using] social media and school,” she said.

Tired of fighting for self-control, Moukoudi downloaded Opal, an app that forces users to solve math problems before reopening distracting apps. It is one of a growing number of companies in the sprawling digital detox industry that is enticing users – ideally paying ones – by promising to keep them off their devices. The industry is valued at nearly $1bn and is estimated to grow to nearly $8bn by 2035.

Many of these companies are hoping to capitalize on gen Z’s growing weariness about the devices and social media platforms they grew up with. Nearly 60% of gen Z respondents identified as having a social media addiction in an April poll, and a third of the generation said they had deleted some of those apps, according to a 2025 survey.
The shift has also been driven by growing anger at tech platforms that have left some in gen Z feeling as if they are being exploited for profit.

Gen Z “was basically optimized for dopamine by very smart systems”, said Kenneth Schlenker, 39, a former product marketer at Google and co-founder of Opal. “But this generation is also realizing what they don’t want and are trying to change how the system impacts them.”

Some are turning to new devices entirely. Kendall Schrohe, 23, a founding partner of the Attention Studio, a consulting firm advising parents and policymakers on responsible tech, said that she traded her smartphone for a Light Phone, which sells for $349 and includes minimal smartphone features.

“These big tech platforms have been hurting people for years, and we are just now feeling the impacts of it,” Schrohe said. “Our generation were the guinea pigs to big tech, and our suffering and addiction to these apps were profited off of.”

Shreya Nallamothu, 19, a computer science student at Duke University, created her own DIY “Brick”, a device to block selected apps, using $8 near-field communication (NFC) tags that she bought online.

“Everyone deserves to have a good relationship with technology, and it shouldn’t be cost-prohibitive,” Nallamothu said. “Often the tech companies’ best interests aren’t in the users’ best interests. Social media has gotten away from what good technology can do, and people have noticed.”

Research that Nallamothu conducted in high school helped convince state senators in Illinois to advance a recent bill to prevent parental exploitation of children on social media and the state to pass a law forcing parents to compensate their kids.

New event-focused apps are also trying to capitalize on the pivot away from social media. Pie (People I Enjoy), an app highlighting local events including bar pop-ups, 5K runs and concert meetups, grew 150% in a single month – jumping from 120,000 users in July to 300,000 in August.
Co-founder Nadya Okamoto describes Pie as an in-person, active social network.
“I think of social media as this passive consumption of content, but Pie is separate from that,” Okamoto said. “Users are actively networking and building your social circle.”

Co-founder Andy Dunn, who also founded menswear brand Bonobos, added: “Everything about the product is designed to make you want to go and be in community with those people. It gives you so much more agency.”

The price of using such digital detox apps can vary. An Opal subscription costs $99.99 a year, while Brick, a physical block that phone users tap to lock and unlock apps, costs $59. Shift, an app that promises to turn a smartphone into a so-called “dumbphone” that can only make calls or send texts, charges a one-time $150 payment.

That is one reason why convincing gen Z digital detoxers to pay for a new app could be tricky. Like approximately 95% of Opal’s 10 million customers, 75% of whom are gen Z, Moukoudi said she is using the free version. “I am not going to pay for an app just to reclaim my life,” the university student said.
For some, simply deleting apps does the trick. Han Choi, 26, deleted all social media apps last year to spend more of his time on trivia nights and workouts.

“People are rejecting the systems that have been put in place by people who stand to profit off our compliance,” Choi said. “The doomscrolling economy is not one that we need to keep participating in.”

items.title: CurrentBody Series 3 review: a fully customisable LED mask that helps exactly where you need it
paragraphs: CurrentBody’s LED masks have long been my favourite. They’re comfortable, simple to use and effective. My previous favourite, the now-discontinued CurrentBody Multi Light Therapy LED mask, offered five treatments that used different light wavelengths to address multiple skin concerns. The company’s latest mask, the new Series 3, has the most detailed customisable treatments I’ve ever seen.

This isn’t the first LED mask I’ve tried that allows its user to select different treatments for different areas of the face. The Lustre Renew Pro Facewear allows you to choose from two treatments across four different zones, with 16 possible combinations. The Series 3 takes this much further, allowing you to choose between six light wavelengths across 125 light points on the mask. If you stick to one wavelength per light point, that’s 6125 combinations available. That number is longer than I can reasonably comprehend, so allow me to call its level of customisation endless.

At £499.99, it certainly isn’t cheap, but it’s the same price as its less-advanced predecessor. Having tested my custom treatment for six weeks, my results were just as good as I had hoped, with the same excellent coverage I’ve come to expect from CurrentBody LED masks. Once you’ve got over the price, there’s very little to grumble about here, given that the Dr Dennis Gross SpectraLite FaceWare Pro costs almost as much and has no personalisation, and cheaper masks such as the Silk’n LED face mask Pro can’t pinpoint precise areas of the face. For anyone looking for the best LED mask money can buy, this is a safe bet.

I’ve tested 18 LED masks, considering overall efficacy, comfort levels and ease of use – all things that help make consistent treatments enjoyable. I always check comfort levels by testing how well the eye guards block out the light from the mask, how easy the straps are to adjust and how comfortable the mask is to wear when lying down, sitting up and moving around.

I also assess how straightforward the mask’s controls are. This was especially important for this mask, which required me to download an app. If it’s going to take up space on my phone, it had better be flawless.

The test also involved noting the condition, texture and appearance of my skin before and after two months of use. I tested the four preset treatments for four nights each to get a quick idea of how they affected my skin, but since personalised treatments are the star of the show here, I used a customisable treatment for the rest of the test. Having tested LED masks before, I was hoping to at least maintain, or, ideally, build on the improvements I’d seen previously.

Let’s not beat around the bush: LED therapy, AKA photobiomodulation, looks a lot like pseudoscience. Scepticism is understandable, so as part of my LED mask testing for the Filter, I spoke to four independent dermatologists, anti-ageing experts and facialists. Their overall outlook on the tech was positive, particularly with regard to managing mild acne, reducing inflammation and firming skin. They advised choosing a mask from a reputable brand that bolsters its claims with clinical studies, and doing consistent treatments alongside a good skincare routine. Or, if you’re already inconsistent with skincare, consider whether you really need an LED mask first.

The most concrete evidence for LED therapy is in the blue, red and infrared wavelengths, used for acne, ageing and wound healing. There is growing interest in green and yellow light for brightening and calming redness. Small studies commissioned by CurrentBody reported modest reductions of 4.1% in pigmentation with green light and 8.6% in redness with yellow light, compared with a 37.1% reduction in forehead wrinkle volume with deep near-infrared light.

The Series 3 has 750 LEDs spread across 125 light points on the face. This is more light points than any previous CurrentBody mask, allowing for greater light coverage. For context, the Shark CryoGlow has more light points (160), although it lacks the range of wavelengths on offer here, with 480 individual LED light sources across three wavelengths. Some entry-level masks offer fewer light points, sometimes under 100, which tend to garner less effective results. In the Series 3, each light point has six LEDs: red, blue, near-infrared, deep near-infrared, yellow and green. Unlike all other masks I’ve tested, which mostly concentrate the most deeply penetrating deep near-infrared light around the eyes and mouth, the Series 3 offers full-face coverage, meaning it can tackle deep wrinkles anywhere you fancy.

There are four preset 10-minute treatments: Advanced Anti-Ageing, Advanced Clearing, Brighten & Balance, and Complexion Corrector. These combine near-infrared light with a different visible light wavelength to achieve their results and work like those offered on the Multi Light Therapy mask.

As mentioned, the star of the show here is the customised treatments, where users can pick out wavelengths with reckless abandon in the app. Helpfully, each colour is labelled with a brief description of its aims: “clear breakouts” for blue light, “calm redness” for yellow and so on. These can be positioned anywhere on the face and combined to create a treatment that’s unique to your needs. And, since you can save up to 10 custom treatments on the mask and more in the app, it also gives users the flexibility to target breakouts or dark spots precisely where they pop up, while continuing with other treatments elsewhere.

But if free salad bars have taught me anything, it’s that people are likely to overdo it if left unsupervised. That’s why CurrentBody has developed MyDose, which automatically calculates the optimum dosage for your chosen light wavelengths. In theory, this means you can safely customise treatments without compromising on results.

The Series 3 also has CurrentBody’s Veritace certification. Every mask undergoes quality control tests in which each of the 750 LEDs is tested to ensure it emits the specified wavelength and power output required before it’s shipped out to you. The mask comes with its own NFC card that lets you view the results; it’s reassuring to have this kind of transparency for a mask that costs this much.

Price: £499.99 Recommended use: 3-5 times per week Settings: Advanced Anti-Ageing, Advanced Clearing, Complexion Corrector, Brighten & Balance, plus near-infinite customised options Light wavelengths: red (633nm), near-infrared (830nm), deep near-infrared (1072nm), blue (415nm), green (532nm), yellow (590nm) Treatment time: 10 minutes Suitable for: all skin types, but darker tones should take care with blue light Battery life: 13 uses Charging time: 4.5 hours Contents: mask, three straps, two removable eye guards, Veritace card, charging cable, storage bag

Like the Series 2 that came before it, the Series 3 is made from flexible silicone that fits comfortably without digging in, and has a chin strap that offers more coverage than other masks. Its straps are adjustable at four points – two on either side of the head – plus there’s an overhead strap that can stop the mask from slipping down on smaller heads. I also found the eye guards did a fantastic job of blocking out the mask’s light during treatment, as I was able to see clearly enough to read or potter around in dim lighting with no issues.

The results from my tests were fantastic. As expected, given the Multi Light Therapy mask’s near-identical treatments, each of the preset treatments performed well. However, the real selling point for me was the personalised treatments.

Like many with PCOS/PMOS, I get hormonal breakouts and hair growth on my chin and upper lip. For a while, I have been worried that using red light in these areas would make this more pronounced, as red light has been shown to stimulate scalp hair growth. With the Series 3, I chose not to use red light in those areas, and instead used blue light on my acne-prone chin, with red, near-infrared and deep near-infrared everywhere else. I also threw in a sprinkling of yellow light on my cheeks to tackle redness.

Given my hatred for beauty tech apps, which are often full of ads, useless subscriptions and grating tech problems, I was glad to find the CurrentBody app refreshingly simple. The app pops up with an illustration of the light points on the face, ready for you to select which of the six light options you would like to shine from each point. The six light options can be applied using a paintbrush, fill bucket and eraser, which made it feel a lot like using a simplified version of Microsoft Paint. The whole process took about five minutes.

I was most relieved to see that, once my personalised treatment had been saved to the device, I never had to open the app unless I wanted to tweak my treatment. There’s space for up to 10 personalised modes on the mask’s controller, on top of the four preset modes, and if for some reason you want more options than that, you can store more treatments on the app. There’s also the option to share treatments with others using a code (mine’s RYPGJ, if you’re feeling nosy).

After six weeks of using my personalised treatment, my skin looked calmer, with less redness on my cheeks, fewer breakouts on my chin and a healthier overall appearance. Mission accomplished. I was also pleased that the mask lasted through 13 full 10-minute treatments before needing a recharge. If you’re short on time, you can’t reduce the treatment time, but I’d be reluctant to mess around with the treatment length too much anyway, as this would add too many variables to the automatic dosing.

I can’t complain about the results on this mask, but it does have a few nitpicky problems. Namely, the chin strap makes it impossible to pack flat when travelling, as opposed to flat silicone LED masks. Its nose flap left a tiny red mark on my nose for a few minutes after treatments, and to my frustration, CurrentBody’s instruction manual does a poor job of explaining how to add the straps.

Furthermore, unlike the Series 2, the controller comes with a small built-in touchscreen to accommodate its more complex treatments. While this is intuitive to use, I found the screen easy to jog accidentally mid-use, which would often pause my treatment. At 190g, the controller is also bulkier than before, and its clip is about an inch shorter, which makes it harder to carry around or clip securely on to clothing.

I also found the battery life indicator a touch unreliable. Occasionally, the mask died before it got the chance to flag up red low-battery levels. This didn’t happen every time, and the charge always lasted through 13 full 10-minute treatments, but it was frustrating nonetheless.

LED therapy is safe and comfortable for most people, but it’s always best to be cautious. CurrentBody recommends doing a skin sensitivity test before starting treatment, and offers a full refund if your skin becomes red or itchy after 24 hours, provided you return the mask within 14 days. For those who keep the mask, there is also a two-year warranty that covers manufacturing faults.

If you have the money, absolutely. The CurrentBody Series 3 fits comfortably, has a generous battery and is the only one with anti-ageing deep near-infrared light all over the face. With this level of customisation available, it’s easily the top LED mask I’ve tested.

This mask is particularly good for those with areas of their skin where one flat treatment won’t cut the mustard. For example, if you just want to fade one dark spot using green light, or treat a localised breakout using blue light, this mask gives you the flexibility to do that. This is a rare instance where I think the app is genuinely worthwhile, too. I didn’t dread booting it up every time I wanted to make an adjustment, and I love that the mask remembers my personalised treatments.
That said, if you aren’t battling deep wrinkles and don’t have problematic skin, you might be better off with a more affordable LED mask.

At about half the price of the CurrentBody Series 3 at the time of writing, the Silk’n LED face mask Pro is an obvious competitor. It has a silicone fit that blocks light well and coverage under the chin. And, if you think a wired controller will bother you, this is controlled and charged via a small, light battery pack that clips on to the mask itself, making it completely wireless. Treatments are all 10 minutes, and the mask had a lovely calming effect on my skin.

That said, it offers no personalisation and far fewer deep near-infrared lights, which are positioned exclusively around the mouth, eyes and across the forehead. I also found the mask’s controls harder to get used to. The seven treatments, many of which look similar at first glance, are controlled via a button on the battery pack, which doesn’t give you any information about the treatment selected. To check which lights are being used, you’ll need to read the instructions and memorise how many presses it takes to get to your desired treatment. This shouldn’t be a huge problem, but it does somewhat hinder usability.

This is the only other customisable LED mask I’ve tested. It’s not perfect, with a far less comfortable fit thanks to a heavy battery pack stuck on the forehead and a smaller-than-average size, but the lower price and simpler customisation options could clinch it for some.

This mask has two preset treatment options – Energise and Revitalise – which use blue, red and near-infrared light. While you can use either as a full face treatment using the mask’s button, boot up the app and you’ll be able to select areas of the face for each treatment. Rather than offering pinpoint precision, like the CurrentBody Series 3, these areas span the eyes, nose, forehead, and cheeks and chin.

I found these treatments effective at calming my skin, but I didn’t find the app or connection as simple as the CurrentBody, since I had to load the app up every time I wanted to personalise the treatment. If you won’t use the app either, you’d be better off buying the Silk’n option above, which is cheaper, more comfortable and includes deep near-infrared light in its anti-ageing treatments.

If 10-minute treatments feel like too much of a commitment, the Dr Dennis Gross SpectraLite FaceWear Pro requires only three minutes a day, making it perfect for those who are time-poor but rich in other aspects. The lights are bright, the fit is supremely comfortable, and it’s wireless, so you don’t need to faff around with a controller.

I was initially sceptical about this mask’s performance, given its shorter treatment times, but the combination of red, deep red, near-infrared, amber and blue lights helped give my skin a smoother, clearer and brighter appearance. For an effective LED mask without bells, whistles or any fancy app-based extras, this is a brilliant, if expensive, choice.
For more: The best LED face masks that are worth the hype I tested the viral Shark CryoGlow LED face mask 100 times Sali Hughes’s favourite anti-ageing creams, serums and treatments

Sarah Matthews is a consumer journalist who specialises in health and beauty reviews. In her four years of product testing, she’s worked her way through countless hair styling tools, hair removal, light therapy and skincare innovations. She’s seen beauty trends come and go, and can sniff out a fad from a gamechanger (that doesn’t mean she’s disciplined enough to always follow her own advice, though)

items.title: UK officials discussing options including free movement with EU ahead of summit
paragraphs: British officials have begun discussions with the EU about a long-term relationship that could include a return to free movement, the business secretary has said while promising the British people “are the boss” when it comes to what the UK will accept.

Jonathan Reynolds said the focus for British negotiations was the EU summit in November to seal an agreement to ease some trading restrictions and a youth mobility deal. But he said the prime minister, Andy Burnham, had made it clear he wanted to see a long-term and stable relationship with the bloc.

“They will be talking to them about what the future options for our relationship might be. But here and now, the focus should be on the summit and the tangible difference improvements we’re going to make,” he told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme.

He said the changes announced at the EU summit, including a food and drink deal and on emissions trading, would make a significant difference. But he added: “What the prime minister has also said, quite rightly, is we face a series of policy changes on the European side that will affect us, and we need to get as little uncertainty as possible.

“We need to have a way to resolve what our long-term relationship will be, and he is going to set that out after the summit. And he is going to be frank with the British people about what the trade-offs are.”

Reynolds said there had been “no assumptions made about the next stage after that. It’s the prime minister quite rightly saying he wants to set out to the British people what the options are to resolve some of the tensions that exist.”

He said no decision would be made without voters being given a say, without specifying whether this would be through a general election or a referendum. “No assumptions have been made on this. The British people are the people who will decide this. They’re the boss on this,” he said.
A number of backbenchers with heavily pro-Brexit seats in the north and Midlands are wary about reopening the arguments for free movement or rejoining the EU.

The Labour MP for Great Grimsby and Cleethorpes, Melanie Onn, was among those urging caution. “I am still not over the kind of very divisive debate that we had when we were leaving the EU post the referendum, and I don’t think that the scars have healed for many people around the country,” she told Today. “So I do think that this is an unnecessary conversation to be having at this time.”

The Reform UK leader, Nigel Farage, told the programme it would be “very, very poor indeed” to begin discussing freedom of movement. “Five months ago, Andy Burnham says to leave-voting Makerfield: ‘I’m not going to reopen these arguments.’ Two and a half years ago, a Labour government got a massive majority in parliament saying we will not be re-entering the single market, the customs union, or opening up the debate on the free movement of people,” he said.
“What I am saying is this: this prime minister has no mandate, and to hear that his officials are negotiating in Brussels already is really very, very poor indeed.”

Burnham made his plea for an “honest discussion” about freedom of movement in an interview with the Sunday Times, making clear that staying out of it would no longer be a red line in talks with the EU.

Burnham also shared his belief that rejoining the single market and accepting free movement could be done without the need for another referendum, if Labour put it in its manifesto. In contrast, he said fully rejoining would need another in-out poll.

The prime minister said: “Freedom of movement had very significant challenges associated with it and I spoke about them in my previous time in parliament. But, at the same time, it was a type of immigration that perhaps wasn’t as difficult [as now].

“Revolving-door migration where people would come and then go back is different. The balance of migration has changed, hasn’t it, since then? I think we’ve just got to have an honest discussion about those things.”

items.title: OHLAB experiments with colour-blocking and cork in old and new buildings of Terreno Barrio Hotel in Mallorca
paragraphs: Mallorca-based architecture and interiors studio OHLAB has overseen the design of a hotel in Palma, including a renovated heritage building from 1935 and a new structure built from cross-laminated timber and cork.

The 41-room Terreno Barrio Hotel was envisioned as “a catalyst for the neighbourhood” of El Terreno, in the west of the Mallorcan city, serving as a community hub as well as a destination for tourists.

“Terreno is not conceived as a tourist object imposed on its context, but as a device for exchange – a hotel that, before being a hotel, aims to be an extension of the barrio,” said OHLAB founders Paloma Hernaiz and Jaime Oliver.
“This is not a slogan; it is the principle that orders programme, thresholds, atmospheres and materiality.”
The hotel’s reception is in the renovated 1935 building, a five-storey apartment block designed by local architect Francesc Casas, along with the restaurant and bar, a club, and a roof bar.
OHLAB refers to this building as “the stage”, the eye-catching focal point of the complex, while the new structure is described as “the bazaar”, its civic heart.
Wrapping a new public plaza, this second block houses the community-led spaces, including a cafe, coworking areas, a bookshop and gallery, pop-up retail, a gym, a spa and a cinema.
OHLAB adopted different strategies for the architecture and interior design of the two structures, creatively exploring the themes of building and material reuse in various ways.

“Here, circularity was understood not only as an environmental or material strategy, but also as an economic, social and territorial one, a way of keeping value within the local ecosystem by activating residents, culture, crafts, suppliers and everyday life,” they said.
In the renovated building, interior design revives the existing structure rather than covering it.
Communal spaces have a theatrical character, with patterned floor tiles and heavy curtains. Highlights include a golden mirror bar and a wool curtain installation by artist Sylvia Sanchez Montoya.
In the bedrooms, colourblocking creates a horizontal divide between top and bottom.
Floors and furniture feature matching terrazzo, produced by local tile manufacturer Huguet using the project’s demolition waste.

Materials are even more prominent in the seven-storey new building, thanks to the choice of materials. Cork clads the courtyard-facing north facade, while the other exterior walls feature timber louvres that shade the windows from direct sunlight.

Inside, the exposed CLT structure is brought to life through more playful use of colour and materials. The cafe and shop is a key example, with shades of brown and lime green extending across to the terrazzo floors and wooden furniture.
The bedrooms in this block have a different character, with murals by Mallorcan artist Albert Pinya, bathrooms housed inside mirrored boxes, and timber flooring that merges with joinery.
OHLAB was appointed by José Taltavull, who developed the concept for the hotel after being brought on board by hotelier Lydia Piñero.
Taltavull appointed graphic design office StudioRoses to oversee the hotel’s visual identity, which fed into OHLAB’s scheme.
Various elements were picked out in the same red as the hotel logo, including the ramped floor between the bar and reception, the stage in the club, and the sculptural stools located in the bar.

Most of the furniture was either designed by OHLAB or sourced from Mallorca-based manufacturers. A DJ table was made from cork leftover from the construction, while Mallorcan artist Pedro Óliver contributed the neon lighting pieces that feature throughout.
Terreno Barrio Hotel is the latest in a series of major openings in Palma in recent years, with the city in the midst of a cultural renaissance.

El Terreno is a major part of that story, particularly since Mallorca-based shoe brand Camper completed its 15,000-square-metre Project Gomila in 2023, which includes the new Jasper Morrison-designed Can Pa bakery.
OHLAB’s other projects in the city include the Can Santacilia residential development and the Paral·lel apartment complex.

items.title: Can Black voting power and Trump fatigue break Mississippi's red wall?
paragraphs: Mississippi Democratic Senate nominee Scott Colom speaks at a rally in Columbus, Miss., headlined by former Vice President Kamala Harris on Oct. 22, 2026. Stephen Fowler/NPR hide caption
COLUMBUS, Miss. — On paper, Mississippi's U.S. Senate race seems like the perfect place for a political upset this year, an assertion President Trump's Monday rally there seems to support.
It has the highest share of Black voters in the country, at close to 40%. It's a rural, agriculture-heavy state that is also among the poorest, so higher prices are felt harder.
But President Trump won the state by 23 points in 2024, and it's extremely racially polarized, meaning not enough white voters back Democrats for the party to win statewide.

In a midterm environment that has seen hundreds of millions of dollars poured into Senate races in conservative-heavy states like Iowa, Texas, Ohio and Alaska, and a last-minute flood of cash to Kansas, the Magnolia state has been left off of many peoples' radar — and largely out of campaign investments.
Scott Colom, a district attorney and the Democratic Senate nominee in Mississippi, told NPR that's a mistake.

"The reality is, Mississippi has never been a lost cause, we've been a betrayed cause," he said. "The Democratic Party has not been trying to win Mississippi. Let's stop kidding ourselves, right? They spent hundreds of millions of dollars in other states. They spent almost nothing in Mississippi."
Colom is challenging incumbent Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith, who blocked his nomination to be a federal judge during the Biden administration.

In the final weeks of the election, both parties have rushed to spend millions of dollars in Mississippi, as national polling shows a pathway where Democratic enthusiasm and elevated Black turnout, combined with fewer Republican base voters and defections from the party, has made deep red races deeply competitive this cycle.
The crowd listens during a rally with former Vice President Kamala Harris and Mississippi's Democratic Senate nominee Scott Colom in Columbus, Miss., on Oct. 22. Stephen Fowler/NPR hide caption
At a rally for Colom in his hometown high school gym Thursday, about a thousand people showed up to hear the candidate — joined by former Vice President Kamala Harris — give his closing message.

Many attendees expressed optimism for his campaign coupled with a vibe of feeling down about those in power, regardless of party affiliation – citing the war in Iran, rising fuel costs and dissatisfaction with Trump's second term.
That includes Celestine Rice, who said many people were realizing a need to focus on bringing change to the political system and representation.
"Before, we didn't realize how bad it was, but now it's obvious," she said. "The moral compass of this country is gone."

Rice said many people took for granted an era where it seemed the country used to be more focused on taking care of its citizens and now they see that "big money, it doesn't trickle down like they said."

The brunt of the Democratic money and manpower headed to Mississippi is driven by a growing number of those who argue the party's future runs through the South, including Harris, Georgia Sen. Raphael Warnock and former transportation secretary Pete Buttigieg.
At the rally, Harris said political changes in the last year and a half were the result of "the most callous, corrupt and incompetent presidential administration we have ever experienced."

"We've been going through that range of emotions from anger to sadness to depression, all of that for a year and a half," she said. "Well guess what? We're 12 days out from an election. And it's time to turn that anger into action."
President Trump embraces Mississippi Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith at a campaign rally on Oct. 26, 2026 in Corinth, Miss. Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images hide caption
About a hundred miles up the road a few days later, Trump, Hyde-Smith and other Mississippi Republicans gathered in Corinth to motivate the party's base to show up and vote next Tuesday.
In a statement ahead of the rally, Hyde-Smith's campaign manager expressed confidence in her reelection bid.

"We are confident that Mississippians will once again send Cindy Hyde-Smith to the U.S. Senate," Jake Monssen said. "Senator Hyde-Smith and President Trump have built a strong working relationship, and she gladly accepted when President Trump offered to help rally voters and support her get-out-the-vote efforts.

"With so much at stake in this election, Mississippians deserve to hear directly from their President about the consequences of electing Democrats, the radical socialist policies being pushed by Scott Colom, and the importance of this election. Team Cindy looks forward to a successful, high-energy event in Corinth," he said.
Speaking ahead of the president, Hyde-Smith touted accomplishments from her time in office and said the choice facing voters "could not be clearer."

"We know what we're looking at: this is socialism versus capitalism, and we know that," she said. "Communism versus democracy, and big government versus the free market. It could not be higher stakes."
Hyde-Smith repeatedly reiterated that it was important for Republicans to get out and vote.
"Endorsements don't win elections, votes win elections," she said.

Mississippi Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith talks to audience members as President Trump holds a campaign rally in support of her reelection campaign on Oct. 26, 2026 in Corinth, Miss. Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images hide caption
For his part, Trump said his visit to Mississippi was because Hyde-Smith was in good shape in her matchup.

"Sometimes when you think somebody's doing so well, nobody votes," Trump said. "'Oh, Cindy's great, she's gonna do no problem, let's stay home.' And then bad things happen, Cindy. That's why I'm here, just get out and vote."

Over the last month, the Republican campaign strategy has been to highlight the investment and attention from national Democrats as proof Colom is too extreme for Mississippi — and have spent heavily on ads saying as much.

"Meet the most radical Senate candidate in our lifetime, Scott Colom," an ad titled "Most Radical" intones. "Twice nominated by Biden, beholden to the far left. As DA, violent crime doubled on his watch."
The Hyde-Smith campaign has spent more than $1.3 million on that ad, according to data from AdImpact.
But Democrats have spent more this month, about $5 million to the Republicans' $3.2 million, with a message that there's no daylight between the unpopular president and down ballot Republicans.

"I mean, the reality is if somebody's doing a good job, it's hard to beat them," he said. "If Cindy Hyde-Smith was focused on the voters, it'd be tough. But it's very clear the voters of Mississippi want to fire her."
The race carries weight beyond Mississippi, or even control of the Senate. It's become a stand in for conversations about the power of Black voters in the South.

Many Southern Republican-led states have rushed to redraw Congressional maps that remove opportunities for Black voters to elect candidates of their choice after a Supreme Court ruling earlier this year rolled back part of the Voting Rights Act.
In Mississippi, Republicans have signaled a desire to redraw state legislative and judicial races after the midterms, and Colom said it could extend even further into local elections.

"What that tells us is you're trying to take away power from the voters and give it to the leaders," he said. "That's not how democracy is supposed to work. The voters have to pick the leaders, not the leaders pick the voters.

In a statewide race that can't be gerrymandered, and in an environment favorable to Democrats, history and math still prove to be a challenge. The last Democratic Senator from Mississippi came in the early 80s. The last successful Black statewide candidate was during Reconstruction.
Even during the 2018 blue wave, Cindy Hyde-Smith won a special election for this seat by roughly 7 points.

Still, there are many factors that have both parties anxiously awaiting results on Nov. 3, including a pervasive anti-incumbent streak that has shown up in polls and primaries this election cycle coupled with a significant increase in Black voter turnout in states that have early voting.
Ashley Kennedy Shelton, who runs a nonpartisan civic engagement group in Louisiana, told NPR earlier this month that people of all stripes have been expressing frustration and a desire for change.

"I think you're going to see voters truly show up, because folks are just tired," she said. "They're like: 'This doesn't work, and it hasn't been working for quite some time.' I think you're going to see it at the ballot box.

items.title: Polymarket has investigated 'dozens' of election-related cases
paragraphs: Prediction markets, like Polymarket and its main rival, Kalshi, have flourished in Trump's second term. Gabby Jones/AFP via Getty Images hide caption
Polymarket has investigated "dozens" of bets on its prediction markets related to the midterm election, according to the company's head of global intelligence and investigations, Shana Bautista.

At least two of these Polymarket investigations have been referred to its regulator, the U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission, according to a person who is familiar with the probes, but not authorized to speak publicly about them.

These investigations into election insider trading and manipulation come as prediction market Polymarket — and its chief competitor Kalshi — have exploded in popularity over the past year. But the fast-growing industry also faces significant legal challenges from states and political pushback from lawmakers who argue betting on the outcome of elections poses serious risks to the democratic process.

In April, Kalshi banned and fined a handful of political candidates from betting on themselves. A month later, NPR reported that campaign staffers had made "thousands" using insider polling information to bet on their own candidates on platforms like Polymarket and PredictIt.

Polymarket's Bautista — a former FBI official and cryptocurrency analyst — told NPR her team of 16 and a new election surveillance system are actively policing election bets ahead of the Nov. 3 midterms.

"If you have information that you have a duty to protect, don't trade on it," Bautista said. "It's explicitly against our terms of use on both platforms, but also is against the law. If you decide that you are smarter and can do it, we will find you."

Bautista joined Polymarket in June. She oversees information gathered from both the U.S.-regulated version of Polymarket, which requires users to provide their real identities, and its bigger brother, Polymarket International, which is essentially unregulated and where trading can be done anonymously and with cryptocurrency. Despite this, Bautista said crypto trades are rarely completely anonymous.
"There's never been a case that we work where we haven't been able to identify, potentially, who these people are," Bautista said.

She said her election surveillance system pulls in "gigabytes" of data on each user from social media, Federal Election Commission data, cryptocurrency companies, banking partners, statistical models and other public information sources. If a user hits a certain number of internally-defined red flags, Bautista gets an alert on her phone.
"We're getting hundreds of alerts a day," Bautista said.

When asked about the specific detection criteria and thresholds, Bautista did not comment citing system security. But she said insider trading and market manipulation all look the same regardless of the financial market.

"We're looking at threat vectors and risk areas that have existed for decades in traditional markets," Bautista said. "But we recognize, too, that when it comes to prediction markets, we're seeing some of the old tried and known tactics, but being applied to a new vector through prediction markets."

Back in May, Kalshi, Polymarket's top rival, announced its own election surveillance system that also uses FEC data. Their system purportedly blocks any campaign staffer listed by the FEC from betting on an election. In July, Kalshi said it had blocked "dozens" of staffers from trading on elections, though at least one staffer told NPR they got around this. The staffer shared records of their recent trades and spoke to NPR on the condition of anonymity for fear of consequences for their future employment.

Prediction markets for elections are uniquely vulnerable to market manipulation and insider trading, said Rajiv Sethi, an economics professor at Barnard College at Columbia University, who has studied prediction markets for decades.

"[Election prediction markets] have the possibility of being a self-fulfilling prophecy," Sethi said. "Elections have the property that what one believes is going to happen can actually affect what happens if a candidate is thought to be losing momentum or the campaign is flagging."
Bautista said her Polymarket team and surveillance system is learning from past cases and putting their feet in the shoes of would-be insider traders and market manipulators.

"If I was worried about somebody trying to materially move an election market to make it look like one option was more likely to happen than the other and I identify a pattern where they're opening several different accounts and they're doing that in short bursts and I see device IDs consistent across different trades placed in short succession with new wallets across five or four different accounts," Bautista said. "If I were to work that case and then action that, the findings of that tactic go back into the process to create the detections."

As prediction markets have exploded in popularity over the last two years, the industry's federal regulator, the CFTC, has done little to police these new financial markets, largely leaving that work to the companies themselves.

items.title: Democrats still poised to make gains, but poll shows warning signs for just how many
paragraphs: A member of the League of Women Voters of Greater Cleveland helps hold the flag during the national anthem before a basketball game on Oct. 26, 2026 in Cleveland, Ohio. Jason Miller/Getty Images hide caption
📲 Get the latest on the midterms & more in the NPR App

Democrats retain significant midterm electoral advantages, with key data pointing to them being the favorites to win control of the U.S. House. But, there are indications of why a potential wave could be limited, a new NPR/PBS News/Marist poll finds.

The poll also sheds light on the issues driving voters across the ideological spectrum. The cost of living continues to be top of mind overall with a third of people saying they've experienced financial hardship in the past year and 4 in 10 saying their personal finances have gotten worse.

"The economy is at the top of my list right now," said Shun Maurice, a 47-year-old from Arizona who participated in the poll. He's an independent who leans toward Democrats and said high food and gas prices are a strain.
"They're too expensive for everybody, no matter who you voted for," he said. "They're just too expensive for the American people in general, and I don't like that."
Preserving democracy also continues to resonate with Democrats and independents, while immigration is the biggest concern for self-described MAGA supporters.

The poll of 1,289 registered voters was conducted Oct. 19-20. When registered voters are mentioned, the margin of error is +/- 3.7 percentage points. When likely voters are mentioned, it is +/- 3.8 points.

This was the first survey this cycle that Marist applied a likely voter screen, and on multiple questions, likely voters were — within the margin of error — slightly less likely than registered voters to disapprove of the president. Likely voters overall were also slightly less likely to want Democrats to run Congress.

Likely voters are something of a special sauce in polling. Survey researchers apply various metrics — like levels of enthusiasm, past voting history and how important voting is to different respondents — to try to identify the subsample of people who are most likely to vote.

In this survey, just 38% of registered voters approved of the job President Trump is doing, with 61% disapproving (-23). Likely voters gave him a 40% to 59% rating (-19), still not very good, but even a slight margin can make a difference in how significant the gains either party might make in the election are.
That said, an equal share — 53% — of registered and likely voters said they "strongly disapprove" of the job Trump is doing, tied with last month as the highest ever in the poll.
Trump's favorability rating is even lower — just 37% of likely voters have a favorable impression of Trump, while 59% have a negative one.

Democrats also had a strong advantage on which party's candidate people said they are more likely to vote for in their district if the election were held today, known as the generic congressional ballot. Among registered voters, it was a 10-point advantage. With likely voters, it was 8 points, still indicative of Democratic gains.

When Democrats have had that kind of lead on the congressional ballot, they have historically done very well. On average, it was +7 in 2018 and +12 in 2006. In both years, Democrats won the House with at least 30 seats flipped.

But that was before the 2020 Census and ensuing regular redistricting — and the rare, mid-decade redistricting in the last year and a half after Trump asked Republican states to redraw their maps to potentially give Republicans more seats. Though Democrats followed suit, both redistricting periods have tilted congressional seats in Republicans' direction and given them a relative advantage nationally.
Perhaps because of some of those structural disadvantages and past performance, there is a notable degree of nervousness among Democrats.

While 98% of Democratic likely voters said they would vote for a Democrat, just 81% thought the Democrat would win, a 17-point difference. Republicans were only 10 points less likely to believe their candidate would win. Notably, among independents, a higher share thought the Democratic candidate would win.

Working in Democrats' favor — and against incumbents: 55% of likely voters said it's more important in this election to vote for candidates with new ideas who will bring about change. (It was a tick higher with registered voters at 57%.)
Chris Agan, a 43-year-old Democrat in Tyler, Texas, who participated in the survey, never saw himself as an impassioned midterm voter, until this year.

"This year is different. This year, it feels like every opportunity to vote is a referendum against the party in power," said Agan, who's backing Democrat James Talarico over Republican Ken Paxton in the race for U.S. Senate.

"We've been seeing a very slow decline in the standard of living in this state, and it's becoming apparently evident to more people at this time," he added. "I think Talarico embodies that realization that there needs to be change."

Double the percentage of likely voters also said their vote would be one against Trump (44%) as opposed to one for him (21%). In the 2024 presidential election, 55% of those who voted for Trump said their vote was for their candidate, according to exit polls.
Trump is not on the ballot, but he has asked voters to "pretend" he is.

Though Trump's unpopularity poses challenges for Republicans, it may not directly translate to more votes for Democrats. Some swing voters don't like the lurch in some corners of the Democratic Party toward democratic socialism.

Matthew Schroder is a 38-year-old independent living in Charlotte, N.C., who was part of the poll. He backed Joe Biden in 2020 and Trump in 2024. Now, he says that while he's unhappy with Trump's job performance, it isn't what's driving his vote this year.

"What I have seen on the left-hand side is a little bit more of an embrace of democratic socialism, which I just oppose completely," said Schroder, who's supporting Republican Michael Whatley over Democrat Roy Cooper in the state's closely watched race for U.S. Senate.

"I know Roy Cooper is considered a moderate, but the fact that the Democratic Party is even letting some of these voices be heard a little bit more … is not something I'm interested in in the least," he added. "It's not a vote of 'yes for Trump' as much as a vote of, Democrats need to completely reject [democratic socialism] and go a completely different direction."

Democratic likely voters are 10 points more likely to say they are "very enthusiastic" about voting (71% vs. 61%). That's actually wider than the difference between Democratic and Republican registered voters in the poll.
The caution for Democrats, though, is that several of their key pillar groups are not very enthusiastic to vote, and Republicans have closed the gap on who is following the election "very closely."

Just 42% of likely voters under 45, 53% of non-white voters and 56% of white women with college degrees said they are "very enthusiastic" to vote. All of those groups disapproved of the job Trump is doing.
Compare that to pro-Trump groups — MAGA voters (68%), white women without degrees (66%) and white evangelical voters (61%).
For independents, 48% report being very enthusiastic to vote.

Traditionally, younger, as well as Black and Latino voters turn out at disproportionately lower rates in midterm elections. But with the realignment under Trump, more white, college-educated voters are voting Democratic and, as a group, they turn out at the highest rates.
When it comes to paying close attention, last month just 34% of registered Republicans said they're following the election very closely, compared to 42% of Democrats.

Now, they're even – 46% of Democrats and 45% of Republicans said they're paying very close attention. When it comes to likely voters, there's no difference either – 51% of Democrats to 50% of Republicans.

On the positive side for Democrats: those who voted for Democrat Kamala Harris in 2024 are 15 points more likely than Trump 2024 voters to say they are very enthusiastic. And Democrats overall have an 8-point advantage over Republicans when it comes to who cares a "great deal" about who controls Congress.
Three-quarters of likely voters are confident that their state and local governments will run a fair and accurate election.

That includes solid majorities of Democrats (88%), Republicans (68%) and independents (75%), but Republicans were 20 points less likely than Democrats to think they would be run well. MAGA supporters were almost 30 points less likely.

Large majorities also said their preferred candidate should accept the results of the election. That included 70% of Republicans, but again, they were 20 points less likely than Democrats to say they should accept the results. A quarter of Republicans said their candidate should probably or definitely challenge the results.

There was also a sharp divide between those who identified as democratic socialists and MAGA supporters — 86% of democratic socialists but only 65% of MAGA supporters said their preferred candidate should accept the result. MAGA supporters were twice as likely to say they should challenge.

Methodology: This NPR/PBS News/Marist Poll was conducted from Oct. 19-20 and surveyed a national sample of 1,289 registered voters. They were reached through a multi-mode design: by phone, text or online. To create a likely voter sample, Marist applied a likely voter weight to all registered voters. When registered voters are mentioned, the margin of error is +/- 3.7 percentage points. When likely voters are mentioned, it is +/- 3.8 points. That means results fall within a range of roughly eight points – about four points lower or higher.

items.title: How artworks from classic films inspired this matte painter and director
paragraphs: Ian Vicknair is a digital matte painter and art director in the visual effects and game industry. With over ten years of experience, he has contributed to major projects like Justice League, Suicide Squad, Witcher, and Splitgate. Shaped by living globally, he specialises in bringing highly detailed environments to life.

We caught up with him to learn more about his career and influences. If you need to upgrade your own setup for digital art, see our guides to the best drawing tablets and the best laptops for drawing.

Growing up was chaotic; I moved from country to country every few years. In a family of teachers, international schools were our lives – living in places like Ethiopia, Brazil, Saudi Arabia, Lithuania, Russia.
This contributed a lot to my art, especially as a matte painter creating wild environments and as a young art director bringing worlds and stories together.
Truthfully… people. Friends, family, intimate relationships have really added meaning to my work because it’s allowed me to learn and explore who I am and what the world is.

Three specific paintings changed me. The first was the aerial reveal of Neverland in Hook (1991), painted by Yusei Uesugi. Second was the Eloi temple from The Time Machine (1960), painted by Bill Brace.
And finally, the Underground Sea from Journey to the Centre of the Earth (1959), painted by Emil Kosa Jr.

It was for an advertisement firm. I had to digitally paint a farm landscape from the future. It had lots of flying tractors and cities in the sky. This is where I learned the term ‘matte painting’ and fell in love.
Since then, it’s been a constant pursuit to matte-paint as much as I can and where I can.
It was for the Backrooms movie directed by Kane Parsons. There is a huge difference between these paintings and my very first one.
The first had masking issues, colour grade issues, file cleanliness, depth of field problems, stitching errors, noise variations… the list goes on.

Mostly yes. The biggest issue is how volatile the industry is. I’m thankful I’m one of those people who can say their job is what they love. It’s made me a stronger person and continues to allow growth.
Paint more! A younger me didn’t manage life too well. I was very busy figuring out who and what I was and where I belonged. I just wish I had stopped a bit and painted more.

Without a doubt. I adore digital work, especially photorealism because you study how pixels work and fluctuate. It’s made me a stronger painter and VFX artist, and now that I’m into directing, it’s given me a stronger eye.

Halo! I had to paint a Halo jump of Master Chief leaping out of a ship and skydiving down onto the surface of this alien world. It was loads of fun learning how to make planets at that level of detail.
Currently, I’m working on a few IP projects and short films. I’d like to get more into art direction and leading teams and making my own stories. I’ll still be painting, though, as that’s my core.
You can see more of Iain's work on his ArtStation profile. .

items.title: Sir Tom Jones 'truly sorry' as he cancels two shows due to illness
paragraphs: Sir Tom Jones said he is "truly sorry" after rescheduling two forthcoming concerts due to "a bad case of the flu".
The 86-year-old singer from Pontypridd, Rhondda Cynon Taf, is currently on his Come Gather Round world tour.
He announced the decision to push back his Monday show in Los Angeles, and Tuesday's concert in San Diego, following doctor's advice.
In a post on Instagram, he wrote: "Following doctor's advice, I unfortunately have to reschedule tonight's show in Los Angeles and tomorrow's show in San Diego."
The San Diego concert will now take place at The Rady Shell, at Jacobs Park, on 3 November, while his Los Angeles show has been moved to 4 November.

On Instagram, he wrote: "I've had a great time these last few weeks, completing 20 shows and singing for wonderful audiences across the USA, but unexpectedly I've been hit with a bad case of the flu."
He added: "I'm truly sorry for any inconvenience caused. I look forward to seeing you all soon.
"All tickets for the original dates will remain valid. However, if customers are unable to attend the rescheduled dates, they are advised to contact their original point of purchase for a refund."
The post was shared just hours before he was expected to perform at the Greek Theatre, with the Los Angeles venue among those wishing Sir Tom well.
The It's Not Unusual and What's New Pussycat? singer recently made headlines after revealing ITV had "made the decision" to "fire" him from The Voice UK coaching panel.

Sir Tom, who has served as an on-off coach on the popular singing competition since its 2012 debut, shared the news on Instagram last month, amid speculation he had been "dropped" from its 2027 series.
The Delilah and She's A Lady singer has achieved three UK number one singles and four chart-topping albums during a music career spanning more than six decades.
His awards include one Grammy, two Brits and an Ivor Novello; Sir Tom also received a knighthood from the late Queen Elizabeth II in 2006 for his services to music.

items.title: Apple event LIVE: Touchscreen MacBook Pro, iPad mini, iMac and more
paragraphs: Multiple early users of the latest iPhone Duo model have reported faults already. But the most interesting part? There seems to be identical damage occurring, with the screen cracking in one very specific location: a thin crack down the centre hinge, and a line of stuck bright white pixels across the right side of the display.
The cause seems to be an area of concentrated components around the hinge, in a different shape from the rest of the hinge, possibly causing excess stress on the screen, as diagnosed by iFixit.
Would this put you off buying Apple's first foldable?

So, this whole big Apple unveil got me thinking... what cultural role does Apple perform these days? I remember when creatives were inspired by the company's marketing and eager to use its products... and although Apple is still the go-to tech company for many creatives, it seems less about being inspired to use the latest MacBook, and more about about the boring stuff, like how dependable the products are.

Looking at the numbers, financially Apple is a juggernaut, generating record profits and multi-trillion-dollar valuations in 2026. But that's come at the cost of transitioning from revolutionary tastemaker to dumpy conservative. Sure, it still commands loyalty, but it's more geared to managing consumer habits than inventing cool new things.

And really a touchscreen MacBook proves the point. Once dismissed by Steve Jobs as ergonomically unnatural, adopting it today shows Apple to be the pragmatic, market-driven iterator that I wish it wasn't. An Apple touchscreen laptop protects market share and feeds upgrade cycles, which of course is essential... But sadly it proves that modern Apple prioritises commercial efficiency over cultural disruption.
Bring me back to the days of the first iPhone.
A MacBook Air refresh could be coming in early 2027, will we get a tease of that at Apple's LA event?

If you can’t hold out until next year for a new, lighter laptop for creative work then read our guide to the 3 laptops graphic designers should consider, it's a good starting point, and so is our video on whether the MacBook Pro M5 is the best laptop for creatives.
You're here for the Apple rumours about the upcoming LA launch 'experience' kicking off Wednesday at 10 am PT (5 pm UK), so which rumours are leading the pack?

Well, Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, who usually gets these things right, expects 14-inch and 16-inch MacBook Pros with touch-enabled OLED screens, a Dynamic Island instead of the notch, and a lighter build.

Our take? We think so too, as reported in our article when we said Apple’s redesigned MacBook Pro can’t come soon enough. If you’re not sold on OLED for creative work, an OLED MacBook Pro is coming in 2026, but I predict disappointment.
So far, Apple has blessed us with a new iPad mini, but who's this dinky device best suited for?

Naturally, the mini is all about portability. Think of on-the-go professionals who need a travel companion for commuting. It's also a great fit for e-book readers and students who want a compact note-taking device. With its OLED screen and faster A20 Pro chip, it's a nice upgrade from previous models, making it great for cosy solo Netflix nights.
Check out our iPad generations guide to find your perfect match.
While we await anticipated new Apple releases this week, let's take a stroll down memory lane and digest some of the best Apple products ever that already exist (use the arrow to swipe through).
Wait! Who really wants a touchscreen MacBook?

Maybe it's because I never brought iPads into my workflow, but I'm finding it hard to see where this demand is coming from (and presumably, there is demand, if Apple is finally releasing after years of rumour).
As I recall, Apple resisted for so long on ergonomic grounds – and also, why mess with a winning formula?!

But maybe this explains more about where Apple is in 2026 than anything else. Because a move to a touchscreen laptop is clearly an attempt to court and flip users of devices like the Surface Pro, Surface Laptop and Lenovo Yogas, etc.
Or is it because Apple now has to cater to a mobile-first generation who demand touchscreens? Tell us below in the comments!

One of the most strongly rumoured launches for this week’s event is a brand new touchscreen MacBook. This is something Apple has resisted for a long time, and something that Steve Jobs was famously against.

"We've done tons of user testing on [a touchscreen MacBook], he announced on stage at the launch of the iPad in 2010, "and it turns out it doesn't work. Touch surfaces don't want to be vertical. After a short period of time you start to fatigue, and after an extended period of time your arm wants to fall off. It doesn't work, it's ergonomically terrible."

So there we have it. "Ergonomically terrible." "Doesn't work." It seems safe to say Jobs wasn't a fan of the idea in 2010. But what about today? Time will tell if Apple manages to make the whole thing work.
Hello and welcome to Creative Bloq’s live coverage of this week’s Apple announcements! We’re expecting big things this week, but Apple has already announced something little: the new iPad mini.

items.title: "Things start in really simple gestures" says Es Devlin of her Design Museum retrospective
paragraphs: British artist and designer Es Devlin explains how ambitious creative projects begin with simple ideas in this exclusive video interview with Dezeen, filmed at Es Devlin: Other Worlds, her first European retrospective at London’s Design Museum.

“This is literally my favourite project. A book which took me seven years to make and it contains everything I’ve ever made,” Devlin told Dezeen, referring to a companion book created to coincide with the exhibition.
The book, as well as the exhibition, brings together three decades of Devlin’s work across theatre, opera, concert stage design and large-scale public installations.
The exhibition explores how Devlin’s projects develop, from early drawings and models to monumental installations experienced by audiences around the world.
In the interview, she explains how she hopes the presentation will demystify the creative process and encourage visitors to pursue their own ideas.
“I really hope that when people leave this exhibition, they’ll see objects and traces of things which make them say, ‘Oh, I could do that’,” she said.
“It’s not a mystery. It doesn’t come by magic. It comes step by step, with attention, curiosity, work and collaboration.”
The exhibition begins with a replica of Devlin’s studio in Peckham, complete with her books, objects, models, drawings, tools and paints.
“I love visiting other artists and designers’ studios,” she said. “I think it’ll make people feel something about what these rooms feel like, where creativity is allowed to happen at all times.”
From the studio, visitors encounter Come Home Again, Devlin’s installation originally presented outside Tate Modern in 2022.
The original work featured illuminated cut-outs of endangered wildlife arranged within a cross-section of the dome of St Paul’s Cathedral.

Reconfigured beneath a mirrored ceiling for the Design Museum exhibition, it is followed by A 30-Year Desk, a series of concentric circular desks displaying archival objects, drawings and models from across her career.

The archive includes material relating to her designs for the 2018 theatre production The Lehman Trilogy, the Forest of Us installation in Miami and the closing ceremony of the London 2012 Olympic Games, alongside more than 30 models of projects that have previously been exhibited in Britain.
The exhibition culminates in An Infinite Library, an eight-metre-wide rotating sculpture containing more than 2,000 books that have shaped Devlin’s worldview.
The artwork was originally installed on the beachfront of the Faena Beach hotel in Miami Beach and has been reimagined for the Design Museum retrospective.
Arranged in bands of colour above a circular mirror, the books are illuminated by projections and accompanied by recordings of Devlin reading selected passages.

Devlin began her career designing sets for small-scale theatre productions in 1996 before moving into opera, dance and concert stage design. Over the past decade, she has increasingly focused on large-scale public artworks and installations.

For Es Devlin: Other Worlds, she brought together material spanning her career, including childhood experiments and paintings made shortly before the exhibition opened, to reveal the ideas and processes behind her finished projects.

“I began to develop an attitude on how to take things that are amassed in piles and are somewhat overwhelming, to spread them out along a timeline and make them digestible and legible to an audience,” she said.
“Actually, these things that seem huge and overwhelming and complicated, they start in really simple gestures.”
Es Devlin: Other Worlds runs at the Design Museum in London until 4 April 2027.
This video was produced for the Design Museum as part of a partnership. Find out more about our partnership content here.
