items.title: The Atlanta Falcons 'Nazi' logo controversy strikes again
paragraphs: A couple of years back, a throwback Atlanta Falcons logo design was raising eyebrows due to an unfortunate resemblance. Although it was a revival of an old design that the NFL team had used in 1960s, the combination of black on red and the hard stylisation of the bird of prey motif reminded some of the aesthetic of a certain fascist regime from the 1930s.

It seems the team wasn't fazed by the controversy one iota. Two years on, it's doubled down with a remixed design that takes the Third Reich resemblance even further. The memes didn't take long to arrive.
@AtlantaFalcons Please explain how you missed this? https://t.co/noRcZcfBVGOctober 22, 2026
@AtlantaFalcons not a good look, meinami https://t.co/3qv6FNS4L1October 23, 2026

On social media, the Atlanta Falcons' new profile picture has been dubbed the "gridiron cross" and the "Bird Reich". "I read that the NFL wanted to conquer the world but I didn’t think they meant it so literally," one person comments on X.

The logo shows the previously used angular black falcon forming an 'F' shape over red, beige, black and cream vertical stripes. It's presumably intended as a temporary design just for this weekend, as the Falcons will play against the 49ers on Sunday wearing retro 1966-inspired uniforms, comprising red helmets, black jerseys and white pants.

To be fair to the Falcons, Nazi Germany never had a monopoly on birds of prey insignia (nor even the swastika, which had a long history before it was adopted by the Third Reich). The bald eagle is also a familiar piece of US iconography.

But after all the comments and ridicule during the last revival of the 1960s design two years ago, there's no way that the team didn't know what was coming this time around. And the addition of the vertical stripes only makes the resemblance to Nazi iconography more apparent, which it must have realised.

I'd be interested to hear from long-term Falcon fans about whether the same comparison was made when the team originally used this logo back in the 1960s. I guess that in those pre-social media days, people didn't pick apart graphic design in the same way they do today.

Even the best sports logos can generate controversy, and the Falcons logos aren't the most disturbing we've seen. That accolade goes to the old Red Sox logo. Meanwhile, the main Atlanta Falcons logo retains its place in our pick of the best NFL logos.

Joe is a regular freelance journalist and editor at Creative Bloq. He writes news, features and buying guides and keeps track of the best equipment and software for creatives, from video editing programs to monitors and accessories. A veteran news writer and photographer, he now works as a project manager at the London and Buenos Aires-based design, production and branding agency Hermana Creatives. There he manages a team of designers, photographers and video editors who specialise in producing visual content and design assets for the hospitality sector. He also dances Argentine tango.

items.title: How Ben & Jerry's became a beacon of brand bravery
paragraphs: If any brand has become synonymous with activism over the years, it's Ben & Jerry's. From renaming its Chubby Hubby flavour Hubby Hubby to celebrate marriage equality, to campaigning to close a prison in St Louis and using its marketing to challenge racial injustice, the ice cream brand has always found creative ways to turn its values into action.

And the brand's founders, Ben Cohen and Jerry Greenfield, have also participated directly in protests. In April 2016, both were arrested at the US Capitol during the Democracy Awakening demonstrations against the influence of money in politics and restrictions on voting rights. More recently, Cohen was arrested in May 2025 during a US Senate protest over military aid to Israel and the humanitarian crisis in Gaza.

At this year's Paradigms conference in Croatia, in a talk exploring the power of brands to drive social change, chief marketing officer Jay Curley argued that businesses should do more than pay lip service to good causes. For the Vermont ice cream maker, activism is baked into the business, alongside the Cookie Dough.

But what happens when a brand gets it wrong, faces a backlash or risks alienating customers? And how do you choose which causes deserve your voice? We caught up with Curley to discuss why brands should stop sitting on the fence, why perfection shouldn’t stand in the way of progress, and how a little creativity can help change the world.
Peace, Love & Ice Cream | Ben & Jerry's - YouTube

I think traditional businesses are risk-averse. They have a traditional belief that it’s better to stay neutral and avoid polarising issues. For some businesses, that might be the right approach. But I feel that brands that stand for something, and have communities they value and connect with, have to show up. Ultimately, I think it’s a general aversion to risk that keeps businesses out of these issues.

Patagonia does a fantastic job. They’re a big inspiration for us. Lush Cosmetics is another company we’ve always considered a kindred spirit. There are also some less mainstream brands, such as Penzeys Spices in the US. They sell herbs, spices and other ingredients, and they’ve been unapologetically bold in standing up for what matters. I’d argue that this has also helped more people notice them.

Most people who work at Ben & Jerry’s are here specifically because of our values. But there’s no values test, and anyone is welcome to work here, so there are certainly times when people disagree. I think that’s okay.
What we try to do is educate and engage people internally on the issues, so they understand what we’re doing and why. If they still disagree, that’s fine.
It starts with our values, and then we look at where we can have an impact. Where could our presence and energy meaningfully contribute to action?

It’s about looking at our values, identifying emerging social movements that could benefit from what we have to offer, and considering what’s pressing in the world that relates to those values and requires our involvement.
We bring those factors together to decide where to focus. We can’t be everywhere at once, so we try to build campaigns where we believe we can make a meaningful difference.

In a way, even when we don’t get everything right, I usually feel that we did the right thing. It also takes a lot of courage to be imperfect. If we waited until Ben & Jerry’s was perfect in every aspect of racial justice as an organisation, we would never use our voice, because we’re never going to be perfect.

I look back at our Black Lives Matter statement from 2016, and there are things we could ideally have tweaked or expressed better. That said, I think it was really important that we spoke out when we did, rather than waiting until everything was perfect.
I’m grateful that we live in a free country where people can choose what they want to buy.

There are plenty of people who may not be deeply aligned with us on a values level but love Cookie Dough, so they buy it. I think that’s fine. Equally, some people decide not to buy our products, and that’s their choice.
My hope is that those people understand what we’re doing and why. If they decide Ben & Jerry’s isn’t for them, that’s fine with us.

Daniel John is Design Editor at Creative Bloq. He reports on the worlds of design, branding and lifestyle tech, and has covered several industry events including Milan Design Week, OFFF Barcelona and Adobe Max in Los Angeles. He has interviewed leaders and designers at brands including Apple, Microsoft and Adobe. Daniel's debut book of short stories and poems was published in 2018, and his comedy newsletter is a Substack Bestseller.

items.title: AI found the flaw. Hackers found the leak: The race to save 'PHP2SHELL'
paragraphs: AI discovered a vulnerability in part of the internet's architecture, called PHP2SHELL. Security researchers rushed to fix it, but news of the vulnerability leaked and hackers have swooped in.

items.title: 6 niche horror posters that are sharper than the originals
paragraphs: Halloween is approaching, which means it's officially scary movie season. But while there are endless stunning horror movie posters out there, sometimes the best aren't necessarily the official designs.

I'm here to argue that variant designs and fan posters are where it's at if you're looking for elite horror movie poster design. Among the recent sludge of formulaic black-and-red horror flick designs, consider these stunning designs your official spooky season palette cleanser.

Created by graphic designer and illustrator Grzegorz Domaradzki (a.k.a. Gabz), this Japanese variant poster for 'An American Werewolf in London' puts a dramatic spin on the minimalist original. Created in 2021, the intricate design is based on a pencil drawing and remastered in Adobe Photoshop. With ferocious illustration in spine-chilling detail, it's a prime example of how straying from minimalist design can bring a film to life.

A contemporary take on Terence Fisher's 1958 Dracula, this limited edition poster is a wonderful homage to Hammer's most iconic release. Created by legendary Swedish illustrator Robert Sammelin, the design captures the terror of the horror classic with bold freehand linework and hazy visuals that blur the line between dreams and nightmares.

Created as part of a limited edition run of custom hand-pulled silkscreen prints, this minimalist take on The Shining's iconic poster demonstrates how Kubrick's iconic cinematography has stood the test of time. Created by Inkcandy, the poster series is inspired by the 'Italian shot', taking its name from Sergio Leone's Italian-Western films – a cinematic trope featuring extreme close-ups of the eyes.

Commissioned by Pearl's Japanese distributor, Happinet Phantom Studios, this stunning poster created by Japanese artist Yuko Higuchi puts a soft, folk art spin on the film. Known for her surreal paintings and dreamlike illustrations, this gentle take on Pearl is a beautiful contrast to the film's violent horror.

Created by award-winning and published Illustrator Matt Ryan Tobin, this stunning illustrated poster for A24's Talk to Me pairs claustrophobic visuals with a stripped-back palette to create a wonderfully stylised design. The design earned high praise, seeing Tobin awarded a 2024 SILVER Clio.

This alternative poster for Ridley Scott's 1979 Alien is a beautifully frightening take on the iconic original design. Created by movie poster artist Dom Bittner, the hand-painted poster brings a whimsical quality to the classic horror – a wonderful contrast to the minimalist design of the franchise's posters.

Natalie Fear is Creative Bloq's staff writer. With an eye for trending topics and a passion for internet culture, she brings you the latest in art and design news. Natalie also runs Creative Bloq’s 5 Questions series, spotlighting diverse talent across the creative industries. Outside of work, she loves all things literature and music (although she’s partial to a spot of TikTok brain rot).

items.title: Cloud House by Peter Morris brings "fairytale flamboyance" to London
paragraphs: Marshmallow-pink walls, sweeping arches and turquoise detailing influenced by a trip to Miami animate architect Peter Morris‘s self-designed home in Gospel Oak, London.
Named Cloud House, the eccentric project combines two offset residences, one for Morris and his partner, producer Emily Kennedy, and a second for a neighbour who shares their love of colour.
According to the architect, the goal of the project was to bring joy to passersby, while giving his “love of postmodernism a chance to reveal itself fully”.
“The key goal was to make a beautiful building which I hoped might create a little moment of joy for anyone walking past it on the street,” Morris told Dezeen.

“It’s easy to dismiss colour and pattern in architecture as frivolous, but there’s something about this visual language that triggers an emotional response that’s different from what you’ll get with elegant modernism,” continued Morris.

“For me, that alone tells us we should push for more variety in the built environment and be open – as Camden Council have been with this project – to the idea of more fairytale flamboyance on our streets,” he continued.
Cloud House occupies the site of a now-demolished Victorian home, adjacent to a distinctive church and school, where the couple have lived since 2016.
Its bold colour palette and cloud-like forms were inspired by the couple’s honeymoon in Miami and the city’s vast collection of art deco architecture.

“Emily and I honeymooned in Miami, where we loved the art deco curves of the buildings, and the pink and turquoise colours everywhere,” Morris explained. “In a way this building is an architectural love letter to my wife, so it felt appropriate to have some of that honeymoon spirit in the mix.”

According to Morris, the project also draws on the curved forms of the neighbouring Grade II-listed school and Grade I-listed St Martin’s Church, which Morris said are “fabulously eccentric buildings”.
“The school, which sits in St Martin’s Hall, has a frontage that looks like a Medieval castle,” he said.

“And the church – described by the historian Nikolaus Pevsner as ‘the craziest of London’s Victorian churches’ – has a knock-out interior, with a brightly coloured chancel ceiling and a nave with dramatic wooden arches.”
Cloud House’s main structure is composed of structural steel and blockwork.

This is clad in decorative arches made of polystyrene, sprayed with a waterproof layer and a textured top coat to match the bright pink render on the elevations, and positioned in place by the architect himself.
Morris’s home is the smaller of the pair, located on the right side of the plot. It measures 133 square metres.
The home is accessed from an entrance on its front elevation. It has a large, open-plan ground floor, comprising a lounge, kitchen and the architect’s studio.
Its two upper floors are each fitted with a bedroom and bathroom, while a roof terrace crowns the home, complete with an outdoor bathtub.
Next door, the adjoining 165-square-metre home is accessed by a side entrance and has an upside-down arrangement.
Its ground floor contains a home office with a kitchenette, and a guest ensuite bedroom at the rear. Above is the main bedroom.
The main bedroom has a dressing room and ensuite, and sits alongside another smaller ensuite bedroom.
Meanwhile, the social space with seating, dining and cooking spaces is on the top floor, with an adjoining terrace. A second larger terrace tops the home.
While the interiors of Morris’s house boldly match its vibrant exterior, the interiors for the neighbour’s home were left blank and ready for them to customise.
Interior highlights of the architect’s home include turquoise epoxy floors, colour-drenched bathrooms and an emerald-green striped kitchen.
Cloud House was featured on the TV show Grand Designs in September and has been shared widely on social media. Morris said the response to the project is sharply divided.

“I know that not everyone will love the Cloud House as much as we do – the reactions to it on social media have been either overwhelmingly positive or overwhelmingly negative, with nothing in between,” he reflected.
“My final goal, and hope, is that some of the people that do love it might one day be keen to commission me to create something colourful and joyful for them too.”
Other pink dwellings featured on Dezeen include a concrete “fun house” on the English coast by RX Architects and a guesthouse in the Azores contained within a converted stable.

items.title: Seven projects by RIBA award-winning Nakshabid Architects
paragraphs: Who is RIBA International Prize winner Nakshabid Architects? In this roundup, we get to know the Dhaka-based studio through seven of its key projects spanning Bangladesh.

Founded by Bayejid Khondoker in 2003, Nakshabid Architects’ extensive portfolio is concentrated in Bangladesh and encompasses both public and private projects – from residential blocks to mosques and museums.

Last week saw the studio’s Green Field Factory named the fifth winner of the biennial award, presented by the Royal Institute of British Architects (RIBA) to the world’s best new building outside the UK.

Praised for its focus on passive design principles and the prioritisation of employee wellbeing, the studio considers its latest award to be a recognition of Bangladesh’s architectural contributions at a global scale.
“We see the prize as a recognition of what architecture from Bangladesh can contribute to global conversations on climate and the dignity of labour,” the studio told Dezeen.

Alongside the award-winning Green Field Factory, recent projects undertaken by the 20-person studio include the government-commissioned renovation of the Bangladesh Military Museum in Dhaka, which reached completion in 2022 with a glass geodesic dome.
Central to its architectural approach, the studio said, is forging connections between a building and its “socio-ecological context” in a bid to reframe functional programmes as places of gathering.
“We believe that architecture must respond directly to its socio-ecological context, transforming ordinary programmes into meaningful collective experiences,” the studio said.
“We approach every project as a shared undertaking, listening closely to the people who will use it, the climate it sits in and the building traditions around it before we draw,” it continued.
“In this way even the most functional programmes become places of gathering, where light, air, landscape and everyday social life are woven into the architecture itself.”
Read on for a look at seven of the studio’s key projects:
The Green Field Factory, a rug factory in Rangpur, was designed by Nakshabid Architects to dismantle workplace hierarchies and is the fifth winner of the RIBA International Prize.
Fronted by a monumental green facade, the seven-storey building was informed by the traditional Bengali home, incorporating natural ventilation and biophilic design principles.
A pair of intersecting arches form an “invisible dome” that frames the interior of Aman Mosque, a cubic prayer hall completed by the studio in Narayanganj.
Set within a sunken circular courtyard, the mosque is defined by its solid concrete volume, which is adorned with triangular perforations that filter light into the space.
A concrete facade punctuated with square openings was designed to limit heat gain and control daylight access at the Shaptak Insignia apartment tower in Dhaka.
Comprising two blocks, the residential block contains 18 units on a 670-square-metre plot, with each apartment complete with a balcony and a stepped terrace.
A pair of slender, red-brick residential towers make up the studio’s Urban Legacy project in Dhaka.
Its jagged form is defined by cantilevered balconies, which are enclosed by horizontal louvres and complete with greenery intended to shade and cool the apartment interiors.
“Cascading vines and planters spill from every terrace and the brick-walled garden base, turning the building into a vertical green landscape,” the studio said.
Aman Cement Factory Mosque, Sirajganj, 2022
An arched entrance guides visitors beyond the tiered brick exterior of the Ullapara Mosque, which Nakshabid Architects completed on the grounds of a cement factory for its workers.
Spread across two storeys, the mosque was built using locally-sourced brick, concrete and glass in a bid to blend “tradition with modernity”.
“[The mosque] has become a place where factory workers and neighbours gather for prayer, social events and community life,” the studio said.
Looking to redefine museum culture in Bangladesh, Nakshabid Architects conceptualised its design for the Bangladesh Military Museum in Dhaka as a “vibrant civic destination”.
Its curving concrete structure contains cafes, galleries, an amphitheatre and an arena, which is sheltered by a 120-feet glass geodesic dome.
Nakshabid Architects intended for the Nurpur Graveyard, a Muslim graveyard in Rangpur, to also offer a place of leisure for the local community.
To do this, the site accommodates a healthcare facility and an education space – or madrasa – with future expansions expected to include a mosque.
“Nurpur Graveyard is a place that diminishes the typical boundaries of graveyards,” the studio said.

items.title: A censored library logo design just took the war on woke to a new level of weird
paragraphs: The weird 'war on woke' being waged in the US has already claimed some high-profile design victims. The most famous examples have been the Cracker Barrel rebrand, which was deemed too modern for conservatives, and the US State Department's use of the famously liberal typeface Calibri.

Several brands have held their nerve in the face of the onslaught. Mars refused to entertain Tucker Carlson's fetish for the green M&M, the Jaguar rebrand is starting to make sense, and Bob's Red Mill seems to be sticking to its decision to 'kill off' Bob.

Alas, it seems a library in North Carolina didn't have such guts. Farmville Public Library has reportedly ditched the logo design it had been using for the past 14 years because three people complained that it looked a little bit like a rainbow, which apparently reminded them of gay people.

THESE PEOPLE HAVE LOST THEIR MINDS!!! For 14 years, the Farmville Public Library's logo was an open book with each page in a different color. Now it's gone. Three residents complained that it "resembled a rainbow" and might suggest support for LGBTQ+ people. https://t.co/09sYGqk7jtOctober 23, 2026

According to Farmville mayor Alex Joyner, the town's library changed its logo after three complaints were made to a town commissioner. I won't comment on the choice of typeface, but the mark itself was perfectly serviceable for a public library: it was cheerful, it stood out, and it obviously depicted a book rather than a weapon of LGBT propaganda.

The mayor himself has taken issue with the decision. He pointed out that the iconic television series Reading Rainbow had made said climatic phenomenon a “significant symbol of libraries across the entire US”. He also complained that the logo was changed “in the dead of night behind a curtain” with no opportunity for public comment.

“The library is a symbol of inclusion and is supposed to be welcome to all. For a handful of people to be able to decide who is welcomed and who is not here is unacceptable in my eyes,” he said, as reported by ABC.

I'd also point out that the logo's seven colours don't even depict a rainbow and aren't the same colours as the pride flag. It's clearly an open book, with each colour depicting a different page. It's a nice way to show that books can contain a wide array of knowledge on diverse subject matters, like how colours are used to depict different subjects in Trivial Pursuit. Although admittedly, Trivial Pursuit is very woke.

The culture war, it seems, has now become a war on colour. Next, we'll be banning box sets of the best coloured pencils. Apple's iconic rainbow logo would never be allowed today, and I'd be surprised if Google doesn't soon receive complaints too: it's workmark contains red, yellow, green and blue. At this rate, everyone is going to have to dress in black, and any splash of colour will become the ultimate act of rebellion.
A public meeting to discuss he logo controversy will be held at Farmville Town Hall on 2 November at 5:30pm.

items.title: "Nobody has it figured out, and that’s the point": Radim Malinic on the power of creative risk
paragraphs: The confidence to be daring is a hurdle that many creatives will grapple with throughout their career, but for Radim Malinic it's an innate power that we all possess. In his latest book ‘Daring Forever’, the creative director and bestselling author dissects the human capacity for courage, curiosity and creativity, and the power it can hold.

From branding books to mindful practice guides, Radim's bestselling works have inspired creatives across the globe with his practical yet inspirational words. Yet another valuable curation of his industry knowledge, Daring Forever is a wonderfully human take on creative empowerment.

"‘Daring Forever’ begins at the edge of something – a blank page, a stage, a life we haven’t quite stepped fully into yet," the press release reads. "The rope feels unattached. The drop looks real. And still, something in us leans forward. The book is a love letter to that lean: to the body that carries us further than we believe it can, to the self we are still learning to accept, to the curiosity that refuses to sit still, and to the gratitude that brings us home to the present."

"After years of interviewing remarkable people, I noticed the same pattern. The ones doing the most daring work were often the most afraid. Nobody has it figured out, and that’s the point," Radim explains. “Your body is the vehicle, and you’re the driver. Most of us were never given the owner’s manual. This book is my attempt to write one.”
“Daring isn’t a personality trait reserved for the fearless. It’s a human capacity we all carry, and it’s never too late to use it,” he concludes.
Daring Forever is now available on Amazon in paperback, Kindle and audiobook form.

items.title: This week we launched the new Dezeen website
paragraphs: This week on Dezeen, we unveiled the updated Dezeen website, which is “richer and more versatile” while better reflecting what Dezeen is today.

We worked with creative technology studio Made by On to refresh the look and feel of the site, building upon the foundation laid by designer Micha Weidmann, who designed the original Dezeen logo and layout. It is the first time the Dezeen website has been since 2016, after originally being launched as a basic WordPress blog by our founder Marcus Fairs in 2006.
“The new website is faster, richer and, we hope, more enjoyable to use,” Dezeen co-CEO Ben Hobson said. “It also better reflects what Dezeen is today.”
In China, international studio Snøhetta unveiled the landmark Shanghai Grand Opera House this week, which it designed to be “as much a civic destination as a performance venue”.
The striking building features a giant spiral staircase that guides visitors to the roof.

The historic town hall in the city of Limoges in France was set on fire, as an estimated 550,000 people in France took to the streets over the weekend to protest the rising cost of living and poor school conditions.
The fire destroyed significant parts of the 143-year-old Limoges Town Hall, with videos showing its slate roofs ablaze and its central bell tower collapsing.

Also in France, architecture studio OMA unveiled the Palais de Justice de Lille, a law court in northern France. The six-sided building has a pointy, hexagonal form, with each elevation finished in coloured glass.
It was designed to mimic a nearby star-shaped fortification, built in 1667 by the French military engineer Sébastien Le Prestre de Vauban.

Design Miami.Paris took place in Paris this week, with technology brand Apple unveiling its Designers of Tomorrow. Among the pieces on show were a banana-palm-paper lantern and furniture with an acid-etched stainless-steel surface.
We also visited Dutch Design Week, which featured an installation that explored “hydrofeminism” and saw students protest against overcrowded workspaces.
Popular projects on Dezeen this week include a David Chipperfield museum for a single artwork, architect Diana Kellogg’s update of her Tribeca home and a textured home in Mexico.
Our podcast this week asked: has Tesla really made a flying car?
This week on Dezeen is our regular roundup of the week’s top news stories. Subscribe to our newsletters to be sure you don’t miss anything.

items.title: UK to invest £100m in 'world first' AI Biosecurity Lab
paragraphs: The UK says it will establish a national AI Biosecurity Lab (AIBL) to help strengthen its defences against emerging biological threats.
As part of Wednesday's Budget, the government will commit £100m to establishing the new, "world first" institute with the support of leading AI firms.
The chancellor will also pledge millions of pounds in spending across a range of initiatives aimed at shoring up the UK's ability to respond to evolving cyber, biological and AI-enabled threats.
"AI will transform daily life: every firm, community, hospital, school, and every aspect of our economy can benefit," John Healey said.
"I understand and share the concerns of working people, so I am setting out a distinctively British approach to AI.
"One that doesn't leave workers behind and defends our national interest, while ensuring the benefits of AI-enabled growth are felt right across the country."
The full details about the role and remit of the new lab are yet to emerge.

But the AI Minister Kanishka Narayan said it would be a "major new global institution" that brings together "world-leading scientific expertise" to ensure the UK can safeguard its citizens and goals as AI develops.
"That means staying ahead of emerging threats, from cyber attacks to biological risks, while building more of the critical technology our security depends on," he said.
"By backing British science, advanced chips and our own AI companies, we can strengthen our national security, rebuild Britain's industrial strength and create good, skilled jobs across the country."
The AI Biosecurity Lab's creation will also be supported by leading AI developers, with OpenAI and Anthropic providing £200m worth of AI model credits that can be spent on the use of their models.
The Chancellor's plans to boost AI spending will also see an additional £120m committed to the UK's AI Security Institute (AISI).

Established by the former Conservative government in 2023, the lab evaluates the risks of the most advanced and powerful models - and has been championed for its role in helping build a collaborative and open approach to AI testing.

The additional funding announced by the Chancellor will aim to help ensure the lab can continue its efforts and work, particularly amid growing calls for technical standards and guardrails for AI development.

It will come alongside a £60m investment in what it coined a "National Cyber Shield" which it said would use agentic AI to boost cyber-defences, and £70m funding towards a National Exposure and Real-Time Vulnerability (NERV) Centre.
This, it said, would harness AI tools to detect cyber vulnerabilities across the UK's critical infrastructure and economy.

It comes after the UK government revealed it was among organisations around the world to have taken some sites offline as a precaution after critical flaws were surfaced in a popular programming language.

Researchers who helped surface the vulnerabilities in PHP - a popular server-side scripting language used in web development for decades - warned platforms which use it could be exposed to potential hacks.
There have been no reports of any successful exploits of the flaw, coined php2shell, so far.
But experts have warned that the incident shows how quickly and easily bugs which have lain long dormant may be surfaced - and potentially exploited - using AI.

items.title: Strictly's new presenters - after frosty reviews have they warmed up?
paragraphs: Josh Widdicombe, Emma Willis and Johannes Radebe have adapted Tess Daly and Claudia Winkleman's "keep dancing" move for three

Strictly Come Dancing's new hosting trio received a very mixed reception when the latest series began a month ago. Ratings have dipped and the jury's still out, but critics say they are slowly getting into the groove.
Changing the hosting team on the BBC's flagship Saturday night entertainment show was never likely to be a waltz in the park.
And going from two presenters to three, and giving them slightly different roles, upset the show's rhythm even more.
Tess Daly and Claudia Winkleman were always going to be a hard act to follow.

Into their sparkly shoes have stepped the safe and smooth Emma Willis; the flamboyant former professional dancer Johannes Radebe; and cheeky comedian Josh Widdicombe, a wildcard who was not hitherto associated with either the dance world or prime-time TV.
Willis and Widdicombe have been paired on the live shows, where he is tasked with injecting humour into the moments before and after each dance - with mixed results, say critics.
Radebe, meanwhile, has taken over from Winkleman upstairs on the mezzanine, bringing his warmth and dance expertise to the celebrity interviews following each routine.
The new hosts joined the judges on the dance floor when the series began
After they made their debuts in September, the Times' Carol Midgley billed them as, external "TV's most awkward ménage à trois".
The Daily Telegraph's Chris Bennion declared, external that Strictly's "new 'throuple' is an utter disaster", adding: "It's a mess, a muddle, a confusing pudding".
Widdicombe has come in for particular flack. He "felt like an awkward spare part" and looked like "the work experience boy", wrote Sasha Morris of the Daily Express, external.
And the Independent's Isobel Lewis said, external Widdicombe "is a problem the show needs to solve".
She believes things have now improved, although the show hasn't completely solved the problem.
"He's basically acting too much like a comedian to be a presenter," the freelance culture journalist tells BBC News.

"I think he's getting more comfortable with it. When it's him and Emma doing the bits when they intro each act, and they're obviously reading off an autocue, they feel way more confident there, and it feels more like it works."
Widdicombe has been at the centre of comic sketches with the other hosts and judges
The problem grows when Widdicombe does what comes naturally as a good comedian, Lewis says, and tries to be spontaneous.
"They've got, like, 20 seconds with each judge. It's such a tight amount of time, and that's what lends it to feeling sloppy and like he's constantly jumping in.

"Unfortunately it reads a bit like trying to steal attention and have the last laugh. I actually don't think that is what he's trying to do as a selfish act. I just think that is his comedic impulse."
She says it's unfair to put the criticism on Widdicombe, and says as time has gone on he feels less awkward, with comments online suggesting some fans are "warming to him".
"But at the beginning there's always that knee-jerk reaction of, 'I don't like this'," Lewis says.
Emma Willis has hosted shows including Big Brother and The Voice
Radio Times TV and podcast editor Caroline Frost agrees that the trio have gradually settled in.
"I think it's fair to say there were some bumps in the road in the first couple of episodes," she says, "but they do appear to be very slowly relaxing into their new roles."
When it comes to Willis and Widdicombe's double act, Frost would like to see more spontaneity, not less.
"They've been relying quite visibly on scripts and gags, and I would like to see them relax into themselves," she adds.

"It's completely understandable that they would be very scripted, very alert to the clock and to all of the other many demands of running a live show of that scale - but the really talented people can do that on the fly.

"Josh is very likeable, and we know he's a very funny man," she notes. "He doesn't need the shackles of the script that he's currently handcuffed to, and I would love to see him take off those cuffs and become more spontaneous."
One episode featured Widdicombe and Willis in a Mary Poppins-inspired sketch

Frost suggests sending Widdicombe upstairs to conduct the post-dance interviews instead of Radebe, who at times struggles to control his exuberant former fellow dancers. "It's a bit like when you get an internal promotion at work," she reflects.
The producers should make the most of Radebe's strengths and make him "a sort of talent pundit", she suggests.
"Have him in the rehearsal rooms, telling us what's going on. He would be a lovely middleman between what we're seeing on the dance floor and what is going on technically."
Ahead of the series, there had been reports that Radebe would be used as a "roving reporter".
Widdicombe previously suggested the trio's roles would be fluid, telling The Rest Is Entertainment it was "going to be like total football... We're going to be moving everywhere".
Radebe has already gained a reputation for his flamboyant fashion
But while some segments are flexible - especially in the Sunday result show - their main roles appear fixed.
Some fans have been won over by Radebe since he took over Winkleman's old domain.
"JoJo has been really brilliant up in... I guess the Claudatorium, but I'm not sure what we call it now," says Flo Sayers, co-host of the Strictly on the Sofa podcast.

"He is the link to previous Strictly, and I think he has taken to that role really well. I like that he's a bit different from Claudia. He's less the comedian and more the supportive friend for the contestants when they've got off the dance floor and they're probably feeling a little bit vulnerable.
"And his fashion has been amazing, so I'm excited to see what he wears every week."
Sayers isn't sure whether the new line-up has contributed to lower ratings - about six million people are tuning in every week this year, down by about a million.
But overall, she believes that the trio are getting used to the demands of the series.
The presenting trio watched on as Dame Sarah Storey and dance partner Julian Caillon were eliminated last weekend
Dr Karen Wood, associate professor at the Centre for Dance Research at Coventry University, agrees and says the trio "are now really starting to feel a bit more settled".
"I think JoJo has transitioned beautifully from professional dancer to host, and obviously he comes with all his fabulousness," she says.

"He's able to talk about the technical details as well as be very supportive to the professional dancers and the celebrities. And his outfits are just marvellous. So I think he suits that role very well.
"Likewise, Emma is holding her own when she's with Josh and when she's not. She's an experienced presenter. You can you can tell.
"And Josh is bringing the humour. I know it's come with some criticism. But last week was the first week that I felt, oh, these two are actually funny."
She concludes: "It's really feeling like they're finding their stride and their rhythm with it. And I think that's going to develop more and more - very much as the celebrities do."
Just as the show's celebrity contestants improve week by week, the same may be true of the hosts - except viewers can't vote them off if they don't like them.
The next episode of Strictly Come Dancing airs on BBC One at 18:30 BST on Saturday.

items.title: Celebrity Traitors left on a knife edge after a trip to the field of screams
paragraphs: Spoiler warning: This article reveals details from episode eight of The Celebrity Traitors, series two.
Original Celebrity Traitor Maya Jama, latest recruit King Kenny and now even the reluctant James Acaster - hurrah! - have developed a real appetite for murder this week.

And going into Friday's episode we knew that their collective cruel intention was to see that one of three faithfuls, Miranda Hart, Romesh Ranganathan or Sebastian "Bash" Croft, did not make it to breakfast.
When it became clear that the murdered Miranda had danced her last dance in the castle - leaving only 10 of the initial 21 players - the pressure began to mount and speculation was rife.
The self-declared Miss Marple wannabe had been stitched up, of course. "Miranda is a good detective," noted James A in a flashback to the turret talk from the night before.
"I don't know who I'm becoming," responded Maya - who has taken to treachery like a duck to water - "but I feel it in my loins, and Miranda is the only one that makes sense."
Miranda, who had been in her element sleuthing away on the show, did not take the news of her untimely death at all well, throwing her murder note to the ground. "No! Absolutely not," she cried.

"I'm so cross with myself, I was wholly focusing on my Joanne issue," she added, with reference to her theory about Joanne McNally being a traitor. One that even Miranda herself had - unwisely - "debunked" at the roundtable.

Ending on a more positive note, the comedian, who has had health issues in recent years, reflected: "Ultimately, in my little personal story, this has been quite extraordinary that I've been able to get back and do the thing that I love professionally and do the things that I love personally.
"Like wandering around a Scottish island and being in nature and laughing and connecting. There were times that I didn't think that would be possible again".
With Miss Marple now out of the picture, James A told viewers that two of the remaining traitor hunters, James Blunt and Michael Sheen are like "Holmes and Watson".
"Luckily they're completely looking in all the wrong places," he added.
Leigh-Anne, having lost her new Big Mix dance partner from episode six, said she was now praying that the heat on her would now cool down.

While Miranda was being murdered on Thursday night, out in the real world another Little Mix star Jade Thirlwell told BBC News - at the Mercury prize ceremony - that her groupmate was a real life "faithful through and through".
Those kind words would be worth little if the now nicely positioned traitors kept going at this rate, however.
"This is actually embarrassing," declared comedian Romesh at breakfast.
"We are getting battered," a sneaky Maya agreed. "This is just getting harder and harder by the second."
Breaking character in the safety of the diary room, the Gentleman actress and presenter admitted: "I'm not gonna lie, I feel terrible about Miranda, I really do and she will be sorely missed.
"But with great honour comes great pressure, and here I am, "OG Traits", still flying it up."
Joanne had earlier joked that Maya would not be killed or banished as "she's too hot. The hot ones always survive."
After breakfast, James B, who has been pretty consistently wrong with his theories throughout the series, continued his fine form, saying of Maya and Kenny: "I think they are the two most innocent."
He joked (it was a joke, right?): "Watching me in this castle must be like watching Sherlock at work."
With less heat on her than Christmas Day in Blackpool, Maya started planting a seed that roundtable "chief investigator" Michael Sheen might be up to something.
"How has that guy not been killed?" asked Romesh.
"It's like not getting rid of [Hercule] Poirot," he added, as the literary detective references kept coming.
Michael and Sharon - fast becoming a dark horse with her theory about Ross Kemp having been killed with perfume - said she was determined to catch a traitor and would "not be taking any prisoners".
On to Friday's mission, as the dwindling group arrived in a "field of screams", as presenter Claudia Winkleman aptly put it, full of scary-looking scarecrows.
"This is like the Wickerman," said Joanne. "A solo scarecrow is sinister enough. A gaggle of scarecrows is terrifying."
The task involved them attempting to retrieve bags of gold from inside the straw men with a pitchfork, in a bid to add thousands of pounds to the charity prize pot.
Joanne's knot-tying badge she claimed to have been awarded in her youth didn't seem to help her much, though, as she struggled initially to grab any gold.
"I have a newfound respect for the farming community," she declared.

But it wasn't only gold on offer, it transpired. An as-yet unrevealed game-changing power would be bestowed upon one player, but only after they had to blow up the proxy pumpkin scarecrow heads of all but three of the most trustworthy contestants.
Things got a bit awkward when poor Sharon "got so mad at the boys" - James B, Michael and Kenny - over which heads should roll.
In the most remarkably stupid moment of the series since Richard E Grant told everyone he was a traitor, the group chose to preserve the heads belonging to Maya, James A and Kenny.

"I had to hold in my laughter," said Maya, privately afterwards. "Of all people, you saved us. I just thought, 'oh my gosh, have we completed this game already? We are trusting. We are unsuspecting. We are killing you all'."
With the others en route back to the castle, Winkleman quipped to the traitors: "This is like an outdoor turret."
The special power was revealed to be a double dagger, enabling one of "the trustworthy trio", as James A is now calling them, to have two votes at the night's roundtable.
King Kenny became King Arthur being crowned keeper of the special blade.
"I think it's in the right hands," declared James B back at the castle, now colder than ever in terms of catching a traitor.
"I feel like whoever it is, they are five sets ahead of us," noted a befuddled Leigh-Anne. "We don't have a clue!"
Romesh then had to remind Joanne that her policy of not voting off Michael because he's "great company" is not really how the game should work.
With the double dagger in play and time running out for the faithful, Michael declared that he had to catch a traitor tonight.
Watch on iPlayer with new episodes every Thursday and Friday
The latest banished and murdered celebs have their say in Uncloaked
As discussions began, double trouble Kenny warned: "Be nice to me everyone!"
Bash, who had flown under the radar until this point, drew some heat along with Leigh-Anne and Sharon at another roundtable led my Don Michael.
"If you're a faithful, why are you still here?" Bash asked the Welshman, who noted he had a shield last time out.

Romesh agreed: "I definitely would have killed you by now if I was a traitor. And I mean that as a massive compliment, because I think, for the morale of the group, you not being here would decimate us."
In an attempt to deflect attention away from himself, Michael stressed how Sharon had been acting like a "totally different person" of late.
Kenny bought it, sticking his double dagger into the Barbie actress. And James B voted the same way due to her "suspicious" actions earlier on.
Scotswoman Sharon received four votes, along with Irish comic Joanne, meaning that - after desperate final pleas from the pair - it went to second round.
"Do whatever youse want, it's a game," offered a seemingly defeated Sharon.
"I wish I didn't take this dagger," said Kenny, ahead of his decisive second thrust of the double blade. "But I'm gonna vote for..."
The producers then left things, quite literally, on a knife edge.
Ten contestant remain (for now): seven faithfuls (soon to be six) and three traitors, putting the cloaked interlopers in a great position going into the final two episodes.
With the hurly-burly done for another week, we will wait with baited breath until Hallowe'en's double header to see how the battle will be lost and won.

items.title: Mobile internet tariffs in Iran rise by 40%
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Persian article.

Iranian mobile operators MCI and Irancell have announced increases of up to 40% in the tariffs for calls, text messages, and mobile internet packages, as the government continues to impose restrictions on internet access.
The companies said in separate statements on Friday that the new rates would take effect at midnight on October 23.
Irancell has also increased the prices of its fixed internet and fiber-optic services by the same amount.
According to the operators, internet packages purchased before the new rates took effect will remain valid at their original prices until their expiration dates.
The sharp increase in internet costs comes as the Iranian government continues to impose widespread censorship and restrictions on internet access.

In its annual Freedom on the Net 2026 report, U.S.-based nonprofit Freedom House gave Iran just 9 points out of 100, placing it alongside China and Myanmar among the world’s worst countries for internet freedom.
The report said Iran experienced the steepest decline in internet freedom among the 38 countries assessed.
During the suppression of nationwide protests in January 2026, Iran almost completely shut down internet access across the country for 20 days.

In February, coinciding with the start of the joint U.S. and Israeli military operation, the government imposed another nationwide restriction on internet access that lasted approximately 88 days. The measure was described as the longest nationwide internet shutdown in Iran’s history.

Freedom House also warned that the Iranian government has turned the country’s internet into a “two-tier” system in which most citizens are denied unrestricted access to the global internet, while a limited group retains that access.

The organization also cited disruptions to Starlink satellite communications, restrictions on virtual private networks (VPNs), and the arrest of internet users. It noted that internet freedom worldwide had declined for the 16th consecutive year.

Earlier, the deputy political commander of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) claimed that if Iran's infrastructure were targeted, internet cables beneath the Strait of Hormuz would not be safe.

The International Cable Protection Committee said five active cable segments belonging to submarine cable systems pass through the strait, a route that carries less than 1% of the world’s international bandwidth.
According to the committee, damage to these cables would primarily disrupt regional communications.

items.title: Afghanistan-Pakistan trade declines sharply as border crossings remain closed
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Dari article.
Trade between Afghanistan and Pakistan has declined sharply amid rising tensions between the neighboring countries and the continued closure of border crossings.
Mohammad Younus Mohmand, Vice President of the Afghan Chapter of the Pakistan-Afghanistan Joint Chamber of Commerce and Industry, said that the bilateral trade has fallen by about 95 percent.
“We no longer have trade with Pakistan. Our transit via Pakistan and Pakistan’s transit via Afghanistan to Central Asia have come to a complete halt,” Mohmand said.

Pakistani newspaper Dawn reported Monday that the figures released by the Trade Development Authority of Pakistan in August showed that bilateral trade between the two neighboring countries fell 95 percent in 2026-27 compared with the previous year.
The TDAP also reported that bilateral trade fell to $358 million in fiscal year 2025-26, down from $1.3 billion in fiscal year 2024-25, a decrease of about 74 percent.
Pakistan closed the main border crossings with Afghanistan on Oct. 12, 2025, after deadly clashes between the Pakistani forces and the Afghan Taliban.
In September, Pakistani government said that it was ready to reopen the border crossings if the Taliban took measures against the militant groups operating from Afghanistan.

Relations between Pakistan and the Taliban deteriorated as Pakistani authorities accused the Taliban of harboring the militant group, Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan, or TTP, which has taken responsibility for attacks inside Pakistan.
The Taliban publicly deny harboring any militant group, but a U.N. report, released in August, said that the Taliban continue to support TTP.
The closure of the border crossings has hurt Pakistani industries, particularly pharmaceuticals, according to government data.

Pakistan's Dawn newspaper, citing Pakistan's Bureau of Statistics, said pharmaceutical exports declined 25.53 percent in the first quarter of 2026-27, which is primarily attributed to the disruption of trade with Afghanistan.
Mohmand said that the Taliban’s government was seeking alternative trade routes, but “Pakistani traders are at a loss.”
“I think the Pakistani traders have lost and continue to lose the 40-million-people market of Afghanistan,” he added.

Azarakhsh Hafizi, an economist and former head of the international relations committee at Afghanistan's Chamber of Commerce and Industries, told VOA that the halt in bilateral trade is “not in the interest of” either Afghanistan or Pakistan.
“Pakistani industries not only reach Afghan markets but also export via Afghanistan to Central Asia,” he added.
Hafizi said that Afghanistan’s exports via Pakistan were valued at around $1 billion and Pakistan was one of the largest destinations for Afghan products in 2024, with exports totaling $659 million.
Momand said that he “hopes the tensions between the two neighboring countries end soon.”

items.title: Adrian Smith + Gordon Gill Architecture designs "fluid" skyscraper Lilli for Miami waterfront
paragraphs: US studio Adrian Smith + Gordon Gill Architecture has unveiled its latest skyscraper for Miami, designed to display “quiet refinement” on a slender site on the city’s waterfront.

Called Lilli, the residential skyscraper development is the latest in Miami from Adrian Smith + Gordon Gill Architecture (AS+GG). The studio is known for designing some of the world’s tallest buildings, including the world’s upcoming tallest skyscraper, the Jeddah Tower.
At 636 feet tall (193 metres), Lilli is planned for a narrow site in Miami’s Edgewater neighbourhood.
The luxury skyscraper will feature rounded edges and will have terraces on the water-facing side, with larger patios running up the opposite face.
Its design is characterised by rounded edges and large spans of glass interrupted by metallic floor plates.
“Our vision is for Lilli’s interior design to feel inseparable from its architecture,” said AS+GG design partner Juan Betancur.

“The fluidity of the building carries through the interior spaces, while a restrained palette of natural materials allows light, landscape, and views of Biscayne Bay to become part of the experience.”
“The result is a sense of quiet refinement that feels distinctly connected to its waterfront setting.”
The skyscraper will house 117 residences of varying sizes, spread across its 53 storeys, as well as amenities including lounges, pools and spas.
The ground floor will have a lobby for residents with large metallic columns and minimalist detailing.
At the top of the skyscraper, a pool will sit on the edge of a terrace underneath a bulkhead with the same reflective metal treatment seen elsewhere in the exterior.
Lilli is the latest in a series of residential skyscrapers being designed by the studio, which recently completed a “yacht-inspired” building in the city.
Residential skyscraper development has proceeded at a steady pace in Miami, with Bugatti recently unveiling its first branded skyscraper in the city.

items.title: Mystery over source of Ebola infection in Nigeria fuels concern about spread of virus
paragraphs: Health officials across Africa are racing to determine how Nigeria’s first Ebola patient ⁠in more than a decade ⁠became infected, amid fears ​the outbreak could spread further after reaching a fourth African country.

The Swiss foreign ministry said on Friday the patient in Nigeria, the Ugandan-born wife of a Swiss diplomat based in Abuja, had not travelled to the Democratic Republic of ⁠Congo, where the outbreak was first detected in mid-May before spreading to Uganda, Kenya and now Nigeria. The woman was believed to have contracted Ebola while travelling with her husband in Uganda, the ministry added.

The new information contradicts accounts from Uganda, which previously said the woman had travelled to eastern DR Congo, and will raise concerns about the ability of authorities to contain the outbreak, which is already the most geographically widespread in history.

The Ugandan government reported Ebola cases in May and June before WHO declared it Ebola-free in August. A Ugandan government spokesperson told Reuters on Thursday that Uganda had no ​Ebola cases and that, if ​it did, it would make that information ​public.
The World Health Organization said investigations were continuing to establish the likely source of infection for the Ebola patient in Nigeria.

The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention is investigating whether the patient may have come into contact with an Ebola patient in Kenya, as both travelled from Uganda’s Entebbe airport on 3 October, said Dr Wessam Mankoula, head of emergency preparedness and response at the organisation.

Catherine Smallwood, a WHO Ebola incident manager in DR Congo, told a UN briefing in Geneva via video ‌link on Friday that WHO staff in DR Congo had no information showing the patient in Nigeria had travelled to the country.

Smallwood said a link to the case in Kenya was possible, ​but added that officials would need to compare the timing with when the Nigeria patient’s symptoms began to tell whether the infection more likely happened at the Ugandan airport or elsewhere.

Marion Koopmans, a Dutch virologist and member of the WHO’s Ebola emergency committee, cast doubt on the theory. “I think that is very speculative unless there is evidence of sharing the same ​space in a manner that could explain that,” she said. “Random presence at the same location, a large airport, is not a supported epidemiological link by any standard of what we currently know.”

The Nigerian health minister, Muhammad Ali Pate, said Nigeria’s case remains contained and that contact-tracing was continuing. “We are trying to contain it so it doesn’t go out to the communities. Hopefully, it won’t get to that and we are working hard to ensure that,” Pate said.

Melaku Yirga, vice-president for Africa at Prosper Global (formerly Mercy Corps), said the confirmation of Ebola in Kenya and Nigeria reinforces the need for countries to work closely together to prevent further transmission.
“What matters most now is speed, sharing information across borders without delay and ensuring frontline health workers and local organiaations have the resources to respond quickly,” he said.

Ebola is a highly contagious and often fatal viral disease that affects humans and non-human primates. It spreads through body fluids or contaminated materials and causes organ damage, blood vessel impairment and sometimes severe internal and external bleeding.

The current outbreak is caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus, which has no approved treatment or vaccine. It was first announced on 15 May and has infected more than 9,500 people and killed nearly half of them.

The outbreak is the largest and deadliest in DR Congo’s history and second only ​globally to ​the 2014-16 outbreak in west Africa, which infected ​more than ‌28,600 people ​and ​killed more than 11,000.

items.title: Hammersmith Bridge is a symbol of our dysfunctional times. The money is there, the joined-up thinking isn’t | Simon Jenkins
paragraphs: London’s Hammersmith Bridge is a metaphor for all that is wrong with British government. Closed to motor traffic and inert for seven years, it is a victim of the anarchy that seeps into every tier of public administration. The bridge sits today on a sublime bend in the Thames, guarded by what looks like Checkpoint Charlie in iron curtain Berlin. With Albert Bridge also now closed, 37,000 extra vehicles seeking to cross the river have brought south London close to perpetual gridlock. No one cares.

London may be the richest, smartest, coolest place in Britain. Yet it is run like a high street vape shop. Its buses are ever slower, homeless people are ever more prevalent, waiting times in hospitals ever longer. No one can decide if they want an HS2 terminus or a Heathrow runway. A robotic Whitehall algorithm has just declared, ludicrously, that the borough of Kensington’s “housing target” must be 5,107 homes a year, up from a previous target of 1,381.

The first thing you notice about a city is its traffic. In other cities, it moves. In London, it crawls. Its congestion is officially rated the worst of any capital in the world. Efforts to improve the sclerotic traffic lights have failed. The recent installation of computer-assisted “smart” lights – the much-vaunted road time optimisers – has contrived to cut just 27 seconds off individual bus journeys. A Guardian investigation last month timed a series of trips, and found the average speed for a No 22 bus between between Putney Common and Oxford Circus was under 6mph, or 16% slower than a decade ago.

The principal reason for this appears to be London’s epidemic of roadworks. In most cities such infrastructure is subject to intense regulation and coordination. The reason is obvious: that the disruption can restrict movement and thus impose costs on third parties. There is no regulation worthy of the word in London.

In 2017 the Economist published what became a notorious map showing roadworks in Paris and London. The first had a scatter of sparse red dots; London’s map was a sea of blood. Estimates are that vehicles in London navigate 1,300 roadworks every day, with the total for 2024 at 490,893. There is no evidence of the slightest coordination of hold-ups.

The chief reason is that a quarter century of privatising utilities has given water and cabling companies virtually unlimited freedom to dig where and when they please. Streets in the most afflicted inner boroughs now awake each morning to what looks like an overnight blitz. A mass of road closures and detour signs have turned the London street into what looks like a permanent construction site. Seeing any work being done is rare and there is no sense of anyone being in charge.

Hammersmith Bridge is a tough case. It legally belongs to the local Hammersmith and Fulham council – not Richmond on the south bank – but it has decided it “cannot absorb” the cost of restoring its decaying structure, put at £300m. It merely allows pedestrians and cyclists to cross. Yet it claims to have spent £54m on it over seven years. Merely doing next to nothing costs millions of pounds a year.

The bridge’s predicament is serious. Built by Sir Joseph Bazalgette in 1887, it was one of the world’s first iron suspension bridges – and the iron’s life has expired. Repair could only be temporary, or over the longer term astronomical. As architecture it is a noble if rather ungainly structure, compared with graceful Albert Bridge downstream. A growing body of opinion is that it would be common sense to replace it.

Designing a new bridge should be a competitive challenge. It needs to respect the buildings and natural environment of Barnes and Hammersmith on either bank. A work of style and dignity should have nothing to do with the concrete gashes of the 20th century’s London and Waterloo bridges. It needs to be very special.

As for who should take the lead, in any other city a river crossing would be the responsibility of its mayor. British mayors spend their time trying for headlines or Downing Street. London’s Sadiq Khan appears to have no view on Hammersmith Bridge, any more than he does on the capital’s roadworks, building conservation or policy on tall buildings.

As for paying for a new bridge, there is an answer. The so-called City Bridge Foundation was formed in the middle ages to maintain London bridges and later City crossings. Its charter limits its responsibility to just five crossings: Tower, London, Southwark, Millennium, and Blackfriars bridges. However, its trustee, the City of London Corporation, could amend the charter so that it could reinvest in infrastructure. It is one of London’s richest charities – with assets in the order of £1.5bn. The foundation currently spends lavishly on causes that have nothing to do with bridges.

This needs changing. The City of London is an out-of-date relic of medieval local government. The legacy of London’s past wealth should be at the disposal of the whole metropolis. The money is there. A new Hammersmith Bridge should rise across the Thames’s most exquisite western reaches, and soon.

items.title: 'It's been relentless': IT workers scramble to fix PHP flaw described as worst crisis in years
paragraphs: Microsoft boss Satya Nadella says he has not seen anything like the PHP emergency "in a long, long time".

Referencing the ongoing global efforts to fix the critical cyber-security flaw in millions of websites, he told a conference "it was a long day and a long night, I know, for all the IT and security folks".

Other IT and cyber experts have told the BBC about their struggles in the last 48 hours, whose stories give us an insight into what it is like at the coalface of a major cyber emergency. But also highlight how misinformation and panic has made things a lot worse.
"It's been relentless," says UK-based system administrator Adam Mudd.
He said he had never had so many messages from people who were worried about their websites.
"The biggest challenge has been juggling clients who want their sites taken offline as a precaution, while trying to coordinate updates and fixes across countless different setups," he said.
"Sometimes it takes me longer to take a website down than to fix the PHP problem."
PHP is a very popular programming language which powers millions of websites.

But two critical flaws were found with the system that led to the emergency response, with national cyber-security authorities urging IT teams to download a security fix urgently or take websites and servers offline.
Mudd says since then he has been under enormous pressure and has lost a huge amount of sleep - working early and not finishing until 22:30 BST to secure his customers' systems.
In Mauritius, IT administrator Loganaden Velvindron said he too was flat out since his team realised just how much software relies on PHP.
"Many versions of php running are completely end-of-life, so we are having to rebuilding web apps and change code in some cases," he said.
He said part of the problem was the announcement about the security vulnerabilities in PHP came as a surprise, without much time to prepare for action.
Jon Jones, Technical director for a digital advertising company, was also spurred into action by the alerts.
"Seeing the warning drop was definitely eye-opening and a new experience we've not dealt with before," he said.
"But, in a way, it was exciting feeling like a bit of a Hollywood action scene."
The PHP Foundation, which manages the programming language, released its software fix and there was a scramble for people to download it.
Jones said it felt like "the race was on" when the patch launched at 15:00 BST on Wednesday.
"It was also a bit nerve-racking as anyone who has applied software updates before would know, there's always a chance than an update can cause other issues," he said.
The rush came as someone had leaked details of the PHP flaw early - and it was heavily rumoured that cyber-criminals were already trying to carry out attacks.
But cyber experts are also now questioning whether or not those rumours were real.
"We were flooded with rubbish intel about hackers being out there actively with working Proof of Concept (PoC) methods," said UK cyber expert Daniel Card.
He said he also been flat out since Tuesday when the rumours of PHP hacks began circulating.
"This isn't the first time we've had a situation like this but it feels like it's been on another dimension," he said.
He agreed that on paper the PHP vulnerabilities were very serious and should be taken seriously, but he and many others are frustrated with the misinformation about hackers being on the loose.
As well as the alerts from government agencies - even the Prime Minister of Japan - cyber-security companies also made errors which didn't help.
One major firm in this space issued warnings saying hackers had a working PoC - only to have to retract it.
In spite of warnings from Cloudflare and AWS that "millions of hacking attempts" had been made every hour, there is also no evidence of large scale data breaches or cyber-attacks.
It is true that hackers have been seen to use AI to attempt to build attack methods, but none of them seem to be working at scale at the moment - something that may well change soon.
AI was also used to find the PHP flaws which had been hidden from human researchers for decades.
The IT workers we spoke to all agreed that these kinds of serious flaws were going to be uncovered more frequently now that AI tools had become so good at hacking.
But some in the industry are concerned about how people were told about the critical vulnerabilities in PHP, as they fear improvements in AI will throw up more incidents like it.

"We're going to find scary vulnerabilities with the amazing capabilities that OpenAI and Anthropic are bringing online, but we need to calibrate the messaging," posted Mark Maunder, founder of Wordfence - a Wordpress security tool.
He said there was a risk of "alert fatigue" which could be a big problem if a fully exploitable and serious vulnerability arose.

items.title: Lowry kicks off, pop goes kinky and the wild man of Florence is tamed – the week in art
paragraphs: LS Lowry The strangest and perhaps most truthful painter of modern Britain gets a thorough looking at. MK Gallery, Milton Keynes, 24 October to 28 February
Allen Jones Kinky pop art from the diehard naughty boy of 1960s British painting – the Hockney of Soho? Gazelli Art House, London, until 18 December
Multiplied Wonders Woodcuts by Jacopo de’ Barbari, Albrecht Dürer and more reveal the power of the reproduced image in the Renaissance. British Museum, London, until 21 March

Beyond Bayeux Yinka Shonibare, Hurvin Anderson and others design tapestries in collaboration with Edinburgh’s Dovecot Studios, in a somewhat opportunistically titled show. Guildhall Art Gallery, London, until 21 March
Anne Redpath Landscapes on Skye with white houses and bright green fields tenderly depicted in gouache and watercolour. National, Edinburgh, until 6 December

Sheep dung, snails and mouse brains are all beautiful … if you look closely enough. This artwork could be a newly discovered planet or an abstract piece by Stanley Donwood for Radiohead’s A Moon Shaped Pool, but the truth is tinier: this is the tip of a ballpoint pen, a winning entry from the Nikon Small World photography competition.
Bowie, bodybuilders and a blubbering Frenchman have changed the way we see masculinity
Light and Magic: The Birth of Art Photography at Tate Modern will stop you in your tracks
Photos of bustling dancefloors show a changing America through the decades
Frieze art fair is open, and we’ve identified 10 things worth seeing
Bondi beach in Sydney is alive with sculpture

Artist Tony Albert is reappropriating racist artefacts of Aboriginalia for his show Not a Souvenir in Sydney
A new book documents the key players in Cameroon’s vast visual art history
A Paris exhibition explores Ghana before and after it was ripped to shreds by colonialism
St Jerome and the Lion: Predella Panel by Fra Filippo Lippi and Workshop, 1455-60

Filippo Lippi was the wild man of early 15th-century Florentine art, if the stories told about him in the Renaissance are anything to go by. It was even said his patron Cosimo de’ Medici had to lock him in the Medici palace to stop his debauchery. There is a core of fact behind the tales, as Filippo – a friar – is known from legal records to have had children with an escaped nun, Lucrezia Buti. Their son Filippino also became an artist. But whatever his life was like, there’s no lack of piety in this painting of the early Christian Jerome, a real historical figure who translated the Bible into Latin. The lion tamely lets the holy man pull a thorn from its paw, in an intricately painted mountainous landscape with a pink church. Jerome concentrates on his work, as you would if you were de-thorning a dangerous big cat. This is just a small panel from the base of an altarpiece but it packs in the emotion and humanity that makes Lippi a great artist, in spite of, or because of, his sins.
